atp hydrolysis (δg°′ ≈ 30.5 kj mol 1) is often said to release energy from a 'high energy bond'. which statement about the terminal p o p bond is correct? breaking it costs energy; the release comes from forming more stable products breaking it releases energy because the bond is unusually weak it is a phosphoester, the most stable kind of phosphorus bond it releases energy because it forms a new p p bond in adp

acetylating aniline gives acetanilide, c6h5nhcoch3. how does the basicity of its nitrogen compare with that of aniline? much less basic, since the lone pair is also shared with c=o much more basic, since the acetyl group donates electrons about the same, since the n still has a lone pair more basic, since the n now has only one h attached

phosphorus can bond to five atoms (as in pcl5), but nitrogen in the same group never does. what is the best explanation? phosphorus is larger and can hold more than eight valence electrons phosphorus is more electronegative than nitrogen, so it bonds more nitrogen has no lone pair left over to use in bonding phosphorus has more valence electrons than nitrogen does

n ethyl n methylpropan 1 amine has three different groups and a lone pair on nitrogen, yet it can't be separated into stable enantiomers. why? the nitrogen rapidly inverts, interconverting the two enantiomers a lone pair cannot count as one of four different groups the molecule has an internal mirror plane passing through n amines are planar, so their n cannot be a stereocenter
which compound is the strongest base? 4 methylaniline 4 nitroaniline 4 chloroaniline aniline

arginine's guanidino side chain has a conjugate acid pk a near 12.5, far above that of a typical alkylamine (about 10.6). why is the guanidino group so basic? its protonated form spreads the + charge over three nitrogens it has three lone pairs, so it can accept three protons its nitrogens are all sp3, so their lone pairs are more available its c=n bond breaks easily, releasing ammonia as a base

lidocaine (shown; conjugate acid pk a ≈ 7.9) must cross a nerve cell membrane in its neutral form to work. why is it less effective when injected into infected, acidic tissue (ph ≈ 6.9)? more of it is protonated, so less crosses the membrane acid hydrolyzes its amide bond within seconds more of it is neutral, so it diffuses away too fast its amine is oxidized to a nitro group at low ph

ethylamine, ch3ch2nh2 (bp 17 °c), boils far lower than ethanol, ch3ch2oh (bp 78 °c), although their molar masses are nearly equal and both form hydrogen bonds. why? n h···n hydrogen bonds are weaker, since n is less electronegative than o ethylamine has no n h bond, so it can't donate a hydrogen bond ethylamine has no lone pair, so it can't accept a hydrogen bond ethylamine is ionic, so its particles don't attract each other

how is ch3conhch3 (n methylacetamide) classified? a secondary amide a primary amide a tertiary amide a secondary amine

acetonitrile, ch3c≡n, has a lone pair on nitrogen but is an extremely weak base (conjugate acid pk a ≈ 10). why? the lone pair is in an sp orbital, held close to the nucleus the lone pair is delocalized around an aromatic ring the nitrogen has a positive formal charge in the nitrile the lone pair is shared with a neighboring c=o group

in the strecker synthesis, an aldehyde reacts with nh3 and hcn. what intermediate is formed before the final acid hydrolysis step? an α aminonitrile an α hydroxy ketone an α amino aldehyde an α keto acid

the c n bond in an amide (about 1.33 a) is noticeably shorter than the c n bond in an amine (about 1.47 a). why? resonance gives the amide c n bond partial double bond character the amide nitrogen is sp3, and sp3 orbitals form shorter bonds the amide nitrogen carries a full negative charge that pulls on carbon hydrogen bonding between amide molecules squeezes the c n bond

amines are generally better nucleophiles than alcohols of similar size. what is the main reason? less electronegative n holds its lone pair less tightly nitrogen has more lone pairs available than oxygen does amines are always negatively charged in organic solvents nitrogen forms stronger bonds to carbon than oxygen does

when ammonia is alkylated with an alkyl halide, the reaction gives a messy mixture of primary, secondary and tertiary amines. why? each alkylated amine is at least as nucleophilic as the amine it came from alkyl halides react with ammonia only by the sn1 mechanism the primary amine product is too weakly basic to be isolated ammonia is a much better nucleophile than any of the alkylamines

fish smells 'fishy' largely because of volatile trimethylamine. why does squeezing lemon juice on the fish reduce the odor? citric acid protonates it to a nonvolatile ammonium salt citric acid oxidizes the amine into an odorless amide lemon oils dissolve the amine and carry it into the air citric acid reduces the amine into an odorless alkane

strong acids protonate amides on the carbonyl oxygen rather than on nitrogen. why? o protonation keeps the resonance, spreading + over o, c and n oxygen is less electronegative than nitrogen, so it is more basic nitrogen in an amide has no lone pair left to share at all protonating oxygen breaks the c n bond, giving a stable product

a kinase phosphorylates a serine side chain ( ch2oh → ch2opo3h2, whose second pk a is about 6). at ph 7.4, how does this change the charge at that site? from 0 to about 2 from 0 to about 1 from 0 to about +1 from 1 to about 3

in terpene biosynthesis, dimethylallyl diphosphate, (ch3)2c=chch2 opp, loses its diphosphate group to form an allylic carbocation. why is diphosphate such a good leaving group here? as an anion it is a weak base, stabilized by resonance and mg2+ it is a strong base, so it pulls away from carbon with great force it is neutral when it leaves, so no charge has to be stabilized it forms a c=o bond as it leaves, releasing a great deal of energy

phthalimide (shown) has an n h with pk a ≈ 8.3, far more acidic than an amine n h (pk a ≈ 35). why? its conjugate base spreads the negative charge onto two c=o oxygens its nitrogen is sp3, holding the lone pair far from the nucleus its n h bond is weaker because it is part of an aromatic ring its conjugate base is stabilized by hydrogen bonds to benzene

why is the o h stretching band of an alcohol in a concentrated sample broad rather than sharp? hydrogen bonding gives a range of o h bond strengths the o h bond breaks and re forms during each scan oxygen's isotopes absorb at slightly different wavenumbers the o h bond absorbs several photons at the same time

name: Separations & purification
t: a mixture of benzoic acid and naphthalene in diethyl ether is shaken with aqueous nahco3. where does the benzoic acid end up? ether layer, as benzoic acid aqueous layer, as sodium benzoate ether layer, as sodium benzoate it precipitates at the interface

three compounds are run on a silica gel tlc plate with a nonpolar solvent. which travels farthest (highest rf)? the most polar compound the least polar compound the compound with the highest molar mass all have the same rf
simple distillation separates liquids based on differences in: boiling point color molar mass only solubility in water

recrystallization purifies a solid by: dissolving it in hot solvent and letting pure crystals form on cooling dissolving it in cold solvent and letting pure crystals form on heating melting it and collecting the pure liquid that distills over dissolving it in solvent and then evaporating it quickly to dryness

in thin layer chromatography, rf is: distance traveled by compound ÷ distance traveled by solvent distance traveled by solvent ÷ distance traveled by compound distance traveled by compound ÷ total length of the plate time for the compound to travel ÷ time for the solvent
in liquid liquid extraction, two layers form because the solvents: don't mix (are immiscible) have the same density react with each other are both water

when should fractional distillation be used instead of simple distillation? when boiling points differ by less than about 25 °c when boiling points differ by more than 100 °c when one compound is a solid when neither compound boils

vacuum distillation is useful for compounds that: have very high boiling points or decompose when heated have very low boiling points and evaporate at room temperature have nearly identical boiling points needing a long column are ionic salts that dissolve readily in water
in normal phase column chromatography (silica, nonpolar solvent), which compound elutes first? the least polar compound the most polar compound the largest compound the most acidic compound
in reverse phase hplc (nonpolar stationary phase, polar solvent), which compound elutes first? the most polar compound the least polar compound the heaviest compound the most volatile compound

gas chromatography separates compounds mainly by: volatility and interaction with the stationary phase charge and migration rate in an electric field molecular size, with the largest eluting first solubility in a polar liquid mobile phase
a good recrystallization solvent dissolves the compound: well when hot and poorly when cold well at all temperatures poorly at all temperatures only when frozen

an organic amine in an ether layer is shaken with aqueous hcl. where does the amine go? into the aqueous layer, as an ammonium salt it stays in the ether it evaporates it forms a solid at the interface
a tlc spot moves 3.0 cm while the solvent front moves 6.0 cm. what is its rf? 0.50 2.0 3.0 0.33
in a tlc experiment on silica, compound x has rf 0.8 and compound y has rf 0.2. which is more polar? y x they're equally polar rf doesn't relate to polarity
a mixture contains benzoic acid, aniline and naphthalene in ether. which aqueous wash removes aniline? dilute hcl dilute naoh pure water saturated nacl

a mixture of benzoic acid, aniline and naphthalene is dissolved in ether. which aqueous wash removes the benzoic acid? dilute naoh (or nahco3) dilute hcl (or h2so4) saturated nacl (brine) pure water (neutral ph)
a mixture of benzoic acid, aniline and naphthalene in ether is washed with dilute hcl and then dilute naoh. which compound stays in the ether layer? naphthalene benzoic acid aniline none
a pure solid's melting point compared with an impure sample is: higher and sharper lower and broader the same unmeasurable

a compound decomposes at 250 °c but boils at 280 °c at 1 atm. how could it be purified by distillation? use vacuum distillation to lower its boiling point use simple distillation at 1 atm use fractional distillation at 1 atm it can't be distilled
size exclusion chromatography separates proteins by size. which elutes first? the largest molecules the smallest molecules the most charged molecules the most hydrophobic molecules

why is brine (saturated nacl) often used as a final wash in an extraction? it pulls dissolved water out of the organic layer it dissolves the organic product it neutralizes acids it raises the boiling point of ether
a pharmacist must separate a drug's two enantiomers. which method could work? chromatography using a chiral stationary phase simple distillation standard silica tlc recrystallization from water alone

why do forensic labs often use gc ms to identify drugs in blood samples? gc separates the components, and ms identifies each by its mass pattern ms separates the components, and gc identifies each by its mass gc identifies compounds by ir bands, and ms confirms their purity gc ms separates proteins by size and identifies them by charge

a drug synthesis gives the product and an unreacted starting carboxylic acid. which simple step removes the acid? wash the organic layer with aqueous nahco3 wash the organic layer with dilute aqueous hcl wash the organic layer with saturated brine dry the organic layer over anhydrous mgso4
in the silica tlc plate shown (solvent front at 6.0 cm), what is the rf of compound b? 0.25 0.75 1.5 4.0

based on the tlc plate (silica, nonpolar solvent), which statement is correct? compound b is more polar than compound a compound a is more polar than compound b the mixture contains only compound a the two compounds have equal rf values

after an extraction, anhydrous mgso4 is swirled into the separated organic layer. what is its purpose? to absorb leftover traces of water to neutralize any remaining acid to raise the solvent's boiling point to make the two layers separate

why are boiling chips added to a flask before a distillation? to promote smooth boiling and prevent bumping to catalyze evaporation of the lower boiling liquid to absorb impurities from the boiling liquid to lower the boiling point of the mixture
in standard (normal phase) tlc, what is the stationary phase usually made of? silica gel, a polar solid a nonpolar hydrocarbon layer the mobile solvent mixture filter paper soaked in hexane

dichloromethane (density 1.33 g ml 1) and water are shaken in a separatory funnel. where is the organic layer? on the bottom, since it is denser than water on top, since organic solvents always float on top, since it is less polar than water mixed in, since dichloromethane is miscible

why does extracting with three 10 ml portions of solvent remove more solute than one 30 ml extraction? each fresh portion removes a fixed fraction of what remains smaller volumes of solvent have a larger partition coefficient three portions add up to more total solvent than 30 ml shaking three times heats the mixture and raises solubility

on a silica tlc plate developed in hexane, all the spots stay near the baseline. which change should move them farther up the plate? add ethyl acetate to make the eluent more polar use pure pentane to make the eluent less polar use a longer plate with the same hexane spot a larger amount of the sample

a developed tlc plate is viewed under a 254 nm uv lamp, and dark spots appear. which compounds are most easily seen this way? aromatic or conjugated compounds saturated hydrocarbons such as hexane only compounds that are colored only compounds containing nitrogen

during recrystallization, why should a hot saturated solution be cooled slowly instead of being plunged straight into ice? slow growth forms purer crystals that exclude impurities fast cooling lets the compound decompose into side products slow cooling raises the amount that can stay dissolved ice changes the melting point of the compound

why is a hot recrystallization solution sometimes filtered (hot filtration) before it is cooled? to remove insoluble impurities while the product stays dissolved to remove soluble impurities before they crystallize to collect the purified product crystals as quickly as possible to cool the solution faster through the filter paper

a mixture of pentane, hexane and heptane is analyzed by gc on a nonpolar column. in which order do they elute? pentane, then hexane, then heptane heptane, then hexane, then pentane hexane, then pentane, then heptane all three at the same retention time
which method is best for separating pentane (bp 36 °c) from toluene (bp 111 °c)? simple distillation recrystallization from water extraction with aqueous hcl size exclusion chromatography
on a tlc plate, the solvent front traveled 7.5 cm from the baseline. a compound has r f = 0.40. how far did its spot travel from the baseline? 3.0 cm 4.5 cm 18.8 cm 7.1 cm

a compound's solubility is 5.0 g per 100 ml of a solvent at its boiling point and 0.50 g per 100 ml at 0 °c. a student dissolves 5.0 g in 100 ml of the hot solvent and cools it to 0 °c. what is the maximum mass of crystals that can be recovered? 4.5 g 5.0 g 0.50 g 2.5 g

in reverse phase hplc (c18 column, water acetonitrile mobile phase), what happens to a nonpolar drug's retention time when the acetonitrile fraction is increased? it decreases, because the eluent is now less polar it increases, because the eluent is now more polar it decreases, because the eluent is now more polar it does not change, since only the column matters

a mixture of biphenyl, benzaldehyde and benzoic acid is run on a silica tlc plate with 4 : 1 hexane : ethyl acetate. what is the order of r f values, highest to lowest? biphenyl > benzaldehyde > benzoic acid benzoic acid > benzaldehyde > biphenyl benzaldehyde > biphenyl > benzoic acid biphenyl > benzoic acid > benzaldehyde

a solute has a partition coefficient k = [organic] ÷ [aqueous] = 4. a 100 ml aqueous solution containing 1.0 g of the solute is extracted once with 100 ml of ether. how much solute moves into the ether? 0.80 g 0.25 g 0.75 g 0.20 g

a solute has a partition coefficient k = [organic] ÷ [aqueous] = 4. a 100 ml aqueous solution containing 1.0 g of the solute is extracted twice, each time with 50 ml of fresh ether. about how much solute is extracted in total? 0.89 g 0.80 g 0.67 g 0.94 g

a mixture of benzoic acid (pk a 4.2) and 4 methylphenol (pk a 10.3) in ether is shaken with aqueous nahco3 (pk a of h2co3 ≈ 6.4). what happens? only benzoic acid moves into the aqueous layer only 4 methylphenol moves into the aqueous layer both move into the aqueous layer as anions neither moves; nahco3 is too weak a base for either

ethanol (bp 78 °c) and water (bp 100 °c) are fractionally distilled, yet the distillate never goes above about 95% ethanol. why? they form an azeotrope that boils with a fixed composition ethanol decomposes before it can be fully separated the column is too short; a longer one would give 100% water and ethanol have nearly identical boiling points

an unknown white solid melts at 121 122 °c, matching benzoic acid (mp 122 °c). a 1 : 1 mixture of the unknown with pure benzoic acid also melts sharply at 121 122 °c. what can be concluded? the unknown is very likely benzoic acid the unknown is a different compound with the same mp the mixture is impure, so the unknown is impure mixed melting points can't identify a compound

a carboxylic acid streaks badly on silica tlc. adding about 1% acetic acid to the eluent gives a tight spot. why? it keeps the compound fully protonated, so it moves as one form it converts the compound into a less polar ester on the plate it deprotonates the compound so it binds the silica less it makes the silica nonpolar, so every compound moves faster

a toxicology lab must extract amphetamine (conjugate acid pk a ≈ 9.9) from a urine sample (ph 6) into an organic solvent before gc ms. what should the lab do first? raise the urine ph to about 12 so the drug is neutral lower the urine ph to about 2 so the drug is charged keep the ph at 6, since the drug is already neutral add nacl only, since ph does not affect amines

to isolate caffeine (shown) from tea, tea leaves are boiled in water containing na2co3, and the cooled extract is shaken with dichloromethane. tannins (acidic phenolic compounds) are also extracted from the leaves. why is na2co3 added? it turns the tannins into anions that stay in the water layer it protonates caffeine so it dissolves in dichloromethane it reacts with caffeine to form an insoluble salt it raises the density of water so the layers switch places

caffeine can be purified by heating it under vacuum so that it passes directly from solid to gas and then collecting it on a cold surface. what is this technique called? sublimation distillation recrystallization evaporation

after an extraction, a chemist uses a rotary evaporator on the organic layer. what does this instrument do? removes volatile solvent under reduced pressure separates the product from impurities by polarity dries the solution by absorbing dissolved water measures the product's boiling point accurately
in gas chromatography (gc), what is the mobile phase? an inert carrier gas such as helium a polar liquid such as water a thin coating on the column wall the vaporized sample mixture itself

why does a fractional distillation column, packed with glass beads or rings, separate liquids better than simple distillation? it allows many vaporization condensation cycles it raises the boiling point of the lower boiling liquid it absorbs the higher boiling liquid permanently it cools the vapor so that no condensation can occur

an ether solution containing a carboxylic acid is shaken with aqueous nahco3 in a separatory funnel. why must the funnel be vented often? co2 gas forms as the acid reacts, building up pressure the ether layer freezes and expands as it is shaken nahco3 releases hydrogen gas when it touches ether venting lets the aqueous layer drain off more quickly

during a distillation, where should the thermometer bulb be placed to measure the boiling point of the distilling liquid accurately? just below the side arm that leads to the condenser deep in the boiling liquid at the bottom of the flask at the far end of the condenser, near the outlet above the flask, well over the top of the side arm

a solid dissolves well in hot ethanol but also fairly well in cold ethanol, and it is insoluble in water. how can a mixed solvent recrystallization be done? dissolve in minimal hot ethanol, add hot water until cloudy, then cool dissolve in cold water, add hot ethanol until clear, then heat dissolve in hot water, add ice cold ethanol, then filter right away dissolve in hot ethanol, then evaporate all of the ethanol away

why can't ethanol be used as the organic solvent to extract a compound from an aqueous solution? ethanol is miscible with water, so no separate layer forms ethanol is denser than water, so the layers are hard to see ethanol is too nonpolar to dissolve organic compounds ethanol reacts with water to form an insoluble product

a student uses twice the minimum amount of hot solvent needed to dissolve a crude solid before cooling. compared with using the minimum, what is the most likely result? lower recovery of crystals, with no gain in purity higher recovery and noticeably purer crystals higher recovery, but crystals that are less pure exactly the same recovery and purity as before

on a silica tlc plate, cyclohexanol cannot be seen under a 254 nm uv lamp. which method can reveal its spot? placing the plate in an iodine chamber or kmno4 stain viewing the plate under a brighter 254 nm uv lamp running the plate again in a more polar eluent heating the plate until all of the solvent boils

a student reduces a ketone (lane sm) to an alcohol and runs a silica tlc plate of the starting material and the reaction mixture (lane rxn), shown. what does the plate indicate? the ketone is used up, and a more polar product (r f 0.25) formed the ketone is used up, and a less polar product (r f 0.60) formed no reaction occurred, since the rxn lane shows only one spot the product is less polar than the ketone, since it moved less

after an extraction, benzoic acid is in an aqueous layer as sodium benzoate. how can the benzoic acid be recovered as a solid? add hcl until the solution is acidic, then filter off the precipitate add naoh until the solution is basic, then filter off the precipitate add anhydrous mgso4 to the aqueous layer, then filter off the solid add more ether and shake, then collect the solid from the funnel

four neutral compounds with the log p values shown (higher = more nonpolar) are analyzed by reverse phase hplc (c18 column, water acetonitrile eluent). in which order do they elute? z, then x, then y, then w w, then y, then x, then z x, then z, then w, then y y, then w, then z, then x
a gc analysis of a three component mixture gives the peak areas in the table. assuming the detector responds equally to each component, what percentage of the mixture is component b? 60% 40% 33% 50%

a 100 ml mixture of hexane (bp 69 °c) and toluene (bp 111 °c) is fractionally distilled. the graph shows the vapor temperature versus the total volume collected. about what percentage of the mixture was hexane? about 40% about 60% about 70% about 20%

a mixture is loaded onto a silica column and eluted with hexane. a nonpolar hydrocarbon comes off, but a polar alcohol stays near the top. what should be done to elute the alcohol? gradually switch to a more polar eluent, such as ethyl acetate switch to a less polar eluent, such as pure pentane keep using hexane, but run it through more slowly heat the column so that the alcohol boils out of it
the table shows a compound's solubility in four solvents, cold and at the boiling point. which solvent is best for recrystallizing it? toluene ethanol water hexane
a student recrystallizes 4.0 g of crude product and recovers 3.2 g of crystals with a sharper, higher melting point. what is the percent recovery? 80% 75% 125% 20%

steam distillation lets oils such as limonene (bp 176 °c) distill along with water at just under 100 °c. why does the mixture boil below the boiling point of either pure liquid? immiscible liquids each add their full vapor pressure to the total water lowers limonene's boiling point by hydrogen bonding to it steam breaks limonene down into smaller, more volatile pieces the mixture forms a single solution that obeys raoult's law

a solute has a partition coefficient k = [organic] ÷ [aqueous] = 1. it is extracted from water with portions of organic solvent equal in volume to the water. what is the minimum number of extractions needed to remove more than 90% of it? 4 2 3 10

an ideal liquid mixture is 50 mol% a (pure vapor pressure 600 torr) and 50 mol% b (pure vapor pressure 200 torr). its vapor is condensed, and the condensate is vaporized again, as on two ideal plates of a fractional column. what is the mole fraction of a in the second vapor? 0.90 0.75 0.56 0.50

an unknown and a known standard, spotted side by side on the same silica plate, give the same r f (0.40) in 3 : 1 hexane : ethyl acetate. on a second plate in 9 : 1 dichloromethane : methanol, again side by side, their r f values are 0.55 and 0.30. what can be concluded? they are different compounds they are the same compound the second solvent was contaminated the first solvent result alone proves identity

propan 1 ol (bp 97 °c) and heptane (bp 98 °c) are injected onto a gc column with a polar stationary phase. which elutes later, and why? propan 1 ol, since it hydrogen bonds to the polar stationary phase heptane, since its higher boiling point keeps it on the column longer heptane, since nonpolar compounds always stick to gc columns best both together, since gc separates only by differences in boiling point

blood alcohol is measured by headspace gc. each sample is mixed with a fixed amount of propan 1 ol before analysis, and the ethanol peak area is divided by the propan 1 ol peak area. why is propan 1 ol added? it is an internal standard that corrects for injection variations it reacts with ethanol to form a product that is easier to detect it raises the boiling point of ethanol so it separates better it removes proteins from the blood so they don't foul the column

a lab isolates a nonpolar drug from urine using a c18 (nonpolar) solid phase extraction cartridge: urine is passed through, the cartridge is rinsed with water, and then methanol is passed through and collected. where is the drug at the end? in the methanol, which pulls the drug off the nonpolar c18 in the water rinse, which washes the drug off the c18 phase still bound to the cartridge, since methanol is too polar in the urine that first passed through the cartridge

name: Motion & forces
t: a 2.0 kg medicine bag falls from rest off a 5.0 m ledge. ignoring air resistance, how fast is it moving just before it lands? (g = 10 m s 2) 5 m s 1 10 m s 1 50 m s 1 100 m s 1

a patient's forearm holds a 10 n weight 0.30 m from the elbow joint. the biceps attaches 0.030 m from the elbow and pulls straight up. what biceps force keeps the forearm in rotational equilibrium? (ignore the forearm's own weight.) 1 n 10 n 100 n 300 n
an object starts from rest and accelerates at 2.0 m/s2 for 5.0 s. what is its final speed? 0.40 m s 1 10 m s 1 2.5 m s 1 25 m s 1
which quantity is a vector? velocity speed mass temperature

newton's first law states that an object: keeps its velocity unless a net force acts on it needs a constant force to keep moving at constant speed accelerates in proportion to the net force on it exerts an equal, opposite force on anything it pushes

newton's third law says that when you push on a wall, the wall: pushes back on you with an equal and opposite force pushes back with a smaller force, since it doesn't move pushes back with an equal force in the same direction pushes back on you only if it starts to move away
what is the si unit of force? newton (kg·m s 2) joule watt pascal
a ball is thrown straight up. at its highest point, its acceleration is: 9.8 m s 2 downward zero 9.8 m s 2 upward it depends on the throw speed
a projectile is launched horizontally. ignoring air resistance, its horizontal velocity: stays constant increases decreases becomes zero at the peak
static friction compared with kinetic friction for the same surfaces is usually: larger (μs > μk) smaller equal zero
an object moves in a circle at constant speed. which statement is true? it is accelerating toward the center it isn't accelerating its velocity is constant the net force points outward

in which situation is a box in translational equilibrium? it slides at constant velocity across a floor it speeds up steadily as it slides down a ramp it is momentarily at rest at the top of a toss it moves at constant speed around a circular path
a car accelerates from 0 to 20 m s 1 in 4.0 s. what is its average acceleration? 5.0 m s 2 80 m s 2 0.20 m s 2 20 m s 2
a 1000 kg car brakes with a net force of 5000 n. what is its deceleration? 5.0 m s 2 0.20 m s 2 5000 m s 2 50 m s 2
an object falls from rest for 3.0 s (g = 10 m s 2). how far does it fall? 45 m 30 m 90 m 15 m
a 60 kg person stands in an elevator accelerating upward at 2.0 m s 2. what does a scale read? (g = 10 m s 2) 720 n 600 n 480 n 120 n
a 10 kg box on a frictionless 30° incline. what is the component of gravity along the incline? (g = 10 m s 2) 50 n 87 n 100 n 10 n
a ball is kicked at 20 m s 1 at 30° above the horizontal. what is the initial vertical velocity? 10 m s 1 17 m s 1 20 m s 1 5 m s 1
a ball is launched with an initial vertical velocity of 10 m s 1 (g = 10 m s 2). how long until it reaches its peak? 1.0 s 2.0 s 0.5 s 10 s
a 2.0 kg mass swings in a horizontal circle of radius 0.50 m at 3.0 m s 1. what is the centripetal force? 36 n 12 n 6.0 n 18 n
a seesaw: a 30 kg child sits 2.0 m from the pivot. where must a 40 kg child sit on the other side to balance? 1.5 m 2.7 m 2.0 m 1.0 m
two blocks (2 kg and 3 kg) are pushed together on a frictionless floor by a 10 n force on the 2 kg block. what force does the 2 kg block exert on the 3 kg block? 6 n 4 n 10 n 5 n
a patient's arm is in traction: a 5.0 kg mass hangs over a pulley pulling horizontally on the arm. what tension does the cable apply? (g = 10 m s 2) 50 n 5.0 n 25 n 100 n

why do crash airbags reduce injury? they lengthen stopping time, so the same momentum change needs less force they reduce the person's total change in momentum during the crash they shorten the stopping time, which lowers the impulse delivered they convert the person's momentum into heat inside the bag

a runner's foot pushes backward on the ground. what actually pushes the runner forward? static friction from the ground, acting forward on the foot the runner's leg muscles, acting directly on the body kinetic friction from the ground, acting backward on the foot the normal force from the ground, acting forward on the foot
the velocity time graph shows a car's trip. how far does it travel in 14 s? 200 m 280 m 140 m 20 m
using the same graph, what is the car's acceleration during the first 4 s? 5 m s 2 20 m s 2 4 m s 2 80 m s 2
the position time graph shows a walker. what is the walker doing between 2 s and 4 s? standing still moving at constant velocity speeding up moving backward

the free body diagram shows a box at rest on a rough incline. which force keeps it from sliding down? static friction (f), up the incline the normal force (n) acting up the incline gravity (mg) acting into the incline kinetic friction acting down the incline
a runner completes exactly one lap of a 400 m oval track and stops at the starting line. what is the runner's displacement? 0 m 400 m 200 m 800 m

an astronaut travels from earth to the moon, where gravity is about one sixth as strong. how do her mass and weight change? mass stays the same; weight drops mass drops; weight stays the same both mass and weight drop to 1/6 both mass and weight stay the same
on a velocity time graph, what does the slope of the line represent? acceleration displacement position jerk (rate of change of acceleration)

a bowling ball and a tennis ball are dropped together from the same height in a vacuum. which lands first? they land at the same time the bowling ball lands first the tennis ball lands first it depends on the height of the drop

from the same table top, ball x rolls off horizontally at 3 m s 1 while ball y is dropped from rest. ignoring air, which reaches the floor first? both reach the floor at the same time ball x, because it is moving faster ball y, because it falls straight down ball x, because it has more total energy

a car rounds an unbanked curve at constant speed on a dry, level road. which force supplies the centripetal force? static friction between tires and road kinetic friction between tires and road the normal force from the road surface the car's weight pulling it inward

a skydiver falls at terminal velocity. which statement about the forces on her is correct? air drag equals her weight, so net force is zero air drag is zero, so gravity is the only force her weight is still larger than the air drag air drag is larger than her weight, so she slows

why is a door much easier to open when you push near the handle rather than near the hinges? a longer lever arm gives more torque per newton the door has less mass near the handle side friction at the hinges is lower near the handle a longer lever arm reduces the door's weight
a car drives 60 km north in 1.0 h, then 20 km south in 1.0 h. what is its average velocity for the whole trip? 20 km h 1 north 40 km h 1 north 40 km h 1 south 30 km h 1 north
a car moving at 20 m s 1 brakes with a constant deceleration of 5.0 m s 2. how far does it travel before stopping? 40 m 20 m 80 m 4.0 m
a worker pushes a 20 kg crate across a floor at constant velocity. the coefficient of kinetic friction is 0.30. what horizontal force is the worker applying? 60 n 200 n 6.0 n 260 n
a stone is thrown horizontally at 15 m s 1 from the top of a 20 m cliff. how far from the base of the cliff does it land? 30 m 15 m 60 m 20 m
a mechanic pulls with 40 n on the end of a 0.25 m wrench, at 30° to the wrench handle. what torque does she apply to the bolt? (sin 30° = 0.50) 5.0 n·m 10 n·m 8.7 n·m 160 n·m
a 2.0 kg block on a frictionless table is tied by a string over a light pulley to a 3.0 kg block hanging over the edge. what is the acceleration of the blocks? 6.0 m s 2 10 m s 2 15 m s 2 4.0 m s 2

a satellite is moved from an orbit 2r from earth's center to an orbit 6r from earth's center. how does the gravitational force on it change? it becomes 1/9 as large it becomes 1/3 as large it becomes 1/36 as large it becomes 1/4 as large
a box slides down a 37° incline with a coefficient of kinetic friction of 0.25. what is its acceleration? (sin 37° = 0.60, cos 37° = 0.80) 4.0 m s 2 6.0 m s 2 2.0 m s 2 8.0 m s 2
a soccer ball is kicked at 20 m s 1 at 53° above level ground. how far away does it land? (sin 53° = 0.80, cos 53° = 0.60) 38 m 24 m 19 m 51 m
a uniform 4.0 m plank of mass 20 kg rests on supports at its two ends. a 60 kg person stands 1.0 m from the left end. what upward force does the left support exert? 550 n 450 n 250 n 400 n
a cart rolls through a vertical loop of radius 2.5 m. what is the minimum speed at the top of the loop for it to stay on the track? 5.0 m s 1 25 m s 1 7.1 m s 1 2.5 m s 1

a lab centrifuge spins samples at a radius of 0.10 m and 100 revolutions per second. about how many times g is the centripetal acceleration? (use π2 ≈ 10.) about 4000 g about 400 g about 60 g about 40,000 g

a 60 kg patient is strapped to a frictionless tilt table raised to 30° from horizontal, with her feet resting on a footboard. what force does the footboard exert on her feet? (sin 30° = 0.50, cos 30° ≈ 0.87) 300 n 600 n 520 n 0 n
on an acceleration time graph, what does the area between the curve and the time axis represent? the change in velocity the displacement the change in acceleration the average speed
which property of an object measures its inertia, its resistance to changes in velocity? its mass its weight its speed its volume

a book rests on a ramp tilted at 20°. in which direction does the normal force from the ramp act on the book? perpendicular to the ramp, away from its surface straight up, directly opposite to gravity parallel to the ramp, pointing up the slope perpendicular to the ramp, into its surface

for a crate sliding across a floor, the size of the kinetic friction force depends mainly on: μ k and the normal force on the crate the area of the crate touching the floor how fast the crate is sliding the crate's acceleration
in a tug of war, two teams pull on opposite ends of a rope with 500 n each, and nothing moves. what is the tension in the rope? 500 n 1000 n 0 n 250 n

a sled can be moved across level snow by pulling a rope angled 30° above the horizontal or by pushing a handle angled 30° below the horizontal, with the same force each way. why is pulling usually easier? pulling lifts slightly, lowering the normal force and friction pulling presses the sled down, giving better grip on snow pushing gives a smaller forward component of the force friction does not depend on how the force is aimed

a car drives over the crest of a rounded hill at constant speed. at the very top, how does the normal force from the road compare with the car's weight? it is less than the car's weight it is equal to the car's weight it is greater than the car's weight it is zero at every speed
ignoring air resistance, a ball launched at 30° above level ground lands 40 m away. at the same launch speed, which other launch angle gives the same 40 m range? 60° 45° 15° 75°

a ball on a string is swung in a vertical circle. at which point is the tension in the string greatest? at the bottom of the circle at the top of the circle at the sides, level with the center it is the same all the way around
the velocity time graph shows a cart moving along a straight track. at what time does the cart reverse its direction of motion? at t = 4 s at t = 0 s at t = 6 s at t = 3 s
a ball is thrown straight up at 20 m s 1. ignoring air resistance, how high does it rise above the launch point? (g = 10 m s 2) 20 m 40 m 10 m 2.0 m
a planet has twice earth's mass and twice earth's radius. an astronaut weighs 600 n on earth. what would she weigh on this planet's surface? 300 n 600 n 1200 n 150 n

a swimmer heads straight across a river, swimming at 3.0 m s 1 relative to the water, while the current flows at 4.0 m s 1. what is her speed relative to the riverbank? 5.0 m s 1 7.0 m s 1 1.0 m s 1 3.0 m s 1
a 160 n sign hangs from two ropes attached symmetrically, each making a 30° angle above the horizontal. what is the tension in each rope? (sin 30° = 0.50) 160 n 80 n 320 n 92 n

after braking hard, a car leaves straight skid marks 40 m long before stopping. the coefficient of kinetic friction between tires and road is 0.50. about how fast was the car going when the skid began? (g = 10 m s 2) 20 m s 1 40 m s 1 10 m s 1 14 m s 1
the velocity time graph shows a cart moving along a straight track. what is the cart's displacement from t = 0 to t = 6 s? 18 m 30 m 24 m 36 m
a student pulls a lab cart with different net forces and measures its acceleration, as shown in the table. what is the cart's mass? 4.0 kg 0.25 kg 2.0 kg 8.0 kg

name: Research design
t: researchers find that people who sleep less report more anxiety. which conclusion is justified? less sleep causes higher anxiety in these people anxiety causes these people to sleep less sleep and anxiety are associated; causality is unknown sleep and anxiety are unrelated in this group
in a controlled experiment, the variable deliberately manipulated is called the: independent variable dependent variable confounding variable outcome measure only
the independent variable in an experiment is: the variable the researcher manipulates the variable that is measured a variable held constant an uncontrolled factor

a control group: doesn't receive the experimental treatment, for comparison receives a higher dose of the treatment for comparison is chosen by the researcher based on who seems healthiest receives the treatment but isn't measured afterward
a hypothesis is: a testable prediction a proven fact an unrelated observation a summary of results

a placebo is: an inactive treatment that looks like the real one an active drug given at a lower dose than usual an established drug used to compare a new one a survey measuring participants' expectations

in a double blind study: neither participants nor interacting researchers know who is treated only the participants are unaware of who receives the treatment only the researchers are unaware of who receives the treatment two independent teams each run the trial on separate groups

a confounding variable is one that: is related to both the iv and dv, giving an alternative explanation is the variable the researcher deliberately manipulates in a study is related only to the dependent variable, adding random noise is held constant across groups so it can't affect the results

random assignment to groups mainly improves: internal validity (supports cause and effect conclusions) external validity (supports generalizing to other people) statistical power (supports detecting small effects) reliability (supports consistent repeated measurements)

random sampling from a population mainly improves: external validity (generalizability) internal validity (causal inference) reliability (consistency of measures) construct validity (measuring the trait)
reliability refers to: consistency of a measurement accuracy of a measurement generalizability ethical approval

validity refers to: whether a test measures what it claims to measure whether a test gives the same results when repeated whether a test's results are statistically significant whether a test's sample is large enough to detect effects
a cohort study: follows a group over time to see who develops an outcome starts with people who already have the disease and looks back randomly assigns treatments studies one person in depth

a case control study compares: cases to similar people without the condition, looking back at exposures exposed and unexposed people, following them forward for outcomes randomly assigned groups given treatment or placebo over time one group's condition rates measured at a single point in time

which design can best show that a drug causes improvement? a randomized controlled trial a case study a correlational survey a cross sectional study
participants improve simply because they know they're being studied. this is the: hawthorne effect placebo effect halo effect bystander effect

in a crossover trial, each participant takes the drug for 4 weeks and a placebo for 4 weeks, in random order, with a washout period in between. what is the main advantage of this design? each person serves as their own control it removes the need for any blinding carryover effects become impossible it needs no ethics review to run

increasing sample size usually: increases statistical power decreases power has no effect on power increases bias

in a normal distribution, about what percentage of data lie within 1 standard deviation of the mean? 68% 50% 95% 99.7%
iq scores have a mean of 100 and sd of 15. about what percentage of people score above 130? 2.5% 5% 16% 0.15%
a test detects 90 of 100 people who have a disease. what is its sensitivity? 90% 10% 100% it can't be determined
a test correctly gives negative results for 950 of 1000 healthy people. what is its specificity? 95% 5% 50% 90%

a 95% confidence interval for a mean blood pressure drop is 2 to 8 mmhg. what does this suggest? the drug likely lowers blood pressure, since the interval excludes 0 the drug has no clear effect, since the interval is so wide the drug lowers blood pressure by exactly 5 mmhg on average 95% of patients had a blood pressure drop between 2 and 8 mmhg

data on a graph show a strong positive correlation between ice cream sales and drowning deaths. what is the best explanation? a third variable (hot weather) increases both eating ice cream before swimming causes drowning drowning deaths lead people to buy more ice cream the correlation is most likely due to chance alone

a screening test for a rare disease (1 in 1000) has 99% sensitivity and 95% specificity. a random person tests positive. is it likely they have the disease? no; most positives are false positives, since the disease is so rare yes; 99% sensitivity means a 99% chance they have the disease yes; 95% specificity means a 95% chance they have the disease yes; with both rates above 90%, the disease is very likely

positive predictive value increases when: the disease is more common in the tested population the disease is rarer in the tested population the test's specificity decreases at a fixed prevalence the test's sensitivity decreases at a fixed prevalence
which plot best shows the relationship between two continuous variables? a scatter plot a pie chart a bar chart of categories a histogram of one variable

a study of 20 patients finds a new drug lowers cholesterol with p = 0.08. what is the most reasonable conclusion? not statistically significant at α = 0.05, possibly due to low power the drug definitely doesn't lower cholesterol in any patient the drug significantly lowers cholesterol at the α = 0.05 level the result proves the null hypothesis of no effect is true
a study reports that a drug reduces heart attack risk from 2% to 1%. what is the absolute risk reduction? 1 percentage point 50 percentage points 2 percentage points 0.5 percentage points
a drug lowers heart attack risk from 2% to 1%. what is the number needed to treat (nnt) to prevent one heart attack? 100 50 2 1

in a randomized trial (bar graph), the drug group improved 35 points and the placebo group 22 points. what is the best interpretation? the drug adds about 13 points beyond placebo the drug caused all 35 points of improvement the placebo group shows the drug doesn't work improvement can't be compared between groups
a researcher wants to display the distribution of ages among 500 clinic patients. which graph is most appropriate? a histogram a pie chart a scatter plot a line graph over time
a patient's blood type (a, b, ab or o) is what kind of variable? categorical (nominal) continuous (ratio) ordinal (ranked) discrete interval

a trial tests whether drug x changes ldl cholesterol compared with a placebo. what is the null hypothesis? drug x and placebo produce the same mean ldl drug x lowers ldl more than the placebo drug x raises ldl more than the placebo the placebo lowers ldl more than drug x

a researcher sets the significance level α at 0.05 before collecting data. what does this mean? a 5% false positive risk is accepted if h0 is true the study has a 5% chance of a false negative the results will be 95% accurate overall the p value must turn out to equal 0.05

a nurse adds 10 mmhg to every blood pressure reading in a data set to correct a miscalibrated cuff. how do the mean and standard deviation change? the mean rises by 10; the sd is unchanged both the mean and the sd rise by 10 the mean is unchanged; the sd rises by 10 both the mean and the sd stay the same

a trial of 50,000 patients finds a new drug lowers systolic blood pressure by 0.5 mmhg more than placebo (p < 0.001). what is the best interpretation? the effect is real but likely clinically trivial the effect is large, since p is very small the result is likely a type i error the drug should replace current therapy

a histogram of age at diagnosis for a disease shows two separate peaks, one in the 20s and one in the 60s. which statement is most accurate? the distribution is bimodal, so the mean alone misleads the distribution is normal with a large sd the distribution is skewed right with one mode the mean age is the most typical age at diagnosis

a researcher lowers the significance level from α = 0.05 to α = 0.01 without changing the sample size. what happens? type i errors fall, but type ii errors rise type i and type ii errors both fall type i errors rise, but type ii errors fall statistical power increases

in a trial, diet a produces a mean weight loss of 4 kg (standard deviation 1 kg) and diet b a mean of 4 kg (standard deviation 3 kg). which statement is best supported? diet b's results vary more from person to person diet b produced more weight loss on average diet a produced more weight loss on average diet b's median loss must be larger than 4 kg

a case control study reports an odds ratio of 1.4 for an exposure, with a 95% confidence interval of 0.8 to 1.9. what is the best conclusion? no significant association, since the ci includes 1 a significant association, since 1.4 is above 1 a significant protective effect of exposure a significant association, since 0.8 is above 0

in a study of exercise and resting heart rate, the correlation coefficient is r = 0.70. about what fraction of the variation in resting heart rate is accounted for by exercise level? about 49% about 70% about 30% about 84%
in a cohort study, 30 of 100 exposed workers and 10 of 100 unexposed workers develop a lung disease. what is the relative risk? 3.0 0.33 20 2.0
a case control study has 100 cases and 100 controls. among cases, 40 were exposed; among controls, 20 were exposed. what is the odds ratio? about 2.7 2.0 about 0.37 4.0
systolic blood pressures in a population have a mean of 120 mmhg and a standard deviation of 10 mmhg. what is the z score for a reading of 135 mmhg? 1.5 15 1.35 1.5
six patients' hospital stays (in days) are 4, 8, 10, 14, 15 and 90. what is the median stay? 12 days 10 days 14 days 23.5 days
a test with 90% sensitivity and 90% specificity is used in 1000 people, of whom 100 have the disease. what is the positive predictive value? 50% 90% 10% 82%
a vaccine trial finds that 10% of the placebo group and 6% of the vaccine group develop the illness. what is the relative risk reduction? 40% 4% 60% 25%

a research team tests 20 different supplements against placebo, each at α = 0.05. in truth, none of the supplements has any effect. about how many 'significant' results should they expect by chance? about 1 about 0 about 5 about 20

a lab lowers the cutoff value at which a blood test is called 'positive' for a disease. what is the most likely effect? sensitivity rises and specificity falls sensitivity and specificity both rise sensitivity falls and specificity rises neither value changes, only prevalence

a sample of 36 patients has a mean cholesterol of 200 mg/dl with a standard deviation of 12 mg/dl. what is the approximate 95% confidence interval for the population mean? 196 to 204 mg/dl 188 to 212 mg/dl 176 to 224 mg/dl 198 to 202 mg/dl

researchers want to make the 95% confidence interval for a mean half as wide as in their pilot study. assuming the sd stays the same, how should they change the sample size? make it 4 times larger make it 2 times larger make it √2 times larger make it 8 times larger

in a population, 30% of people carry gene variant a and 40% carry variant b, and the two are inherited independently. what is the probability that a randomly chosen person carries a or b (or both)? 0.58 0.70 0.12 0.82

in a cohort study, coffee drinkers have twice the risk of heart disease of non drinkers (rr = 2.0). when the data are split by smoking status, the rr is 1.0 among smokers and 1.0 among nonsmokers. coffee drinkers are much more likely to smoke. what is the best conclusion? smoking confounds the coffee heart disease link coffee causes heart disease only in smokers coffee doubles risk in each smoking group smoking reduces the risk caused by coffee

newborn birth weights at a hospital are approximately normal, with a mean of 3.4 kg and a standard deviation of 0.5 kg. about what percentage of newborns weigh between 2.9 kg and 4.4 kg? about 82% about 68% about 95% about 75%
patients rate their pain as none, mild, moderate or severe. what kind of variable is this? ordinal nominal continuous ratio
for the ages of patients in a study, the first quartile (q1) is 20 years and the third quartile (q3) is 35 years. what is the interquartile range? 15 years 55 years 27.5 years 7.5 years

in a blood donor population, 45% have type o blood and 40% have type a. each person has exactly one blood type. what is the probability that a randomly chosen donor is type o or type a? 85% 18% 45% 5%
the box plot shows patients' wait times at a clinic. what does the line inside the box mark? the median wait time the mean wait time the most common wait time the range of wait times

in a wealthy country, most deaths occur between ages 70 and 95, but a small number of people die in childhood or young adulthood. how do the mean and median age at death most likely compare? the mean is lower than the median the mean is higher than the median the mean and median are equal the median is pulled down by the young deaths

in a data set of resting heart rates, one value was entered as 700 beats per minute instead of 70. the error is corrected. how do the mean and standard deviation change? both the mean and the sd decrease the mean decreases; the sd stays the same the mean stays the same; the sd decreases both the mean and the sd increase

researchers find r = 0.62 between height and weight, with heights measured in inches. they convert every height to centimeters (multiplying by 2.54). what is the new correlation coefficient? 0.62 1.57 0.24 1.00

the scatter plot shows relative risk of death versus body mass index in a cohort. the correlation coefficient for these data is close to zero (r ≈ 0.0). what is the best interpretation? there is a strong relationship, but it isn't linear body mass index and risk of death are unrelated the relationship is strong and negative the correlation must have been calculated wrongly

two trials use the same sample size and α = 0.05. trial 1 tests a drug that truly lowers blood pressure by 20 mmhg; trial 2 tests a drug that truly lowers it by 2 mmhg. which trial has more statistical power? trial 1, because larger effects are easier to detect trial 2, because small effects need fewer patients both have equal power, since n and α are equal neither, because power depends only on the p value

from the same data, a researcher calculates both a 95% and a 99% confidence interval for a mean. how does the 99% interval compare? it is wider it is narrower it is the same width it is shifted to higher values
one lab section of 20 students has a mean exam score of 80, and another section of 30 students has a mean of 90. what is the mean score of all 50 students? 86 85 84 87

the box plots show recovery times for patients given drug a or drug b. which statement is supported? drug a has the lower median and the larger iqr drug b has the lower median and the larger iqr both drugs have the same median recovery time drug a has the lower median and the smaller iqr

exam scores are normally distributed. a student scores exactly 1 standard deviation above the mean. about what percentile is this? about the 84th percentile about the 68th percentile about the 34th percentile about the 95th percentile

a screening test is given to 1000 people, with the results shown. what is the test's negative predictive value (the chance that a person with a negative result is truly disease free)? about 98% about 90% about 80% about 47%

a rapid test gives a false positive result 5% of the time in healthy people. a healthy person is tested twice, and the two results are independent. what is the probability that both tests are falsely positive? 0.25% 10% 5% 2.5%

in a study, the best fit line relating systolic blood pressure (sbp, in mmhg) to age (in years) is sbp = 0.5 × age + 100. what sbp does the line predict for a 60 year old? 130 mmhg 160 mmhg 110 mmhg 150 mmhg

a new drug truly lowers relapse rates, but a small trial finds p = 0.30, and the authors conclude the drug has no effect. what has happened? a type ii error a type i error a correct decision, since p > 0.05 proof that the null hypothesis is true
the table shows how many emergency room visits each of 30 patients made last year. what is the median number of visits? 1 visit 0 visits 2 visits 5 visits

normal oral body temperatures in a group have a mean of 37.0 °c and a standard deviation of 0.50 °c. if every value is converted to fahrenheit (°f = 1.8 × °c + 32), what are the new mean and standard deviation? mean 98.6 °f; sd 0.90 °f mean 98.6 °f; sd 32.9 °f mean 98.6 °f; sd 0.50 °f mean 66.6 °f; sd 0.90 °f

hospital a delivers about 10 babies per day, and hospital b about 100 per day. over a year, which hospital will most likely record more days on which over 70% of the babies born are girls? hospital a, since small samples vary more hospital b, since it delivers more babies in total both equally, since each birth is 50% girls neither, since 70% girls can't happen by chance

across all applicants, admission test scores correlate moderately with first year medical school grades. at one school that admits only applicants with the very highest scores, the correlation is much weaker. what is the most likely reason? the narrow range of scores weakens the correlation the test measures different skills at that school larger samples always produce a smaller r grades are always less reliable at selective schools

a study reports a sample's mean ± standard deviation (sd) and mean ± standard error of the mean (sem = sd ÷ √n). if the sample size grows from 25 to 100, what most likely happens? the sd stays about the same; the sem halves both the sd and the sem are cut in half the sd halves; the sem stays about the same both the sd and the sem stay the same
the table shows smoking status and disease in 1000 adults. if a person with the disease is chosen at random, what is the probability that they are a smoker? 60% 15% 3% 20%

in a randomized trial, patients take a placebo or one of two doses of a cholesterol drug. the graph shows the mean drop in ldl cholesterol with 95% confidence intervals. which conclusion is best supported? both doses beat placebo; high vs low dose is unclear the high dose is clearly better than the low dose only the high dose clearly beats the placebo the low dose is no better than the placebo

fasting glucose in healthy adults is roughly normal, with a mean of 90 mg/dl and a standard deviation of 5 mg/dl. a clinic's software flags any result above 95 mg/dl for review. among 2,000 healthy adults, about how many results will be flagged? about 320 about 640 about 50 about 1,000

name: Amino acids & proteins

a researcher unfolds an enzyme with urea and β mercaptoethanol, then slowly removes both. the enzyme refolds and becomes fully active again. what does this show? the primary sequence contains all the information needed for folding chaperones must be present for the protein to refold correctly disulfide bonds, not the sequence, dictate the folded structure urea and β mercaptoethanol never fully denatured the enzyme

which two standard amino acids have side chains that end in an amide group ( conh2)? asparagine and glutamine aspartic acid and glutamic acid serine and threonine lysine and arginine
which amino acid has a side chain made of an aromatic ring bearing an oh group (a phenol)? tyrosine phenylalanine tryptophan serine

by convention, in which direction is a peptide sequence such as gly ala ser written? from the free n terminus to the free c terminus from the free c terminus to the free n terminus from the most to the least hydrophobic residue from the smallest to the largest side chain

an aspartate side chain and a lysine side chain lie next to each other on a protein's surface at ph 7. which interaction most likely forms between them? a salt bridge (ionic attraction) a covalent disulfide bond a new peptide bond a hydrophobic (nonpolar) contact

protein folding in water is favorable even though the folded chain is more ordered than the unfolded one. what mainly drives nonpolar side chains to the interior? ordered water around them is released, gaining entropy nonpolar side chains form covalent bonds in the core nonpolar groups hydrogen bond strongly to each other burial lowers the entropy of the surrounding water

in a β pleated sheet, where do the side chains of consecutive residues along one strand point? alternately above and below the plane of the sheet all toward the neighboring strand to form h bonds all outward from a central axis, as in a helix all into the sheet's plane, between the strands

in collagen, every third residue is glycine. replacing one of these glycines (as in some forms of brittle bone disease) weakens the triple helix. why? only glycine's tiny side chain fits in the crowded helix center glycine forms the disulfides that link the three chains glycine is the residue that vitamin c dependent enzymes hydroxylate glycine's charged side chain repels water from the helix

a cysteine thiol in a peptide has pk a = 8.3. at ph 7.3, what is the approximate ratio of thiolate ( s ) to thiol ( sh)? 1 : 10 10 : 1 1 : 1 1 : 100
a single chain protein contains about 150 amino acids. using an average residue mass of 110 da, what is its approximate mass? about 16.5 kda about 1.65 kda about 165 kda about 11 kda

glycine (pk a 2.3 for cooh and 9.6 for nh3+) is drawn in the form shown. in which solution is this the main form? ph 1, where its net charge is +1 ph 6, where its net charge is 0 ph 12, where its net charge is 1 ph 6, where its net charge is +1
the tripeptide shown is drawn as it exists at ph 7. reading from the n terminus to the c terminus, what is its sequence? ala ser phe phe ser ala ala thr phe ala ser tyr

poly l lysine is a random coil at ph 7 but folds into an α helix at ph 12. what best explains this? deprotonated side chains no longer repel each other high ph forms disulfide bonds that brace the helix high ph hydrolyzes peptide bonds into short helices side chains form salt bridges with each other at ph 12

lowering the ph of a folded protein's solution from 7 to 2 often unfolds it. which effect contributes most directly? carboxylates gain h+, breaking salt bridges peptide bonds break, destroying the primary structure h+ ions reduce the protein's disulfide bonds amino groups lose h+, adding negative charge

enzymes from bacteria living in hot springs often stay folded near 90 °c. compared with similar human enzymes, which feature best explains this stability? more salt bridges and disulfides, and a tighter core more glycine, making the chain more flexible fewer hydrophobic residues in the interior core more proline placed in the middle of α helices

a synthetic 20 residue peptide with two cysteines is stirred in air at ph 8. mass spectrometry then shows the main species is 2 da lighter than the starting peptide, and it is still a single chain. what happened? an intramolecular disulfide formed, losing two h atoms two peptides joined by a disulfide, losing water a peptide bond was hydrolyzed, losing a hydrogen both cysteine thiols were oxidized to sulfonic acids

in a neurodegenerative disease, a normal brain protein and its disease form have the identical amino acid sequence. the disease form resists proteases, is insoluble, and forms stacked fibrils held by h bonds between backbone strands. what best describes the change? α helical regions refolded into stacked β sheets a point mutation changed the protein's sequence peptide bonds were replaced with disulfide bonds β sheets unfolded into a soluble random coil
which amino acid has a guanidinium group (a carbon bonded to three nitrogens) at the end of its side chain? arginine lysine histidine asparagine
which amino acid has an indole side chain (a benzene ring fused to a five membered ring containing n h)? tryptophan tyrosine phenylalanine histidine

tight β turns reverse a polypeptide chain's direction within four residues. which two amino acids are especially common in these turns? glycine and proline tryptophan and phenylalanine leucine and isoleucine glutamate and lysine

hsp70 type chaperones help many newly made proteins reach their native fold. how do they mainly do this? they bind exposed hydrophobic stretches, preventing aggregation they form covalent bonds that lock in the native fold they supply the folding information missing from the sequence they cut peptide bonds in misfolded regions of the chain

which backbone bonds in a polypeptide rotate relatively freely, giving the chain its flexibility? the n cα and cα c(=o) bonds the c(=o) n peptide bond only the bonds inside side chains the c=o double bond of each residue

vitamin c is a cofactor for prolyl hydroxylase, which modifies collagen. why are collagen fibers weak in scurvy (vitamin c deficiency)? fewer hydroxyproline residues mean fewer h bonds holding the triple helix without vitamin c, glycine can't be placed at every third position vitamin c itself forms the disulfide cross links between collagen strands ribosomes can't add proline to the chain without vitamin c
five amino acids, each with a free (unlinked) molar mass of 128 da, are joined into a linear pentapeptide. what is the pentapeptide's mass? 568 da 640 da 550 da 586 da
using only the 20 standard amino acids, how many different linear tripeptide sequences are possible? 8000 60 1140 400

in a 16 residue segment of a soluble protein, the hydrophobic residues fall at positions 1, 4, 5, 8, 11, 12 and 15, and all the others are charged or polar. which structure does this pattern most likely form? an α helix with one nonpolar face a β strand with one nonpolar face a transmembrane helix buried in a bilayer a random coil, since the pattern is scattered

a lysine side chain normally has pk a ≈ 10.5, but one lysine buried in a nonpolar pocket of an enzyme has pk a ≈ 6. what best explains the shift? burying a charge is unfavorable, so the neutral nh2 form is favored a nearby asp stabilizes the neutral nh2 form of lysine a nonpolar pocket makes nh2 a much stronger base the local ph inside a hydrophobic pocket is higher

on a plot of allowed backbone angles (φ and ψ), glycine occupies regions that are forbidden to every other amino acid. why? its side chain is only h, so few angles cause steric clashes it is achiral, so its n h cannot form hydrogen bonds its side chain forms a ring that bonds to the backbone n its peptide bonds lack any partial double bond character

the aligned backbone c=o and n h groups give an α helix a dipole, with a partial positive charge at its n terminal end. which residues tend to stabilize a helix when placed near its n terminus? aspartate and glutamate lysine and arginine leucine and isoleucine glycine and proline

a segment on the edge of a β sheet has the sequence val thr ile ser val thr leu ser, and one face of the sheet packs against the protein's core. which arrangement fits this segment? val, ile, leu face the core; thr and ser face water all eight side chains face the core of the protein the segment folds into an α helix with a nonpolar face thr and ser face the core; val, ile and leu face water

an enzyme has a single trp, which emits light near 330 nm when buried in a nonpolar environment and near 350 nm when exposed to water. the enzyme is incubated in increasing concentrations of urea (data shown). which conclusion is best supported? activity is lost as the trp becomes water exposed, with a midpoint near 3 m urea activity drops before any unfolding, so urea must block the active site directly the trp is exposed to water in the native enzyme and becomes buried with urea unfolding increases steadily and evenly across the whole range from 0 to 6 m

a 12 residue peptide contains one serine, one tyrosine and no threonine. after incubation with a kinase and atp, mass spectrometry shows its mass rose by 160 da. a phosphatase that acts only on phosphotyrosine then lowers the mass by 80 da. what do the results show? both the ser and the tyr each gained one phosphate the tyr gained two phosphates; the phosphatase removed one the ser gained two phosphates, and the tyr was not modified a single pyrophosphate group was added to the serine

sickle cell disease based on the passage, which condition would most likely trigger sickling in a patient? breathing supplemental o2 in a hospital being at high altitude, where o2 is low drinking extra water to stay hydrated resting at sea level, where o2 is normal
sickle cell disease in one region, 1 in 100 newborns has sickle cell disease. assuming hardy weinberg equilibrium, what fraction of the population are carriers? 0.01 0.09 0.10 0.18

name: Enzymes
t: a drug binds an enzyme's active site and competes with the substrate. how does it affect km and vmax? km increases; vmax unchanged km unchanged; vmax decreases both decrease km decreases; vmax increases

a noncompetitive inhibitor binds equally well to the enzyme and the enzyme substrate complex at an allosteric site. what is its effect? km increases; vmax unchanged km unchanged; vmax decreases km decreases; vmax decreases no effect on kinetics
what does an enzyme’s km represent in michaelis menten kinetics? concentration of enzyme at saturation substrate concentration at half vmax activation energy maximum catalytic rate
enzymes speed up reactions by: lowering the activation energy raising the activation energy making δg more negative shifting the equilibrium toward products

what distinguishes a coenzyme from a metal ion cofactor? a coenzyme is a small organic molecule, often derived from a vitamin a coenzyme is always a protein a coenzyme is a metal ion a coenzyme is permanently consumed in each reaction
a hydrolase is an enzyme that: uses water to break bonds transfers a phosphate from atp moves electrons between molecules rearranges atoms within one molecule

a kinase is an enzyme that: transfers a phosphate group, usually from atp, to a substrate removes a phosphate group from a substrate by hydrolysis uses inorganic phosphate to cleave a bond in a substrate hydrolyzes atp to pump ions across a cell membrane

the induced fit model of enzyme action states that: the active site changes shape as the substrate binds the active site is rigid and fits the substrate exactly enzymes bind every substrate equally substrates change the enzyme's primary structure
a low km value means an enzyme: has a high affinity for its substrate has a low affinity for its substrate has a high vmax is inhibited
