when a cell has plenty of atp and nadh, what happens to pyruvate dehydrogenase and isocitrate dehydrogenase? both are inhibited both are activated pdh is activated; isocitrate dh is inhibited neither changes

a person with chronic alcoholism and thiamine (vitamin b1) deficiency develops lactic acidosis. why? pyruvate dehydrogenase can't work, so pyruvate is converted to lactate pyruvate carboxylase can't work, so pyruvate is converted to lactate lactate dehydrogenase needs thiamine, so lactate can't be reoxidized complex iv needs thiamine, so cells switch to anaerobic glycolysis
how many co2 molecules are released when one glucose is fully oxidized through pyruvate dehydrogenase and the citric acid cycle? 6 2 4 3

newborns have brown fat containing thermogenin (ucp1). how does it keep them warm? it lets h+ bypass atp synthase into the matrix, releasing gradient energy as heat it boosts atp synthase output, and the extra atp is hydrolyzed to make heat it blocks complex iv, so electrons release their energy as heat instead it oxidizes glycogen stores in the cytosol, releasing their energy as heat

rotenone blocks complex i. in a cell exposed to rotenone, which fuel can still feed electrons into the etc? succinate, through complex ii (fadh2) nadh, through complex i pyruvate, directly at complex iv none; all electron flow stops
which citric acid cycle enzyme converts citrate (shown) into its isomer, isocitrate? aconitase citrate synthase isocitrate dehydrogenase fumarase
which mobile carrier moves electrons from complex iii to complex iv? cytochrome c coenzyme q (ubiquinone) nadh fadh2
fumarase adds water across the double bond of fumarate (shown). what is the product? malate succinate oxaloacetate citrate

in mitochondrial atp synthase, where is atp actually made? in the f1 head, which faces the matrix in the f0 ring, within the inner membrane in the f1 head, which faces the intermembrane space in cytochrome c oxidase, next to the synthase

which citric acid cycle enzyme complex most closely resembles pyruvate dehydrogenase in structure, cofactors and reaction type? α ketoglutarate dehydrogenase isocitrate dehydrogenase (nad+) succinate dehydrogenase malate dehydrogenase
which pair of signals activates isocitrate dehydrogenase? adp and ca2+ atp and nadh acetyl coa and citrate succinyl coa and gtp

pyruvate dehydrogenase kinase (pdk) is stimulated by high nadh and acetyl coa. what does pdk do? phosphorylates pdh, inactivating it phosphorylates pdh, activating it dephosphorylates pdh, activating it hydrolyzes pdh's lipoic acid arm

why does fadh2 from succinate yield fewer atp (about 1.5) than nadh (about 2.5)? its electrons enter at coq, skipping complex i's proton pumping fadh2 carries only one electron instead of the usual two its electrons skip complex iv, so o2 is never reduced by them fadh2 must first be carried out of the matrix by a shuttle

why must nadh made in the cytosol by glycolysis use a shuttle such as malate aspartate to deliver its electrons? the inner mitochondrial membrane has no nadh transporter cytosolic nadh is chemically different from matrix nadh nadh would be destroyed by o2 if it crossed directly only fadh2 can cross the inner membrane on its own, unlike nadh

when citric acid cycle intermediates are drawn off for biosynthesis, which reaction most directly refills oxaloacetate? pyruvate carboxylase: pyruvate → oxaloacetate pyruvate dehydrogenase: pyruvate → acetyl coa pepck: oxaloacetate → phosphoenolpyruvate citrate lyase: citrate → acetyl coa + oaa in cytosol
using about 2.5 atp per nadh and 1.5 atp per fadh2, about how much atp comes from complete oxidation of one pyruvate in the mitochondrion? about 12.5 atp about 10.0 atp about 15.0 atp about 25.0 atp

electrons from succinate pass through complexes iii and iv, which together pump about 6 h+ per electron pair. if about 4 h+ are needed per atp made and exported, how many atp form per fadh2? about 1.5 about 2.5 about 6 about 0.7

antimycin a blocks electron flow through complex iii. in treated mitochondria, what is the redox state of the carriers? coq is mostly reduced; cytochrome c is mostly oxidized coq is mostly oxidized; cytochrome c is mostly reduced both coq and cytochrome c are mostly reduced both coq and cytochrome c are mostly oxidized

arsenite binds tightly to the two thiol groups of reduced lipoic acid. which pair of metabolites would most likely build up? pyruvate and α ketoglutarate citrate and isocitrate succinyl coa and oxaloacetate malate and fumarate

malonate (shown) resembles succinate and competitively inhibits succinate dehydrogenase. in treated mitochondria, which change is expected? succinate builds up, but high succinate can overcome the block fumarate builds up, and extra succinate deepens the block succinate builds up, and no amount of succinate can help citrate falls sharply because malonate inhibits citrate synthase

during muscle contraction, cytosolic ca2+ rises and some enters the mitochondria. how does this affect the citric acid cycle? it activates pdh phosphatase, isocitrate dh and α ketoglutarate dh it inhibits pdh phosphatase, isocitrate dh and α ketoglutarate dh it activates citrate synthase but inhibits succinate dehydrogenase it activates pdh kinase, which shuts off pyruvate dehydrogenase
oxidizing one acetyl coa in the citric acid cycle yields 3 nadh and 1 fadh2. passing all these electrons to oxygen consumes how many o2 molecules? 2 1 4 8

in isolated mitochondria, oligomycin stops o2 consumption, and adding the uncoupler dnp restores it. after cyanide, dnp does not restore o2 consumption. why? cyanide blocks electron flow itself; oligomycin only blocks h+ re entry dnp is destroyed by cyanide before it reaches the membrane cyanide blocks atp synthase's proton channel, as oligomycin does oligomycin blocks complex iv, and dnp reactivates that complex
acetyl coa labeled with 14c at both carbons enters the citric acid cycle. in the first turn, how many of the labeled carbons are released as co2? none one two three

the mammalian atp synthase c ring has 8 c subunits. each full rotation moves 8 h+ through f0 and makes 3 atp in f1. about how many h+ pass through the synthase per atp made? about 2.7 about 0.4 about 8 about 24

no citric acid cycle reaction uses o2, yet the cycle stops within seconds when o2 runs out. why? without o2, nadh isn't reoxidized, so nad+ and fad run out o2 is a required allosteric activator of citrate synthase without o2, acetyl coa is converted straight into lactate o2 is needed to regenerate oxaloacetate directly from malate

complex ii passes electrons from succinate (e°′ ≈ +0.03 v) to coq (e°′ ≈ +0.05 v). why doesn't complex ii pump protons? the tiny potential drop releases too little energy to pump h+ complex ii sits in the outer membrane, away from the gradient electrons move uphill here, so the step must be driven by atp complex ii hands electrons straight to o2 without any pumping

a patient rescued from a house fire has severe lactic acidosis, and blood drawn from a vein is bright red with an unusually high o2 content. cyanide poisoning is suspected. why is venous o2 high? complex iv is blocked, so tissues extract little o2 from the blood cyanide binds hemoglobin directly and greatly raises its o2 affinity cyanide uncouples the chain, so o2 is pumped back into blood lactic acidosis shifts the curve left, trapping o2 on hemoglobin

isolated mitochondria are given succinate and pi, and o2 use is slow. adding adp makes o2 use jump; it slows again once the adp has been converted to atp. what does this show? electron transport is tightly coupled to atp synthesis adp is the final electron acceptor of the chain succinate can't be oxidized until adp activates complex ii adp uncouples mitochondria and lets protons leak in

fluoroacetate, a poison found in some plants, is converted in cells to fluoroacetyl coa, which citrate synthase turns into fluorocitrate. fluorocitrate inhibits aconitase. which metabolite would build up in poisoned tissue? citrate isocitrate succinate oxaloacetate

the last reaction of the citric acid cycle regenerates oxaloacetate from malate. which enzyme catalyzes it, and what reduced carrier forms? malate dehydrogenase, forming nadh malate dehydrogenase, forming fadh2 fumarase, forming nadh malic enzyme, forming nadph

the proton motive force that drives atp synthase is made of which two components? a ph gradient and an electrical potential across the inner membrane a na+ gradient and a k+ gradient across the outer membrane a ph gradient and an osmotic gradient across the outer mitochondrial membrane an electron gradient and a phosphate gradient across the matrix

cytochromes in the electron transport chain carry electrons using: an iron ion in a heme group that cycles between fe3+ and fe2+ a flavin ring that accepts two electrons and two protons a quinone ring dissolved in the inner membrane's lipid layer a zinc ion that cycles between zn2+ and zn+ in the protein

which two citric acid cycle enzymes release co2? isocitrate dehydrogenase and α ketoglutarate dehydrogenase citrate synthase and aconitase, the first two enzymes of the cycle succinate dehydrogenase and fumarase succinyl coa synthetase and malate dehydrogenase

the adenine nucleotide translocase swaps atp4 out of the matrix for adp3 coming in. why does this exchange favor atp export? atp carries one more negative charge, and the matrix side is negative atp is smaller than adp and diffuses through the protein faster the matrix is more acidic, so atp becomes protonated and is pushed out atp binds the outer membrane, pulling it across the inner membrane

some electrons leak from complexes i and iii and reduce o2 by a single electron. what is formed, and which enzyme converts it first? superoxide (o2 ), converted to h2o2 by superoxide dismutase water, released into the matrix by cytochrome c oxidase hydroxide ion (oh ), converted to hydrogen peroxide by catalase ozone (o3), converted to o2 by glutathione peroxidase

complex iii receives electrons from reduced coenzyme q (coqh2) and passes them to cytochrome c. why does it need a special mechanism (the q cycle)? coqh2 carries two electrons, but cytochrome c accepts only one cytochrome c carries two electrons, but coqh2 gives only one coqh2 must be sent back to complex i to be reduced again complex iii must first split o2 before it can accept any electrons

compared with the intermembrane space, the mitochondrial matrix during active respiration is: more alkaline and electrically negative more acidic and electrically positive more alkaline and electrically positive more acidic but still electrically negative
which vitamin coenzyme pairing is correct? pantothenic acid (b5) → coenzyme a riboflavin (b2) → nad+ and nadp+ niacin (b3) → fad and fmn thiamine (b1) → lipoic acid

the first step of β oxidation, acyl coa dehydrogenase, makes fadh2 in the matrix. where do these electrons enter the electron transport chain? at coenzyme q, via electron transferring flavoprotein at complex i, via nadh made from the fadh2 at cytochrome c, after passing through complex ii at complex iv, which passes them directly to o2

vitamin b6 deficiency can cause anemia because the first enzyme of heme synthesis, ala synthase, needs pyridoxal phosphate to join glycine with which citric acid cycle intermediate? succinyl coa oxaloacetate α ketoglutarate fumarate

using the table and δg°′ = nfδe°′ (f ≈ 96.5 kj mol 1 v 1), what is δg°′ when complex i passes two electrons from nadh to coenzyme q? about 71 kj mol 1 about 36 kj mol 1 about 220 kj mol 1 about +71 kj mol 1

mitochondria oxidizing glutamate and malate (nadh linked substrates) are placed in an o2 electrode chamber, and 250 nmol adp is added (graph). the fast o2 use stops when the adp is used up. what is the p/o ratio (adp phosphorylated per o atom reduced)? 2.5 5.0 1.25 1.5

a child with pyruvate dehydrogenase deficiency has lactic acidosis that worsens after carbohydrate rich meals. which diet best supplies acetyl coa to the brain without needing pdh? a high fat, low carbohydrate (ketogenic) diet a high carbohydrate diet with frequent small meals a high protein diet rich in alanine a diet high in sucrose and fructose

atractyloside blocks the adenine nucleotide translocase. what happens when it is added to mitochondria actively making atp from added adp? o2 consumption falls, because adp can no longer reach atp synthase o2 consumption rises, as it does when an uncoupler is added atp synthesis continues normally, using the adp already present in the matrix electron flow stops at complex iv, just as it does with cyanide

glutamate can be oxidized after conversion to α ketoglutarate. using 2.5 atp per nadh and 1.5 per fadh2, how much atp is made as one α ketoglutarate goes around the cycle to oxaloacetate? 7.5 atp 10 atp 6.5 atp 12.5 atp

a fluorescent dye accumulates in mitochondria in proportion to the membrane potential. researchers add oligomycin to respiring cells, then the uncoupler fccp. how does the signal change? it rises slightly after oligomycin, then collapses after fccp it collapses after oligomycin, then rises sharply after fccp it doesn't change after oligomycin, then rises sharply after fccp it falls slightly after each drug but never collapses fully

mitochondria swollen in a hypotonic buffer rupture their outer membrane. they then oxidize succinate very slowly, and adding purified cytochrome c restores the normal rate. what explains this? cytochrome c, a soluble carrier in the intermembrane space, was lost succinate dehydrogenase leaked out of the damaged outer membrane cytochrome c is needed to carry succinate into the matrix rupture let cytochrome c enter the matrix, where it blocks complex ii

the table shows o2 use by isolated mitochondria with different electron donors and inhibitors (rotenone blocks complex i, antimycin a blocks complex iii, cyanide blocks complex iv). where does the artificial donor ascorbate/tmpd feed electrons into the chain? into cytochrome c, past complex iii into coenzyme q, past complex i into complex i, like nadh does directly to o2, without needing complex iv

glucose labeled with 14c at c4 is broken down by glycolysis, and the pyruvate is oxidized by pyruvate dehydrogenase. where is the label found right after the pdh step? in the co2 released by pyruvate dehydrogenase in the methyl carbon of acetyl coa in the carbonyl carbon of acetyl coa in the oxaloacetate the acetyl group joins

measured p/o ratios are about 2.5 for nadh and 1.5 for succinate, not whole numbers. why aren't they integers? electron flow and atp synthesis are linked only by the h+ gradient, so h+ ratios needn't divide evenly each nadh makes exactly 3 atp, but half of all mitochondria in a sample are damaged atp synthase makes half an atp per h+ that passes through its f0 ring some nadh makes 2 atp and some makes 3, so the average is a fraction

when atp and nadh are high, isocitrate dehydrogenase is inhibited and citrate accumulates in the matrix. how does this affect metabolism in the cytosol? citrate is exported, slowing pfk 1 and activating acetyl coa carboxylase citrate is exported, speeding pfk 1 and inhibiting acetyl coa carboxylase citrate stays in the matrix and is converted directly into glucose citrate is oxidized in the cytosol to make extra nadh for the etc

two children have lactic acidosis (table). one has a defect in the electron transport chain and the other has pyruvate dehydrogenase deficiency. which interpretation fits best? child a has the etc defect, since a high lactate:pyruvate ratio means high nadh child b has the etc defect, since a normal ratio means nadh is being reoxidized child a has pdh deficiency, since pyruvate is low when pdh can't remove it neither ratio helps, because lactate is the same 6.0 mm in both of these two children

many tumor cells take up lots of glucose and secrete lactate even with o2 present, partly because pdh kinase keeps pdh phosphorylated. the drug dichloroacetate inhibits pdh kinase. what change is expected in treated tumor cells? lactate output falls and o2 consumption rises lactate output rises and o2 consumption falls both lactate output and o2 consumption fall glucose uptake stops, because hexokinase is inhibited

a cyanide poisoning antidote includes a nitrite that converts some hemoglobin (fe2+) into methemoglobin (fe3+). how does this help? methemoglobin's fe3+ binds cyanide, pulling it off complex iv methemoglobin carries extra o2 to the cells that cyanide has poisoned the nitrite reduces cyanide to harmless ammonia in the blood plasma methemoglobin activates complex ii so electrons bypass complex iv

isolated mitochondria were placed in an o₂-electrode chamber with succinate, and adp, oligomycin and 2,4-dinitrophenol (dnp) were added in turn (figure 1). which explanation best accounts for the rapid o₂ consumption after dnp is added? dnp reverses the oligomycin block so that atp synthase can again make atp. dnp carries protons across the inner membrane, dissipating the gradient so electron transport runs without atp synthesis. dnp donates electrons directly to cytochrome c oxidase. dnp inhibits complex iv, forcing the chain to use o₂ faster.

the liver makes ketone bodies but can't use them for energy. why? the liver lacks thiophorase, which converts acetoacetate to acetoacetyl coa ketone bodies can't cross liver cell membranes to reach the mitochondria the liver lacks hmg coa synthase, which is needed to oxidize ketone bodies ketone bodies inhibit β oxidation, so the liver avoids burning them

fatty acid synthesis needs acetyl coa in the cytosol, but acetyl coa is made in mitochondria. how does it get out? it joins oxaloacetate to form citrate, which is exported and cleaved in the cytosol it diffuses directly through the inner mitochondrial membrane into the cytosol it is converted to malonyl coa, which is then exported to the cytosol it is converted back to pyruvate, which is exported and then reconverted

positive nitrogen balance (more nitrogen taken in than excreted) is expected in: a growing child or a pregnant woman a patient with severe burns a person who is starving an adult with stable weight and diet

a patient with severe liver failure becomes confused after a high protein meal. which explanation is most likely? the failing liver can't convert ammonia to urea, so ammonia accumulates and affects the brain the meal raises blood glucose too high, causing a hyperosmolar state in the brain the failing liver overproduces urea, which crosses into the brain and is toxic breakdown of the dietary protein produces ketone bodies that impair the brain

a newborn has very high blood ammonia, and testing shows a defect in ornithine transcarbamylase (otc), an early urea cycle enzyme. which treatment strategy makes the most sense? limit dietary protein and give drugs that let nitrogen be excreted by other routes give a high protein diet so more substrate drives the urea cycle forward give extra fatty acids so their carbons can carry nitrogen into urea give extra ammonium salts to stimulate the remaining urea cycle enzymes

muscle and brain release much of their excess nitrogen into the blood as glutamine rather than free nh4+. why? it moves two n atoms in a nontoxic form to liver and kidney free nh4+ cannot dissolve in blood plasma at any ph glutamine is converted directly to urea by arginase in muscle glutamine synthetase makes atp while it traps ammonia

oleate (18:1, cis δ9) and stearate (18:0) are each fully oxidized. using 1.5 atp per fadh2, how does oleate's atp yield compare with stearate's? about 1.5 atp less, since one fad linked step is skipped about 2.5 atp less, since one nad+ linked step is skipped about 10 atp less, since one acetyl coa is lost the same, since both have 18 carbons in the chain

in hyperammonemia, brain cells detoxify nh4+ by adding it to α ketoglutarate to make glutamate, and then to glutamate to make glutamine. why can this impair brain atp production? α ketoglutarate is drained from the citric acid cycle, slowing the cycle glutamine directly inhibits atp synthase in brain mitochondria the reactions produce large amounts of nadh, which uncouples the chain ammonia is converted into urea in the brain, using up all its atp

in untreated type 1 diabetes, ketone bodies build up even though blood glucose is high. what best explains this? low insulin allows lipolysis, and low malonyl coa frees cpt i high glucose is converted directly into ketone bodies by the liver high insulin activates hmg coa lyase in the liver mitochondria muscle can't release glucose, so it makes ketones in its place

a child has fatty diarrhea and very low blood cholesterol and triglycerides. blood tests detect no chylomicrons, vldl or ldl, and biopsied intestinal cells are packed with fat droplets. which defect best explains these findings? inability to load lipid onto apob to form chylomicrons and vldl absent pancreatic lipase, so dietary fat is never digested missing ldl receptors, so ldl can't be cleared from the blood absent lipoprotein lipase, so chylomicrons can't be emptied

during chronic metabolic acidosis, such as prolonged ketosis, the kidney takes up more glutamine and raises glutaminase activity. what is the benefit? the nh4+ released is excreted, removing acid and regenerating hco3 the glutamine is stored in kidney cells as an emergency nitrogen reserve the glutamate released raises blood ph by binding free h+ ions in plasma the nh4+ released is converted to urea by the kidney's own urea cycle

a drug taken in the first trimester causes limb malformations, but the same dose in the third trimester does not. what best explains this? limbs and organs form in the first trimester, the period most sensitive to teratogens the placenta forms only in the third trimester, so early drugs reach the fetus freely the fetus has no circulation in the first trimester, so drugs accumulate in tissues drugs can't cross the placenta in the third trimester, so the fetus is unexposed

scientists turn adult skin cells into induced pluripotent stem cells (ipscs). why are these useful in medicine? they can become many cell types and match the patient's own genome they are totipotent, so they can also form placental tissue they never form tumors, since they come from adult cells they can become only skin cells, which simplifies grafting

in a lab, blocking a signal from the notochord prevents the neural tube from forming. this supports which idea? induction: ectoderm needs the notochord's signal to form neural tissue apoptosis: the notochord's signal kills ectoderm that isn't neural gastrulation: the notochord's signal forms the three germ layers endoderm origin: the neural tube develops from endoderm cells

a person's neurons and liver cells make very different proteins, yet carry the same genome. what best explains this? each cell type expresses a different set of genes each cell type deletes the genes it does not use neurons and liver cells carry different mutations neurons read codons with a different genetic code

somites, the paired blocks of mesoderm beside the neural tube, give rise to: vertebrae, skeletal muscle and dermis the brain, spinal cord and retina the lining of the gut and lungs the heart, kidneys and gonads

fraternal (dizygotic) twins are, on average, about as genetically similar as: any two ordinary full siblings a pair of identical twins two half siblings two first cousins

a mutant fruit fly grows legs on its head where its antennae should be. a mutation in which kind of gene is most likely? a homeotic (hox) gene a gene controlling apoptosis a gene encoding a cyclin a gene for neural crest migration

an infant has severe constipation because one segment of the colon lacks the nerve cells normally found in its wall. failed migration of which embryonic cells best explains this? neural crest cells endoderm cells somite cells trophoblast cells
if the anterior (head) end of the neural tube fails to close, which condition results? anencephaly spina bifida hydrocephalus cleft palate
a zygote completes four rounds of cleavage with no growth. compared with the zygote, about what volume does each cell have? 1/16 1/4 1/8 1/32

why does most of the blood leaving the fetal right ventricle bypass the lungs through the ductus arteriosus? fluid filled fetal lungs have very high vascular resistance fetal lungs exchange gases faster than the placenta the pulmonary artery is not connected until birth fetal blood is too rich in o2 to enter the lungs

when the dorsal lip of the blastopore from one amphibian embryo is grafted onto the belly side of another, a second body axis forms, built mostly from host cells. what does this show? the graft induced nearby host cells to change their fate the graft's own cells divided to build the second axis host belly cells were already determined to form an axis the graft fused with host cells to form hybrid cells

an ovarian tumor contains hair, teeth and gut like epithelium, which represent all three germ layers. from which kind of cell did it most likely arise? a pluripotent germ cell a unipotent skin stem cell a differentiated smooth muscle cell a trophoblast cell of the placenta

in somatic cell nuclear transfer, a nucleus from an adult sheep's udder cell was placed into an egg whose own nucleus had been removed, and a whole lamb developed. what does this show about differentiated cells? their nuclei still hold the genes needed for a whole body differentiation is caused by a permanent loss of many genes udder cells are totipotent while inside the adult body only dna from an egg nucleus can direct development

a patient receives a transplant of hematopoietic stem cells. which cells can these donor stem cells normally replace? red cells, white cells and platelets blood cells as well as neurons and liver cells red blood cells only, but not white cells lymphocytes only, but not red blood cells

a premature newborn has a patent (still open) ductus arteriosus. prostaglandin e2 normally keeps the ductus open before birth. indomethacin, an nsaid, inhibits cyclooxygenase. why can indomethacin help close the ductus? it blocks prostaglandin synthesis, letting the ductus constrict it raises prostaglandin levels so the ductus constricts it lowers blood o2 so the ductus muscle contracts it reopens the foramen ovale to divert the blood

sickle cell disease is caused by a mutation in the β globin gene. affected infants usually have few symptoms until about 6 months of age. what best explains this delay? fetal hemoglobin (α2γ2), which lacks β chains, still dominates antibodies from the mother destroy sickled red cells until then the β globin gene acquires its mutation only after birth newborn red cells contain no hemoglobin for six months
after passing through the corona radiata, a sperm must cross which glycoprotein layer to reach the egg's plasma membrane? the zona pellucida the trophoblast layer the endometrium the amnion
which part of the blastocyst gives rise to the chorion, the embryo's contribution to the placenta? the trophoblast the inner cell mass the blastocoel the zona pellucida
the epithelial lining of the lungs' airways and alveoli develops from which germ layer? endoderm ectoderm mesoderm neural crest

in adult humans, remnants of the embryonic notochord persist as: the nucleus pulposus of the intervertebral discs the spinal cord running through the vertebral canal the bony bodies of the vertebrae the dorsal root ganglia beside the cord

right after one sperm fuses with the egg, the egg releases the contents of its cortical granules. what does this accomplish? it changes the zona so no other sperm can bind it sets off the sperm's acrosome reaction it starts the embryo's implantation in the uterus it supplies the zygote with stored nutrients

early frog embryos divide every 30 minutes, much faster than adult cells. what mainly allows this? they skip g1 and g2 and use stores in the egg they skip s phase and divide without copying dna their cells grow much faster between divisions their chromosomes are much shorter than adult ones

a pregnant woman is expected to deliver at 30 weeks, and her doctors give her a corticosteroid injection. what is the main purpose? to speed maturation of the fetal lungs and surfactant to close the fetal ductus arteriosus well before birth to suppress the fetus's developing immune system to raise the fetus's level of fetal hemoglobin

a human blastocyst reaches the uterus but cannot 'hatch' out of its zona pellucida. what is the most likely outcome? it cannot implant in the endometrium it implants in the fallopian tube instead it splits to form identical twins it develops into a fetus without a placenta

inner cell mass cells from a black furred mouse embryo are injected into the blastocyst of a white furred mouse. the pup that is born has patches of black and white fur, and black strain cells are found in many organs. what does this show? the injected cells were pluripotent and joined the host embryo the injected cells could only become pigment cells the host embryo's cells were all killed and replaced fur color is determined by the mother's uterus

an xy individual has testes that make testosterone and anti mullerian hormone (amh) normally, but androgen receptors that don't work. which anatomy is expected? female external genitalia, internal testes and no uterus male external genitalia with a uterus and tubes female external genitalia with ovaries and a uterus male external genitalia with internal ovaries

female fruit flies homozygous for a bicoid mutation produce embryos with no head structures, even when those embryos receive a normal bicoid allele from their father. why? bicoid mrna is placed in the egg by the mother the father's bicoid allele is always silenced the bicoid gene is located on the y chromosome bicoid protein acts only after the larva hatches

according to gate control theory, rubbing an injured area reduces pain because: touch signals activate spinal circuits that 'close the gate' on pain pain signals 'open the gate' so that touch signals cannot get through rubbing depletes pain receptors so they stop sending signals rubbing releases histamine that numbs the damaged tissue
kinesthesia (proprioception) is the sense of: body position and movement balance and head rotation internal organ states skin pressure and vibration

a patient with damage to the dorsal (where/how) visual pathway can name objects but can't reach for them accurately. what does this suggest? object identification and spatial guidance use separate pathways the ventral pathway, not the dorsal one, guides reaching movements damage to either pathway impairs naming and reaching equally reaching depends on the motor cortex, not on visual pathways

the muller lyer illusion makes two equal lines look different in length. researchers found the illusion is stronger in people raised in 'carpentered' environments with many right angles. what does this support? perception is shaped partly by experience and culture perception of length is innate and the same across cultures people in carpentered settings have more accurate depth vision the illusion arises from differences in retinal structure
in the signal detection table, what belongs in the cell marked ? false alarm hit miss correct rejection
the graph shows just noticeable differences for weights. what is the weber fraction? 0.02 (2%) 0.2 (20%) 2 g for every weight 50

when you look directly at a word on a page, its image falls on the fovea. why is vision sharpest there? it is densely packed with cones that resolve fine detail it has the highest density of rods in the retina it is where the optic nerve exits the eye it contains the most hair cells of any region

each eye has a 'blind spot' where no image is detected. why? the optic nerve leaves there, so it has no photoreceptors the retina there contains only rods and no cones at all the lens cannot focus light onto that region ganglion cells there absorb all incoming light

which vestibular structures detect linear acceleration and head tilt relative to gravity, as when an elevator starts to rise? the utricle and saccule (otolith organs) the semicircular canals the cochlea and basilar membrane the ossicles of the middle ear

a 100 hz tone makes auditory nerve fibers fire about 100 times per second, matching the sound wave. this observation supports which theory of pitch? frequency theory place theory opponent process theory gate control theory

hubel and wiesel recorded from single neurons in the visual cortex of cats and found cells that fired strongly only to a bar of light at a particular angle. these cells are called: feature detectors mirror neurons photoreceptors ganglion cells

looking out the side window of a moving train, a passenger sees nearby fence posts race past while distant mountains seem to drift slowly. this depth cue is: motion parallax retinal disparity convergence linear perspective

in what order does a visual signal pass through the cells of the retina on its way to the brain? photoreceptors → bipolar cells → ganglion cells ganglion cells → bipolar cells → photoreceptors bipolar cells → photoreceptors → ganglion cells photoreceptors → ganglion cells → bipolar cells
on a slide, 12 dots are arranged in three tight clusters of four, and viewers report seeing 'three groups.' which gestalt principle explains this? proximity similarity closure continuity

in the organ of corti, how is sound energy transduced into neural signals? hair cell stereocilia bend, opening ion channels the ossicles fire action potentials toward the brainstem fluid in the semicircular canals stimulates the rods the eardrum releases neurotransmitter onto nerve fibers

a radiologist worried about unnecessary biopsies reports a tumor only when a shadow on a scan is very clear. compared with a colleague who reports any suspicious shadow, she will likely have: fewer false alarms but more misses more hits and more false alarms fewer misses and fewer false alarms greater sensitivity (d′) for real tumors

a patient's hearing returns to normal after a doctor removes impacted earwax. before treatment, the patient had which type of hearing loss? conductive hearing loss sensorineural hearing loss central auditory processing loss noise induced hair cell loss
a row of lights on a theater sign flashes on and off in sequence, and viewers see a single light moving along the row. this is the: phi phenomenon autokinetic effect motion parallax ponzo illusion

viewing a drawing that can be seen either as a white vase or as two dark faces in profile, a student finds her perception flipping back and forth. this drawing mainly demonstrates: figure ground organization sensory adaptation shape constancy bottom up feature detection

a patient with a stuffy nose from a cold says her coffee 'tastes like nothing,' although she can still tell it is bitter. why? much of flavor comes from smell, which is now blocked taste buds stop working whenever the nose is blocked bitterness is detected only by olfactory receptors the cold virus has destroyed her taste receptor cells

during a neurological exam, a doctor tests whether a patient can feel a vibrating tuning fork pressed against the ankle bone. which receptors mainly detect this high frequency vibration? pacinian corpuscles free nerve endings merkel discs golgi tendon organs

a white shirt still looks white to you under the yellowish light of an indoor lamp, even though it reflects more yellow light there than outdoors. this is: color constancy shape constancy an opponent process afterimage sensory adaptation of rods

after a training course, radiology residents detect more true fractures and make fewer false alarms than before. in signal detection terms, the training most likely: increased their sensitivity (d′) made their response criterion more liberal made their response criterion more conservative raised their absolute threshold for detection

older adults usually lose hearing for high pitched sounds first. based on place theory, where in the cochlea is the damage most likely? hair cells near the base, close to the oval window hair cells near the apex, far from the oval window hair cells of the semicircular canals the ossicles, which stiffen with age

hubel and wiesel kept one eye of newborn kittens closed for the first few months. when it was reopened, few visual cortex neurons responded to that eye, and the kittens behaved as if blind in it. closing one eye in adult cats had little effect. this shows that: visual development depends on input during a critical period the retina of the closed eye was permanently destroyed visual cortex connections are fixed at birth regardless of input depth perception is learned through reinforcement

after carbon monoxide poisoning damaged her ventral visual stream, patient d.f. could not say whether a slot was vertical or horizontal, yet she rotated a card correctly to post it through the slot. what does this show? vision for action can work without conscious object perception her dorsal stream was destroyed while her ventral stream survived she had lost all input to her primary visual cortex her deficit was in moving her hands, not in vision

in gibson and walk's visual cliff studies, most crawling infants (about 6 14 months old) would not cross onto the glass over the 'deep' side, even when their mothers called. why can't this result alone prove that depth perception is innate? the infants had months of visual experience before testing the infants could feel the glass, so vision was irrelevant the mothers' calls made the infants too anxious to move too few infants were tested to support any conclusion

in a hearing study using identical faint tones, group 1 earns $1 for every hit, while group 2 loses $1 for every false alarm. group 1 has a 90% hit rate and 40% false alarm rate; group 2 has 60% and 10%. which conclusion is best supported? the payoffs shifted the response criterion, not hearing sensitivity group 1 has better hearing sensitivity than group 2 does group 2 has a lower absolute threshold for tones than group 1 the money changed how loud the tones physically were

a patient with a growing pituitary tumor keeps bumping into door frames on both sides, though his central vision is clear. the tumor presses upward on the middle of the optic chiasm. which visual field loss is expected? loss of the outer (temporal) half of each eye's visual field complete blindness in one eye, while the other eye stays normal loss of the left half of the visual field in both eyes loss of the inner (nasal) half of each eye's visual field
receptors that respond to potentially damaging stimuli, such as intense heat or a cut, and send pain signals are called: nociceptors photoreceptors proprioceptors pacinian corpuscles
which basic taste responds to glutamate, as found in broth, aged cheese and soy sauce? umami (savory) sour (acidic) bitter (alkaloid) salty (sodium)
the hue of a light, whether it looks red, green or blue, depends mainly on the light's: wavelength amplitude intensity duration of exposure
a stimulus that is too weak to be consciously detected is described as: subliminal supraliminal habituated transduced

reading in the back seat of a moving car, a passenger becomes nauseated. how does sensory conflict theory explain this? the eyes signal stillness while the inner ear senses motion engine noise overstimulates the cochlea's hair cells the eyes adapt to the page and stop sending signals leg proprioceptors detect vibration from the road

when you watch a red ball roll across a table, separate brain areas analyze its color, motion and shape at the same time. this is called: parallel processing serial processing top down processing sensory adaptation

a car horn sounds to your left. it reaches your left ear slightly earlier and slightly louder than your right ear. the brain uses these differences mainly to: locate where the sound is coming from determine the pitch of the sound judge how loud the horn actually is filter the horn out as background noise

when you shift your gaze from a distant mountain to a book in your hands, the ciliary muscles contract and the lens becomes rounder. this process is called: accommodation convergence dark adaptation transduction

a screen shows a grid of evenly spaced dots. every other column is red and the rest are blue, and viewers report seeing vertical columns rather than rows. which gestalt principle explains this? similarity proximity closure common fate

in a photo of a long, straight railroad, the two rails seem to come together near the horizon, which makes the far part of the track look distant. which depth cue is this? linear perspective retinal disparity binocular convergence motion parallax

a stroke damages a patient's right optic tract, which lies behind the optic chiasm. which visual loss is expected? the left visual field of both eyes the right visual field of both eyes all vision in the right eye only the outer half of each eye's visual field

a patient whose cochlear hair cells were destroyed by a toxic antibiotic receives a cochlear implant. the device restores some hearing because it: stimulates the auditory nerve directly with electrodes amplifies sound so the remaining hair cells respond replaces the small bones of the middle ear sends sound vibrations through the skull bones
the table shows one listener's responses in a hearing test with 50 tone present and 50 tone absent trials. what is the listener's false alarm rate? 30% 15% 27% 70%

the table shows hypothetical two point thresholds for one volunteer: the smallest distance at which two touching points feel like two separate points rather than one. which region most likely has the densest touch receptors with the smallest receptive fields? fingertip back forearm palm of hand

a man lacks working medium wavelength ('green') cones and confuses reds with greens, yet his vision is otherwise normal. which theory does his condition most directly support? trichromatic theory opponent process theory place theory gate control theory

as you slowly bring your finger toward your nose, you feel your eyes turning inward. the brain uses signals from these eye muscles to judge distance. which depth cue is this? convergence accommodation relative size interposition

participants are shown an ambiguous drawing that can be seen either as a rat or as a man's face. those who first viewed pictures of animals usually see a rat; those who first viewed human faces usually see a man. this shows the effect of: perceptual set sensory adaptation feature detection retinal disparity

after a rare illness destroyed the sensory nerves that report limb position, a man could move his arms and legs smoothly only while watching them; in the dark, his movements fell apart. which sense had he lost? proprioception (kinesthesia) vestibular sense (balance) nociception (pain) somatic motor control

in a lab, a faint light is flashed at different intensities, and the graph shows the percentage of trials on which a volunteer reported seeing it. what is the volunteer's absolute threshold? about 4 units about 2 units, where detection begins to rise about 6 units, where detection nears 100% about 8 units, the strongest stimulus tested

the graph shows a typical dark adaptation curve: the dimmest light a person can detect, measured over time after entering a dark room (lower values mean greater sensitivity). what happens at the kink labeled b, at about 8 minutes? rods become more sensitive than cones and take over cones become more sensitive than rods and take over the pupil stops dilating and sensitivity stops changing the fovea begins to detect light for the first time

in the ponzo illusion, two identical bars are drawn between two lines that converge like railroad tracks (as shown), and bar 1, nearer the point where the lines meet, looks longer. which explanation is most widely accepted? depth cues make it look farther, so size constancy enlarges it bar 1 actually casts a larger image on the retina feature detectors fire more to bars near converging lines sensory adaptation shrinks bar 2 after a few seconds

recordings show that touch receptors under a ring on a finger fire less and less within seconds of steady pressure. in another study, a toddler stops turning toward a repeated harmless sound, even though her auditory nerve still fires to every sound. what best describes these two cases? the first is sensory adaptation; the second is habituation both are habituation, a learned drop in attention the first is habituation; the second is sensory adaptation both are sensory adaptation in the receptors themselves

in the 1890s, george stratton wore lenses that turned his visual world upside down. at first he was clumsy and disoriented, but after several days he could move around fairly normally, and on removing the lenses he was briefly disoriented again. what does this show? the brain can adapt perception to a changed visual input the retina flipped its image back over within hours perception is fixed at birth and cannot be changed depth perception depends only on the vestibular sense

a radiologist and an ai tool each read the same 1000 mammograms; the table shows their hit and false alarm rates. the tool's developer says it is 'clearly better at detecting cancer because it catches more cancers.' which response best applies signal detection theory? its higher hit rate came with many more false alarms it must be more sensitive, since its hit rate is higher the radiologist has the more liberal response criterion their criteria can't differ, since they read the same scans

researchers studied older children and teenagers in india who were born blind from treatable cataracts and had them surgically removed. right after surgery, they could identify shapes by touch and by sight, but they could not tell which seen shape matched one they had only touched. within about a week, their matching improved greatly. what do these findings suggest? linking touch and vision needs visual experience but is learned quickly touch and vision are fully linked at birth without any experience the surgery damaged the visual cortex for several weeks after the critical period, no new visual learning is possible

loud music and high pitched hearing the musicians' pattern of hearing loss most likely reflects damage to which structures? hair cells in the cochlea bones of the middle ear the tympanic membrane the primary auditory cortex
loud music and high pitched hearing according to figure 1, at which frequency do the two groups differ the most? 4 khz 8 khz 6 khz 0.5 khz

loud music and high pitched hearing which is the strongest reason this study cannot show that playing in bands caused the musicians' hearing loss? participants chose their own groups, so the groups may differ in other ways the thresholds were measured in decibels instead of in watts the sample included only adults between 20 and 30 years of age, not older adults every participant heard the same set of pure tone frequencies

loud music and high pitched hearing why might the musicians struggle with speech in background babble even though their thresholds at 0.5 2 khz are normal? high frequency consonant sounds that help tell words apart are harder to hear low pitched vowel sounds can no longer reach their auditory cortex at all their middle ear bones vibrate too slowly to carry words to the cochlea background talking causes sensory adaptation only in damaged ears
loud music and high pitched hearing based on paragraph 4 and figure 1, what was the mean 4 khz threshold of the 20 musicians who rarely wore earplugs? 36 db hl 28 db hl 20 db hl 40 db hl

in the liberal–soft block, the payoff rules most likely changed participants': absolute threshold for the 1,000-hz tone response criterion, making them more willing to answer "yes" sensitivity to the tone relative to the background noise sensory adaptation to the continuous white noise

which result in figure 1 best indicates that the louder tone increased sensitivity rather than changing response bias? the hit rate rose from 60% to 80% while the false-alarm rate stayed at 20%. the hit rate in the neutral–loud block equaled the hit rate in the liberal–soft block. the false-alarm rate in the neutral–loud block was lower than in the liberal–soft block. the hit rate was higher than the false-alarm rate in every block.

what was the main purpose of counterbalancing the order of the three blocks? to ensure that participants could not tell which block was which to make the sample representative of adults with normal hearing to keep practice and fatigue effects from being confounded with block type to equalize the number of tone and no-tone trials within each block

based on figure 1, which of the following differences are most likely meaningful? i. the false-alarm rate in the liberal–soft block vs the neutral–soft block ii. the hit rate in the liberal–soft block vs the neutral–loud block iii. the hit rate in the neutral–soft block vs the neutral–loud block ii only i and ii only i and iii only i, ii and iii

a radiologist is told that missing a tumor will lead to a lawsuit, while an unnecessary follow-up scan has no cost to her. based on the passage, she is most likely to show: fewer hits and fewer false alarms more hits and fewer false alarms more hits and more false alarms no change in hits or false alarms

compared with the high-prevalence condition, the low-prevalence condition mainly changed screeners': sensitivity, making knives harder to perceive response criterion, making them more conservative response criterion, making them more liberal sensitivity, making knives easier to perceive

which conclusions are supported by table 1? i. the payoff manipulation shifted the criterion without meaningfully changing sensitivity. ii. low prevalence reduced screeners' perceptual ability to detect knives. iii. screeners in the low-prevalence condition missed a larger proportion of knives than screeners in the high-prevalence condition. i only ii only i and iii only ii and iii only

a critic notes that hit rates in the low-prevalence condition are less trustworthy than those in the high-prevalence condition. which statement best supports this criticism? screeners in the low-prevalence condition saw fewer total images. each low-prevalence hit rate was based on only 30 target trials, so it is estimated less precisely. low-prevalence screeners were not randomly assigned to their condition. false-alarm rates cannot be calculated when targets are rare.

the finding that expectations about how often knives appear changed screeners' decisions is best described as an example of: top-down processing sensory adaptation weber's law bottom-up feature detection

if airports adopted the researchers' proposal to insert artificial threat images, raising the effective target prevalence, signal detection theory predicts that screeners would show: more hits and fewer false alarms, because d′ would increase fewer hits and fewer false alarms, because c would increase more hits and more false alarms, because c would decrease no change in hits, because prevalence affects only reaction time

a participant can just barely tell the difference between a 200-g weight and a 204-g weight. according to weber's law, what is the smallest difference she should be able to detect from a 500-g weight? 4 g 8 g 10 g 20 g
which of the following are monocular depth cues? i. convergence ii. relative size iii. linear perspective i only i and ii only ii and iii only i, ii and iii

a participant can just detect the difference between a 100-g weight and a 104-g weight. according to weber’s law, about how heavy must a comparison weight be for her to just detect a difference from a 500-g weight? 504 g 510 g 520 g 540 g

two radiologists each read the same 100 mammograms, 50 with a tumor and 50 without (table). which statement best describes their performance? reader 2 is better at telling tumors from normal tissue because reader 2 has fewer false alarms. reader 1 is better at telling tumors from normal tissue because reader 1 has more hits. reader 1 says “tumor” more readily than reader 2, producing more hits and more false alarms. reader 1 uses a stricter response criterion than reader 2.

a hospital tells its radiologists that missing a cancer is far more costly than ordering an unnecessary biopsy. if their ability to discriminate tumors from normal tissue does not change, which outcome is expected? both hit rate and false-alarm rate decrease. hit rate increases and false-alarm rate decreases. hit rate stays the same and false-alarm rate increases. both hit rate and false-alarm rate increase.

an amateur astronomer notices that a faint star is easier to see when she looks slightly to one side of it than when she looks straight at it. which explanation is best? looking to the side widens the pupil, letting in more light. cones, which are more sensitive in dim light, are concentrated in the peripheral retina. the fovea contains the optic disc, which has no photoreceptors. rods, which are more sensitive in dim light, are concentrated in the peripheral retina rather than the fovea.

a pituitary tumor presses upward on the middle of the optic chiasm. which visual deficit is most likely? loss of central vision only, in both eyes complete blindness in one eye loss of the right half of the visual field in both eyes loss of the outer (temporal) half of the visual field in both eyes

after damage to a small region of visual cortex, a patient identifies colors and shapes normally but sees moving cars as a series of still snapshots. this case best supports the idea that the visual system: analyzes features such as motion, color and form in parallel, partly separate pathways processes all visual features in a single serial stream relies on top-down expectations to detect motion detects motion only through the retina’s rods

a slide shows 12 identical dots arranged as three tight clusters of four, with wide gaps between the clusters. viewers report seeing “three groups.” which gestalt principle best explains this? similarity proximity closure continuity

a student easily reads a handwritten note even though one letter in the word “hospital” is a smudge. which process does this best illustrate? feature detection bottom-up processing sensory adaptation top-down processing

an audiologist finds that a factory worker has lost hair cells near the base of the cochlea, close to the oval window. which difficulty is the worker most likely to report? hearing high-pitched sounds, such as a whistle or some consonants hearing low-pitched sounds, such as a bass drum keeping his balance when turning his head hearing sounds of every pitch equally poorly

a patient feels dizzy only when she spins in a chair, not when she rides an elevator that speeds up and slows down. which structure is most likely affected? semicircular canals utricle and saccule cochlea proprioceptors in skeletal muscle

to find the absolute threshold for a faint tone, a researcher presents a tone on every trial and asks, “did you hear it?” the threshold is defined as the intensity detected on 50% of trials. which change would best reduce the effect of response bias on this measure? increase the loudness of every tone include catch trials with no tone so that false alarms can be measured tell participants that a tone is present on every trial test only participants who are trained musicians

in a visual cliff study, 9-month-old infants who have been crawling for several weeks refuse to cross the “deep” side, but same-age infants who do not yet crawl show little wariness. a researcher concludes that crawling experience causes wariness of heights. which follow-up study would best test this causal claim? test the same crawling infants again at 12 months of age randomly assign pre-crawling infants to receive self-produced movement experience in a baby walker or no such experience, then test both groups compare infants whose parents fear heights with infants whose parents do not survey parents about the age at which their infants began to crawl

a researcher records action potential frequency from two touch receptors in a fingertip while constant pressure is applied from 1 s to 5 s (figure). which interpretation is best supported? both receptors stop firing within 1 s of pressure onset, showing complete adaptation. receptor y is rapidly adapting, because its firing falls steadily during the pressure. receptor x is rapidly adapting and signals changes in pressure, whereas receptor y is slowly adapting and signals sustained pressure. receptor x fires only when pressure is removed, so it detects the absence of touch.

after bumping her elbow, a child rubs the spot and says it hurts less. which theory best explains this effect? gate control theory: touch fibers activate spinal interneurons that inhibit pain transmission opponent-process theory: pain neurons are inhibited by color-opponent cells place theory: rubbing shifts pain signals to a different region of the cortex weber’s law: rubbing makes the pain intensity harder to discriminate

a painter wants a flat canvas to look deep, using cues that work even for a viewer with one eye closed. which cues could she use? i. making distant trees smaller than near ones ii. convergence of the eyes iii. drawing parallel road edges that meet at the horizon i only ii only i and iii only i, ii and iii

name: Learning & memory
t: participants study a 20 word list. when recall is tested after a 30 second distraction task, which effect is most likely to disappear? the primacy effect the recency effect both effects neither effect
after switching to a new phone, a patient keeps typing her new passcode when she tries to recall her old one. this is: proactive interference retroactive interference source monitoring error decay

a patient feels nauseated every time she smells the hospital where she received chemotherapy. in classical conditioning terms, the hospital smell is the: unconditioned stimulus unconditioned response conditioned stimulus conditioned response

a man takes ibuprofen because it makes his headache go away, and he becomes more likely to take ibuprofen in the future. this is: positive reinforcement negative reinforcement positive punishment negative punishment
which reinforcement schedule produces behavior that is most resistant to extinction? fixed ratio fixed interval variable ratio continuous
a child receives praise immediately after completing homework and then studies more often. this illustrates: negative punishment positive reinforcement habituation extinction
which memory system briefly retains a small set of information being actively manipulated? procedural memory only working memory long term episodic storage only sensory adaptation
habituation is: a decreased response to a repeated, harmless stimulus an increased response after a painful stimulus learning by watching others learning through rewards
learning by watching others is called: observational learning classical conditioning habituation insight learning
the memory system with an almost unlimited capacity is: long term memory sensory memory short term memory working memory
memory for facts and events that can be consciously recalled is: explicit (declarative) memory implicit memory procedural memory priming
knowing how to ride a bike is an example of: procedural (implicit) memory episodic memory semantic memory flashbulb memory

in classical conditioning, extinction occurs when: the conditioned stimulus is repeatedly presented without the unconditioned stimulus a previously weakened conditioned response reappears after a rest period the conditioned response spreads to stimuli similar to the conditioned stimulus the conditioned stimulus is paired with a new, stronger unconditioned stimulus
after extinction, a conditioned response suddenly returns following a rest period. this is: spontaneous recovery generalization discrimination acquisition
a child bitten by one dog becomes afraid of all dogs. this is: stimulus generalization stimulus discrimination extinction spontaneous recovery

positive punishment is best illustrated by: getting a speeding ticket after driving too fast losing phone privileges for breaking curfew receiving praise for good work taking aspirin to remove a headache

shaping is: reinforcing successive approximations of a desired behavior reinforcing a behavior only after a fixed number of responses pairing a neutral stimulus with one that triggers a reflex learning a behavior by observing and imitating a model

organizing information into meaningful groups (for example, remembering 1 800 555 0199 in chunks) improves: the effective capacity of short term memory the duration of visual sensory (iconic) memory procedural memory for motor skills implicit memory through priming
a student remembers material best when tested in the same room where they studied. this shows: context dependent memory state dependent memory only retroactive interference the serial position effect
a patient can't form new long term memories after surgery but remembers childhood well. this is: anterograde amnesia retrograde amnesia infantile amnesia source amnesia
studying a little each day over two weeks leads to better retention than cramming the night before. this is the: spacing effect serial position effect misinformation effect primacy effect

people remember more words when they think about each word's meaning than when they count its letters. this supports: levels of processing: deeper, semantic encoding aids recall decay theory: unused memory traces fade over time encoding specificity: matching study and test contexts aids retrieval chunking: grouping items expands short term capacity

long term potentiation (ltp) is thought to underlie learning because it: strengthens synapses that are repeatedly activated together weakens synapses that are rarely activated together increases the number of neurons in the hippocampus speeds signal conduction by adding myelin to the most active axons

eyewitnesses who heard the word 'smashed' estimated higher car speeds than those who heard 'hit'. this illustrates: the misinformation effect proactive interference state dependent memory flashbulb memory

a dog salivates to a bell, but not to a buzzer, after learning that only the bell predicts food. later the dog salivates to a light that was repeatedly paired with the bell (never with food). which phenomenon explains the light? second order (higher order) conditioning stimulus generalization to similar cues spontaneous recovery of the response stimulus discrimination between cues

the graph shows recall by list position right after studying. why are the first words recalled well? they were rehearsed more and reached long term memory they were still in sensory memory they were most recently heard they were shown in a larger font

if recall were tested after a 30 second distraction task, which part of the curve would change most? the right end (recency effect) would drop the left end (primacy effect) would drop the middle would rise sharply the whole curve would rise

the forgetting curve shown is typical for newly learned material. when is the most information lost? in the first hour or so after learning after about one week after about one month forgetting is steady over time

in the classical conditioning graph, the response returns partway (the segment labeled ?) after a rest period following extinction. what is this called? spontaneous recovery stimulus generalization second order conditioning habituation

the graph shows cumulative responses under two reinforcement schedules. schedule 2 shows a 'scallop' pattern, with responding speeding up just before each reward every 10 minutes. which schedule is schedule 2? fixed interval variable ratio variable interval continuous reinforcement

thorndike placed hungry cats in puzzle boxes and found that actions that led to escape and food became more frequent over trials. he summarized this as the: law of effect premack principle yerkes dodson law weber's law

a friend asks you a question while you are reading. a second after saying 'what?', you realize you can still 'hear' her words and answer. which memory store held the sound briefly? echoic memory iconic memory procedural memory semantic memory
remembering the details of your own high school graduation ceremony is an example of: episodic memory semantic memory procedural memory implicit priming

a medical student who learned spanish in high school is now studying italian. she keeps recalling spanish words when she tries to remember new italian vocabulary. this is: proactive interference retroactive interference anterograde amnesia decay of sensory memory

in sperling's experiments, a 3 × 4 grid of letters flashed for a fraction of a second. participants could report only about 4 or 5 letters in total, but when a tone right after the flash signaled which row to report, they could report most letters in any row. this shows that iconic memory: briefly holds most of the display but fades within a second holds only about four items, like short term memory lasts several minutes if attention is paid to it stores the letters by their sound rather than by their appearance

rats explored a maze for days with no food reward and showed little improvement. once food was placed in the goal box, they quickly ran the maze as well as rats that had been rewarded all along. tolman called this: latent learning shaping spontaneous recovery instinctive drift

an infant stops looking at a picture of a red circle after seeing it many times, but looks for a long time again when a blue square appears. the renewed looking is called: dishabituation sensitization spontaneous recovery stimulus generalization
a factory worker is paid $5 for every 10 garments she finishes. which reinforcement schedule is this? fixed ratio fixed interval variable ratio variable interval

after living through an earthquake, a woman now startles strongly at minor noises, such as a door closing, that never bothered her before. this is: sensitization habituation extinction latent learning
a teenager comes home after curfew, so his parents take away his car keys for a week, and he stops coming home late. this is: negative punishment negative reinforcement positive punishment extinction

a patient with migraines learns that taking medication at the first sign of a visual aura prevents the headache from developing at all. her medication taking is best described as: avoidance learning escape learning positive reinforcement positive punishment

a student who drank coffee while studying recalls more on the exam when she has also had coffee beforehand. this best illustrates: state dependent memory context dependent memory proactive interference the spacing effect

two groups study a science passage for the same total time. group 1 rereads it three times; group 2 reads it once and then takes two practice recall tests. a week later, group 2 remembers more. this illustrates: the testing effect (retrieval practice) the spacing effect (distributed study) the serial position effect the misinformation effect

in watson and rayner's 'little albert' study, a steel bar was struck loudly behind an infant whenever he reached for a white rat. before any pairing, the infant's crying at the loud noise was the: unconditioned response conditioned response unconditioned stimulus conditioned stimulus

children watched a film of an adult hitting a bobo doll. in one version the adult was punished, and those children later imitated less aggression. when all children were then offered treats for copying the adult, the differences between groups largely disappeared. what does this show? children learned the behavior even when they did not perform it punishing the model kept the children from learning anything imitation requires direct reinforcement of the child's own acts observational learning occurs only for nonaggressive acts

participants hear a list: bed, rest, awake, tired, dream, snooze, blanket. many later confidently 'remember' hearing the word sleep, which was never presented. this finding shows that: memory is reconstructive, so related ideas can create false memories sleep related words are processed more deeply than other words are participants were simply guessing with low confidence the list was too long for short term memory capacity

dogs that first received shocks they could not escape later failed to jump a low barrier to escape shocks, even though escape was easy. dogs that had received the same shocks but could stop them by pressing a panel learned to escape quickly. which conclusion is best supported? learning that outcomes are uncontrollable can suppress later coping inescapable shock damaged the dogs' ability to move any exposure to shock at all makes later escape learning much slower the dogs had habituated to shock and no longer felt it

after a concussion, a football player cannot remember the 30 minutes before the hit, but his memories from the previous week and from childhood are intact. what does this pattern suggest? his most recent memories had not yet been fully consolidated he has anterograde amnesia from hippocampal removal his older memories are held in sensory memory his older memories are held in short term memory

patient h.m. had much of the medial temporal lobe on both sides removed to treat seizures, including the front portions of both hippocampi and the amygdalae. over several days he practiced tracing a star while seeing it only in a mirror. his accuracy improved steadily, yet each day he said he had never done the task before. which conclusion is best supported? procedural learning does not depend on the hippocampus his hippocampus was required for learning the motor skill his surgery mainly caused retrograde amnesia for childhood he was faking his memory loss to avoid further testing

rats drank sweet water while each lick also triggered a flash of light and a click. then one group was made ill by x ray exposure, and another received foot shocks. later, the ill rats avoided the sweet taste but not the light and click, while the shocked rats avoided the light and click but not the taste. what does this show? animals are biologically prepared to link certain cues to certain outcomes any stimulus can be paired equally well with any consequence at all taste aversions need many separate pairings before they appear rats cannot detect lights and sounds while they are drinking
in 1956, george miller proposed that short term memory holds about how many items (or chunks) at once? 7 ± 2 2 ± 1 20 ± 5 an unlimited number
which of the following is a primary reinforcer? water for a thirsty animal a gold star on a sticker chart a paycheck for work praise from a teacher

wolfgang kohler's chimpanzee sultan failed to reach bananas outside his cage with one short stick. after a pause, he suddenly fitted two sticks together and raked the bananas in. this is an example of: insight learning latent learning shaping classical conditioning
a multiple choice exam asks students to pick the correct term from four choices. which kind of memory retrieval does it mainly test? recognition free recall cued recall relearning

in a conditioning study, a tone is played just after food is given rather than before it. after many such pairings, dogs salivate very little to the tone. why? the tone never predicted the food, so it signaled nothing backward pairings produce stronger conditioning than forward the food became a conditioned stimulus for the tone dogs cannot learn associations between sounds and food

on a psychiatric unit, patients earn plastic tokens for making their beds and attending group sessions, then trade the tokens for snacks or extra tv time. the tokens act as: secondary (conditioned) reinforcers primary (unlearned) reinforcers negative reinforcers unconditioned stimuli

to learn the term 'osteoclast,' one student repeats it 20 times. another notes that ' clast' means 'break' and pictures cells chewing through bone. why will the second student probably remember the term better? elaborative rehearsal links new items to meaning repetition keeps items in sensory memory longer repeating a word 20 times overloads working memory visual images are stored only as procedural memory

a pharmacist knows a drug's name starts with 'm' and has three syllables, but she can't come up with it until it pops into her head an hour later. this experience shows: a retrieval failure, not loss of the memory decay of the memory trace over time a failure to encode the name in the first place anterograde amnesia for recently learned names

a student keeps checking her email for a reply from an admissions office. replies arrive at unpredictable times, and checking is rewarded only once a reply has come in. which reinforcement schedule is this? variable interval variable ratio fixed interval continuous reinforcement

a patient vividly remembers her doctor warning her about a drug's side effect, but she actually read the warning in a pamphlet in the waiting room. this error is best described as: a source monitoring error retroactive interference anterograde amnesia a flashbulb memory error

in a hypothetical memory study modeled on ebbinghaus's method, a participant needs the numbers of trials shown to recite a list perfectly. a week later she can't recall any of the list. what is her savings score? 60% 40% 8% 250%

patients with severe anterograde amnesia study a list that includes the word motel. later they can't recall the list, but when asked to complete 'mot___' with the first word that comes to mind, they often write motel. this shows that: priming, a form of implicit memory, is intact their explicit memory for the list is intact they are faking their memory loss on purpose procedural memory has replaced semantic memory

to memorize the 12 cranial nerves, a student imagines walking through her house and placing one nerve in each room. during the exam, she mentally walks the same route. which strategy is she using? the method of loci the peg word method chunking maintenance rehearsal

participants who judged whether each trait word (like 'kind') described themselves later remembered more words than participants who judged whether each word described someone else or who judged its meaning. this is the: self reference effect serial position effect misinformation effect spacing effect

a man with years of heavy alcohol use and poor nutrition can't form new memories and confidently fills in memory gaps with made up stories. deficiency of which vitamin is the main cause of this syndrome? thiamine (vitamin b1) vitamin c vitamin d cobalamin (vitamin b12)

during a depressive episode, a patient mostly recalls failures and sad events from her past; when her mood improves, she recalls more happy events. this illustrates: mood congruent memory retrograde amnesia proactive interference the serial position effect

a first year medical student watches a skilled surgeon tie a complex suture on video many times. he pays close attention, remembers each step and wants to succeed, but still can't tie the knot himself. which of bandura's conditions for observational learning is missing? reproduction: the skill to do it attention to the model retention of what was observed motivation to perform it

the graph shows hypothetical lever pressing rates during extinction (no more rewards) for two groups of rats. during training, one group was rewarded for every press, and the other for an unpredictable one third of presses. which line most likely shows the partially reinforced group? line b, which declines slowly line a, which declines quickly neither; both groups would extinguish equally fast line a, since more rewards build more persistence

the table shows a design like leon kamin's blocking experiments in rats. both groups received identical phase 2 training, yet group 1 learned little fear of the tone. why? the light already predicted shock, so the tone added no information in group 1 the tone came too late after the shock to be learned group 1 had extinguished its fear before phase 2 rats cannot learn about two stimuli at the same time

participants verify 'a canary can sing' faster than 'a canary has skin.' according to collins and quillian's hierarchical network model of semantic memory, why? 'has skin' is stored at a more distant level (animal) 'has skin' is a false statement about canaries shorter sentences are always verified faster singing is stored in procedural memory instead

the day after the september 11, 2001 attacks, students wrote down how they heard the news and also an everyday event from the same time. over the following months, both memories became less consistent at about the same rate, but students stayed far more confident in their 9/11 memories. what is the best conclusion? emotional memories feel vivid but are not necessarily more accurate flashbulb memories are recorded permanently and exactly everyday memories decay while emotional memories never change confidence is a reliable sign that a memory is accurate

in 1924, jenkins and dallenbach tested recall of nonsense syllables after intervals spent either asleep or awake. the graph shows an illustrative version of the pattern they reported. which theory of forgetting does this pattern most directly support? interference from waking activity causes much forgetting memories decay at a fixed rate with the passage of time sleep blocks the encoding of new information forgetting happens only within the first hour

keller and marian breland trained a raccoon to drop coins into a box for food. over time, the raccoon instead began rubbing the coins together and dipping them in and out of the box, even though this delayed its food. what does this show? instinctive behaviors can intrude on operantly trained ones operant conditioning can train any behavior equally well the raccoon had learned the task through insight food stopped working as a reinforcer for the raccoon

rats learn to find a platform hidden just under the water in a pool by using cues around the room. the graph shows hypothetical escape times for control rats and rats given a drug that blocks nmda glutamate receptors in the hippocampus. in a separate test, drug treated rats found a clearly visible platform as fast as controls. what is the best conclusion? nmda blockade impairs spatial learning, not swimming or sight the drug impairs vision, so the rats can't see room cues the drug weakens the rats, so they swim more slowly nmda receptors are needed for every kind of movement

the table shows hypothetical results from a dual task study of working memory. participants hold a list of spoken digits in mind while doing a second task. which conclusion best fits baddeley's working memory model? verbal and spatial tasks use partly separate storage systems all tasks draw on a single short term store of 7 items spatial tapping harms verbal memory more than speaking repeating a word improves memory by adding rehearsal

quizzing versus rereading which statement best describes the results in figure 1? the better method depended on the delay before the final test rereading produced better recall than quizzing at both delays tested quizzing produced better recall at both delays tested recall declined by the same amount in both conditions

quizzing versus rereading from the 5 minute test to the 1 week test, about what fraction of their recall did the reread and quiz groups lose? about 55% for reread and 17% for quiz about 44% for reread and 12% for quiz about 45% for reread and 83% for quiz, respectively about 17% for reread and 55% for quiz
