quizzing versus rereading the drop in recall seen in the reread group is consistent with ebbinghaus's forgetting curve, which shows that: forgetting is fastest soon after learning and then slows down forgetting happens at a steady rate that never levels off memories are stable for a week and then fade quickly forgetting occurs only when new learning interferes

quizzing versus rereading why did the researchers have each student take only one final test instead of testing everyone at both 5 minutes and 1 week? an early test would itself act as retrieval practice for reread students testing twice would make the study take far too long for the student volunteers one test per student ensured that predicted recall was the same a single test removed the need for random assignment to delays

quizzing versus rereading which statement about the students' predictions is best supported by table 1? reread students greatly overestimated their recall; quiz students were nearly accurate quiz students greatly overestimated their recall; reread students were accurate both groups underestimated how much they would recall after one week both groups predicted their week later recall within two percentage points

the higher rate of misleading-detail answers after the misleading summary is best explained by which concept? source-monitoring error proactive interference memory decay over 48 hours state-dependent memory

which statement best describes the results in figure 1? the warning reduced misleading-detail answers equally in both summary conditions. the warning eliminated the effect of the misleading summary. the warning had a much larger effect after the misleading summary than after the neutral summary. the type of summary had no effect once participants were warned.

which change to the procedure would introduce a confound into the comparison between summary conditions? using a different video of a crime for both summary groups testing all participants after 1 week instead of 48 hours having the misleading summary also be twice as long as the neutral summary adding four more non-critical questions to the test for all participants

which conclusions are supported by the data? i. the warning eliminated the misinformation effect. ii. the warning reduced the misinformation effect. iii. some participants chose misleading details even after being warned that the summary contained errors. i only ii only i and iii only ii and iii only

what do the data in table 1 most strongly suggest about eyewitness testimony? a witness's confidence is a poor guide to whether a specific memory is accurate. misleading details are recalled with much lower confidence than true details. confident witnesses are rarely influenced by post-event information. confidence ratings measured the same thing as the warning manipulation.
in operant terms, the reset of the voucher value after a positive breath sample is best classified as: positive punishment negative reinforcement negative punishment extinction

which comparison at week 24 is best supported by figure 1? escalating vouchers produced clearly higher abstinence than standard care, but not clearly higher than fixed vouchers. escalating vouchers produced clearly higher abstinence than both other conditions. fixed vouchers produced clearly higher abstinence than standard care. all three conditions had statistically indistinguishable abstinence.

the drop in abstinence in both voucher conditions after week 12 is best explained by: spontaneous recovery of a conditioned response extinction after removal of the reinforcer habituation to the counseling sessions latent learning of smoking cues

which statements about the design of this study are correct? i. random assignment protects against group differences that arise after assignment, such as unequal dropout. ii. because dropouts were counted as smoking, reported abstinence rates are, if anything, underestimates. iii. verifying abstinence with breath co reduces bias that could come from self-report. i and ii only i and iii only ii and iii only i, ii and iii

the researchers want to apply these findings to smokers who have not sought help to quit. the main limitation is a threat to: internal validity, because the conditions were not randomly assigned construct validity, because breath co does not measure smoking statistical conclusion validity, because the sample was too large external validity, because participants were treatment-seeking clinic patients

many patients receiving chemotherapy, which causes nausea, begin to feel nauseated as soon as they enter the clinic's waiting room. in this example, nausea triggered by the waiting room is the: unconditioned stimulus unconditioned response conditioned stimulus conditioned response

rats were reinforced with food for lever pressing in sessions 1–5. food was withheld from session 6 onward. session 11 followed a 24-hour rest (figure). which statement best describes session 11? a reliable rise above session 10, consistent with spontaneous recovery a rise within measurement error, so no change from session 10 can be concluded a return to the acquisition rate, consistent with full relearning an extinction burst, because responding increased right after food was withheld

a patient receiving chemotherapy begins to feel nauseated as soon as she walks into the infusion clinic, before any drug is given. in classical conditioning terms, the clinic is the: unconditioned response unconditioned stimulus conditioned stimulus conditioned response

a dog trained to salivate to a bell stops salivating after many trials of the bell with no food. a week later, the bell alone again produces some salivation. this return of the response is called: discrimination generalization acquisition spontaneous recovery

a patient with chronic headaches learns that a pain reliever makes the throbbing stop, and she now reaches for the medicine sooner each time a headache begins. which process best explains the increase in this behavior? positive punishment positive reinforcement negative punishment negative reinforcement

a slot machine pays out after an unpredictable number of plays, averaging one win every 20 pulls. this reinforcement schedule is most likely to produce: a high, steady response rate that is very resistant to extinction a pause after each reward followed by a burst of responding responding that speeds up only as a fixed time interval ends rapid extinction once rewards stop

which of the following are examples of negative punishment? i. a teen loses phone privileges for a week after missing curfew. ii. a driver buckles his seatbelt to stop the car’s beeping. iii. a driver pays a $100 fine for speeding and later drives more slowly. i only ii only ii and iii only i and iii only

children watch a video in which an adult hits an inflatable doll and is then praised. later, left alone with the doll, many of the children hit it the same way. this result best illustrates: habituation classical conditioning observational learning insight learning

participants see 40 words. half are asked of each word, “is it in capital letters?” and half are asked, “does it fit the sentence ‘she ate the ___’?” a surprise recall test follows. in this study, the dependent variable is: the list of 40 words shown to participants the type of question asked about each word the number of words recalled on the surprise test whether the recall test was a surprise

participants heard 10-word lists and recalled them either immediately or after 30 seconds of counting backward (figure). which conclusion is best supported? neither condition showed a recency effect, so short-term memory played no role. the delay removed the primacy effect, showing that the first words are held only in short-term memory. the delay lowered recall by the same amount at every position, showing general forgetting. the delay removed the recency effect but left the primacy effect intact, consistent with recency depending on short-term memory.

a nursing student studied spanish in high school and began italian in college. now, when she tries to recall spanish words, italian words come to mind instead. this is an example of: decay proactive interference retroactive interference source amnesia

a patient with severe anterograde amnesia practices tracing a star while viewing it in a mirror. over three days his speed and accuracy improve steadily, yet each day he insists he has never done the task. this best shows that: procedural (implicit) memory can form without explicit memory of the learning sessions the patient’s hippocampus is functioning normally episodic memory is required for every kind of learning his improvement reflects sensory adaptation to the mirror

rats injected with an nmda-receptor blocker before training fail to learn the location of a hidden platform, but rats given the blocker after they have already learned the location find it normally. which interpretation is best supported? the blocker impairs swimming ability rather than memory. nmda receptors are needed to retrieve memories but not to form them. nmda receptor activity is needed to form new memories, through processes such as long-term potentiation, but not to retrieve established ones. nmda receptors are inhibitory gaba receptors that normally prevent learning.

participants watch a video of a car crash and are randomly assigned to answer either “how fast were the cars going when they smashed into each other?” or “…when they hit each other?” the “smashed” group gives higher speed estimates. why is random assignment important here? it ensures that the results apply to all eyewitnesses in real courtrooms. it makes it likely that differences in estimates come from the verb rather than from preexisting differences between groups. it ensures that participants do not know the hypothesis. it makes each participant’s speed estimate more reliable from one test to the next.

a professor finds that students who chose to spread their studying over several days scored 12 points higher on an exam than students who chose to cram the night before. which is the most serious threat to concluding that spacing caused the higher scores? the same professor graded the exams for both groups. students who choose to space their studying may differ in motivation or organization from those who cram. both groups took the same exam at the same time. a 12-point difference may be too large to be real.

divers learned word lists either on a beach or underwater and were then tested in the same setting or the other one (figure). which conclusion is best supported? being underwater impaired recall no matter where words were learned. learning on land produced better recall in both test settings. recall was best when the learning and testing environments matched. the test setting had no effect on recall.

a student who moves into a dorm beside a train track is startled by the first few passing trains, but after two weeks she barely reacts, even though the trains are just as loud. which form of learning does this describe? extinction sensitization habituation operant conditioning

name: Cognition, consciousness & language
t: an eeg shows mostly high amplitude, low frequency delta waves. the sleeper is most likely in: stage n1 (light sleep) stage n2 (sleep spindles) stage n3 (slow wave sleep) rem (paradoxical sleep)
a patient after a stroke speaks slowly in short, effortful phrases but understands what others say. which brain area was most likely damaged? wernicke's area broca's area occipital lobe cerebellum
persisting with a familiar problem solving strategy despite a better option is an example of: classical conditioning sensory threshold absolute refractory period mental set
focusing on one conversation in a crowded room demonstrates: selective attention operant extinction retroactive interference sensory transduction
a mental shortcut used to make quick judgments is called a: heuristic algorithm schema prototype
which state of consciousness is associated with vivid dreaming and muscle paralysis? rem sleep stage n1 stage n3 wakefulness
which brain waves are typical of an awake, alert person? beta waves delta waves theta waves sleep spindles

a person with narcolepsy: suddenly falls asleep during the day, sometimes entering rem directly has persistent trouble falling asleep or staying asleep at night repeatedly stops breathing during sleep and wakes briefly each time acts out vivid dreams because the normal muscle paralysis of rem fails
judging how likely an event is by how easily examples come to mind is the: availability heuristic representativeness heuristic anchoring effect confirmation bias

judging that someone who loves poetry is more likely a literature professor than a truck driver, ignoring how many of each exist, reflects the: representativeness heuristic (ignoring base rates) availability heuristic (ease of recalling examples) anchoring bias (relying on a first starting value) confirmation bias (seeking supporting evidence)
searching only for evidence that supports what you already believe is: confirmation bias functional fixedness overconfidence hindsight bias
failing to see that a coin could be used as a screwdriver is an example of: functional fixedness mental set insight divergent thinking

which drug class slows central nervous system activity? depressants (like alcohol and benzodiazepines) stimulants (like cocaine and amphetamines) hallucinogens (like lsd and psilocybin) mild stimulants (like caffeine and nicotine)
stimulants like amphetamines mainly increase the activity of: dopamine and norepinephrine gaba acetylcholine only glycine

according to piaget, a child who understands that pouring water into a taller glass doesn't change its amount has reached the: concrete operational stage sensorimotor stage preoperational stage formal operational stage

the idea that the language you speak shapes how you think is the: whorfian (linguistic relativity) hypothesis nativist (universal grammar) theory learning (behaviorist) theory of language interactionist theory of language
chomsky's nativist theory proposes that children learn language because they have: an innate language acquisition device only rewards from parents only imitation no biological readiness

according to the activation synthesis hypothesis, dreams are: the brain's attempt to interpret random neural activity in rem disguised expressions of unconscious wishes and conflicts a process for consolidating memories from the previous day mental rehearsal of threats to prepare for waking life

adults who are sleep deprived often show 'rem rebound' when they finally sleep. this means: they spend more time in rem sleep than usual they spend less time in rem to recover n3 first they enter rem later in the night than usual they spend more time in stage n1 than usual

a patient speaks fluently but uses made up words and has great difficulty understanding speech. which language area is most likely damaged? wernicke's area broca's area the arcuate fasciculus only the motor cortex
a person keeps using a math method from class even when a much simpler shortcut exists for a new problem. this is an example of: a mental set functional fixedness insight the availability heuristic
iq scores are normally distributed with mean 100 and sd 15 (shown). about what percentage of people score between 85 and 115? 68% 95% 50% 34%
the scatter plot shows sleep and anxiety scores. which correlation coefficient is most likely? r ≈ 0.9 r ≈ +0.9 r ≈ 0 r ≈ 0.1
a volunteer sits quietly with her eyes closed, awake and relaxed. which eeg waves will most likely dominate? alpha waves beta waves delta waves theta waves
the difference between the words 'bat' and 'pat' comes from a change in a single: phoneme morpheme syntax rule pragmatic cue

which brain structure, located in the hypothalamus and receiving input from the retina, acts as the body's master circadian clock? suprachiasmatic nucleus (scn) pineal gland reticular formation lateral geniculate nucleus
sleep spindles and k complexes on an eeg are hallmarks of which sleep stage? stage n2 stage n1 stage n3 rem sleep

in piaget's three mountain task, a 4 year old is asked what a doll on the far side of a mountain model can see, and she describes her own view. this reflects: egocentrism in the preoperational stage missing object permanence in the sensorimotor stage failed conservation in the formal operational stage abstract reasoning in the concrete operational stage

as people age from 30 to 70, which pattern of intelligence is typical? crystallized intelligence holds steady; fluid intelligence declines fluid intelligence holds steady; crystallized intelligence declines both fluid and crystallized intelligence rise steadily both fluid and crystallized intelligence drop sharply

a theorist argues that a gifted dancer, a skilled counselor and a math prodigy each show a different kind of intelligence that iq tests miss. this view best matches: gardner's theory of multiple intelligences spearman's general intelligence (g) factor chomsky's language acquisition device cattell's fluid crystallized distinction

a parent smiles and praises a toddler each time she says 'mama,' and the child says it more often. which theory of language development emphasizes this process? skinner's learning (behaviorist) theory chomsky's nativist (innate) theory the whorfian hypothesis the critical period hypothesis

a clinician reasons: 'all patients with this mutation develop the disease. this patient has the mutation. so this patient will develop the disease.' this is: deductive reasoning inductive reasoning the availability heuristic belief perseverance

viewers who are counting basketball passes in a video often fail to notice a person in a gorilla suit walking through the scene. this is: inattentional blindness change blindness sensory adaptation functional fixedness

a 5 year old sits up screaming about an hour after falling asleep, seems terrified, can't be comforted and has no memory of it the next morning. during which sleep stage do these episodes typically occur? stage n3 (slow wave sleep) rem sleep stage n1 (light sleep) while falling asleep (hypnagogic)

most participants choose a sure option when it is described as '200 of 600 people will be saved,' but choose a risky gamble when the same sure option is described as '400 of 600 people will die.' this shows: the framing effect the availability heuristic belief perseverance functional fixedness

a 14 year old says, 'if gravity were twice as strong, basketball players couldn't dunk.' reasoning systematically about such hypothetical situations is characteristic of piaget's: formal operational stage concrete operational stage preoperational stage sensorimotor stage
a patient who has taken opioid painkillers for months now needs a higher dose to get the same pain relief. this is: tolerance withdrawal sensitization reuptake inhibition

participants name the ink color of words. they are slower when the word red is printed in green ink than when xxxx is printed in green. why? reading is automatic and interferes with naming the color green ink is harder for cones to detect than other colors participants deliberately read every word before answering color naming is automatic and blocks reading the word

chomsky's sentence 'colorless green ideas sleep furiously' sounds grammatical to english speakers even though it means nothing. it shows that: syntax can be judged separately from meaning meaning is needed to judge whether grammar is correct phonemes carry the meaning of whole sentences language determines how speakers perceive colors

genie was kept isolated with almost no exposure to language until she was found at age 13. afterward she learned many words but never mastered grammar. her case is most often cited as evidence for: a critical (sensitive) period for language acquisition language being learned purely through reinforcement the whorfian hypothesis of linguistic relativity grammar being easier to learn than vocabulary

linda is described as a former philosophy major deeply concerned with social justice. many people rate 'linda is a bank teller and a feminist' as more likely than 'linda is a bank teller.' which error is this? the conjunction fallacy, driven by representativeness the availability heuristic, driven by vivid memories anchoring, driven by the first description heard the framing effect, driven by gain versus loss wording

a student who scrolls on her phone in bed until 1 a.m. has trouble falling asleep. which explanation is best supported by research on circadian rhythms? bright, blue rich light suppresses evening melatonin release screen light raises melatonin and causes rem rebound darkness signals the scn to stop releasing melatonin phone use causes narcolepsy like sleep attacks

alcohol enhances gaba a receptor activity. a heavy daily drinker who suddenly stops drinking develops tremors, anxiety and even seizures. which explanation fits best? the brain adapted to constant inhibition and is now overexcited withdrawal raises gaba activity in the brain far above normal levels alcohol had been acting as a cns stimulant all along sudden abstinence lowers glutamate activity too far

an emergency physician instantly 'recognizes' a patient's chest pain as heartburn because he looks like many heartburn patients she has seen, and she misses a heart attack. a checklist that makes doctors list alternative diagnoses reduces such errors. in dual process terms, the checklist works by: engaging slow, deliberate system 2 to check fast system 1 speeding up fast, intuitive system 1 judgments replacing slow, deliberate reasoning with a quick heuristic increasing the physician's functional fixedness

after a stroke, a patient speaks fluently and understands spoken questions well, but cannot repeat a phrase such as 'no ifs, ands or buts' and makes sound errors when trying. damage to which structure is most likely? the arcuate fasciculus linking wernicke's and broca's areas broca's area in the inferior left frontal lobe wernicke's area in the superior left temporal lobe the corpus callosum linking the two cerebral hemispheres

participants watched a wheel of fortune rigged to stop at either 10 or 65, then estimated the percentage of african countries in the united nations. median estimates were 25% after seeing 10 and 45% after seeing 65. which conclusion is best supported? an obviously random number still biased their estimates participants reasonably treated the wheel as a useful clue the 65 group happened to know more about world geography recent news stories made african countries more available

a nurse calculates a drug dose by working through a fixed formula, step by step, that always gives the right answer if followed correctly. which problem solving strategy is this? an algorithm a heuristic trial and error insight
as a person drifts from relaxed wakefulness into stage n1 sleep, which eeg waves become most prominent? theta waves delta waves beta waves alpha waves
how many morphemes (smallest units of meaning) are in the word 'unhappiness'? 3 1 2 4
caffeine makes people feel more alert mainly by blocking receptors for which substance, which builds up during waking and promotes sleepiness? adenosine melatonin serotonin gaba

a 2 year old says 'daddy go car' and 'more juice,' leaving out small words such as 'the' and 'is.' this stage of language development is called: telegraphic speech babbling the one word (holophrastic) stage overregularization

a toddler who knows what horses are sees a zebra at the zoo and shouts 'horsey!' in piaget's terms, she is using: assimilation into an existing schema accommodation by creating a new schema conservation of an object's properties object permanence

charles spearman noticed that people who score well on one kind of mental test tend to score well on other kinds too. he explained this pattern by proposing: a general intelligence factor (g) many fully independent intelligences emotional intelligence rising scores across generations
in freud's theory of dreams, the hidden, symbolic meaning of a dream, as opposed to its literal storyline, is called its: latent content manifest content activation synthesis collective unconscious
lsd causes hallucinations mainly by acting on receptors for which neurotransmitter? serotonin gaba acetylcholine endorphins

after noticing that each of 40 patients given a new drug developed a rash, a resident concludes that the drug probably causes rashes. this is an example of: inductive reasoning deductive reasoning functional fixedness a mental set

the hypnogram shows a healthy adult's typical night of sleep, with rem periods marked as bars. how does sleep in the second half of the night differ from the first half? rem periods lengthen and n3 becomes rare n3 lengthens and rem periods disappear the sleeper stays in n1 for the rest of the night each sleep cycle becomes about 30 minutes long

a man who snores loudly wakes many times each night gasping for air, and his partner notices long pauses in his breathing. he is very sleepy during the day. which sleep disorder is most likely? obstructive sleep apnea narcolepsy with cataplexy primary insomnia night terrors

in simulated driving studies, drivers talking on a hands free phone missed more red lights than when not on the phone, about as often as drivers holding a phone, while listening to the radio caused little impairment. what is the best explanation? the conversation divides attention, not just the hands hands free phones block the sound of traffic holding a phone is the only real source of danger radio listening requires more attention than talking

cocaine raises dopamine levels in the nucleus accumbens and produces euphoria. it does this mainly by: blocking reuptake of dopamine into the releasing neuron activating dopamine receptors directly as an agonist blocking the enzyme that makes dopamine from l dopa releasing dopamine from neurons of the substantia nigra

a father speaks to his infant in short, high pitched, exaggerated sentences and builds on her babbling as if they were taking turns. researchers who argue that such social exchanges drive language learning, together with the child's developing brain, favor which theory? social interactionist theory nativist theory (chomsky) learning theory (skinner) linguistic relativity (whorf)
at dinner, a guest asks, 'can you pass the salt?' everyone understands it as a request, not a question about ability. which aspect of language explains this? pragmatics phonology syntax morphology

a nursing student earns average iq scores but excels at real world problems, such as reorganizing a shift when two coworkers call in sick or finding a way to get a reluctant patient to take medicine. in sternberg's triarchic theory, she is strongest in: practical intelligence analytical intelligence creative intelligence crystallized intelligence

an experienced driver arrives home and realizes she can't remember any details of her familiar 20 minute drive, even though she drove safely. this best illustrates: automatic processing of a well practiced task controlled processing of a demanding task retrograde amnesia for recent events selective attention to the road

in dichotic listening studies, people repeat aloud a message played to one ear and can report almost nothing about a message in the other ear. yet neville moray found that about one third of listeners noticed when their own name was spoken in the ignored ear. what does this suggest? unattended input is still processed to some degree for meaning unattended input is fully blocked before any processing people can consciously attend to both messages equally well hearing a name is a reflex controlled by the cochlea

in a study by simons and levin, an experimenter asked a pedestrian for directions. mid conversation, two workers carried a door between them, and the experimenter was secretly replaced by a different person. about half the pedestrians did not notice the change. what does this demonstrate? change blindness: we store few details of what we see inattentional blindness for an unexpected extra object perfect visual memory for faces we have just seen sensory adaptation to faces after a few seconds

the graph illustrates the flynn effect: when people take an iq test scored against old norms, average scores in many countries have risen by roughly 3 points per decade. what is the best explanation for this rise? environmental changes, since genes can't change that fast genetic changes in the population over a few decades iq tests becoming harder over time smaller families lowering average intelligence

travelers flying from los angeles east to paris usually have worse jet lag than those flying the same distance west. which explanation is best supported by circadian research? the body clock must move earlier, and it shifts later more easily flying east exposes travelers to more cabin pressure changes melatonin is only released after westward flights the suprachiasmatic nucleus stops working during eastward flights

under hypnosis, crime witnesses often report more details than before, but later checks show that many of the new details are wrong, while the witnesses' confidence increases. what does this imply about hypnosis? it raises suggestibility and confidence, not accuracy it reliably recovers accurate memories that were repressed it has no effect at all on what witnesses report it works only on witnesses who are not paying attention

in a classic problem from tversky and kahneman (data in the table), 85% of a city's cabs are green and 15% are blue. a witness who identifies cab colors correctly 80% of the time says a hit and run cab was blue. most people say the chance the cab really was blue is 80%. what is the actual probability, and why do people get it wrong? about 41%; they neglect the base rate of blue cabs about 80%; the witness's accuracy settles it about 15%; the witness adds no information about 68%; both percentages must be multiplied

johnson and newport tested the english grammar of chinese and korean immigrants who had all lived in the united states for several years, and compared them with native english speakers. the graph shows illustrative values matching the pattern they reported. which conclusion is best supported? grammar learning is easiest during a sensitive period in childhood years of exposure explain the scores, not the age of arrival adult learners eventually reach native like levels of grammar children and adults learn grammar equally well
sleep and memory the process the authors describe, in which new memories are stabilized after learning, is called: encoding consolidation retrieval habituation
sleep and memory which eeg pattern would most likely be prominent during the sleep stage linked to better recall? alpha waves beta waves delta waves sleep spindles only

sleep and memory which is the biggest weakness in this study's design? the groups learned and were tested at different times of day the word pairs may have been too easy for participants in both groups recall was measured as the number of pairs remembered both groups studied the identical list of word pairs

sleep and memory besides missing sleep, what else could explain the wake group's lower recall? proactive interference from information learned before the word pairs retroactive interference from new information encountered during the day sensory adaptation to the word pairs during the waking hours learned helplessness from failing to recall pairs during the day
according to the multicomponent model, articulatory suppression most directly interferes with the: visuospatial sketchpad phonological loop episodic buffer long-term semantic store

the pattern of results in figure 1 is best described as: a main effect of secondary task only, with both secondary tasks impairing both primary tasks equally a main effect of primary task only, with verbal span always higher than spatial span no effect of secondary tasks, since all spans remained above four items an interaction, in which each secondary task impaired mainly the primary task of its own type

why did the researchers counterbalance the order of the six task-by-condition combinations? to prevent practice and fatigue effects from being confounded with condition to allow results to generalize to people outside the university to ensure that each participant was assigned to only one condition to keep participants unaware of the study's hypothesis

which statements are supported by figure 1? i. spatial tapping reduced spatial span more than articulatory suppression did. ii. the data do not show a clear effect of articulatory suppression on spatial span. iii. because the design was within-subjects, the results can be generalized to all adults. i only iii only i and ii only i, ii and iii

suppose a third secondary task, generating a random sequence of digits aloud, heavily taxes the attentional control system. based on the model, this task should: impair verbal span only impair spatial span only impair both verbal and spatial span impair neither span

after a stroke, a patient speaks fluently with normal rhythm, but her sentences contain made-up words and make little sense, and she has great difficulty understanding what others say. damage is most likely in the: left inferior frontal lobe (broca's area) left posterior superior temporal lobe (wernicke's area) right occipital lobe arcuate fasciculus only, with both language areas intact

to test whether caffeine speeds reaction time, researchers tested 30 participants after a placebo drink on monday and after a caffeinated drink on tuesday. reaction times were faster on tuesday. what is the most serious flaw in this design? the sample is too small to include both conditions. practice effects are confounded with caffeine because every participant received the conditions in the same order. using the same participants in both conditions increases individual-difference variability. reaction time is not a valid measure of alertness.

in a problem-solving study, participants must attach a candle to a wall using a box of tacks and matches. when the tacks are given inside the box, 40% solve the problem within 10 minutes by tacking the empty box to the wall as a shelf. when the tacks are given beside an empty box, 85% solve it. which interpretation is best supported? participants given the full box solved the problem more often because they had more materials. presenting the box as a container made it harder to see the box’s other use, showing functional fixedness. the difference reflects the availability heuristic, because the tacks were easier to see. both groups solved the problem equally well, so presentation had no effect.

after a week of news coverage of a plane crash, a traveler decides to drive 800 miles instead of flying because she now believes flying is more dangerous, even though driving has a much higher fatality rate per mile. her judgment best illustrates: functional fixedness the representativeness heuristic anchoring the availability heuristic

in a town, 70 of every 100 adults are farmers and 30 are librarians. a randomly chosen resident is described as “quiet, tidy and fond of books.” most people answer “librarian” without considering how many farmers there are. their reasoning best illustrates: anchoring, relying on the first number given the availability heuristic, relying on recent examples the representativeness heuristic, with neglect of the base rate functional fixedness, seeing only one use for the information

a physician who suspects pneumonia notes every test result that fits pneumonia and dismisses a normal chest x-ray as a technical error. her reasoning best illustrates: the gambler’s fallacy the framing effect hindsight bias confirmation bias

a sleep technician sees an eeg with bursts of 12–14 hz activity (sleep spindles) and sharp k-complexes, with no rapid eye movements. the patient is most likely in which stage? rem sleep n3 (slow-wave) sleep n2 (stage 2) sleep relaxed wakefulness with eyes closed

a sleep lab recorded the minutes of n3 and rem sleep in each roughly 90-minute cycle across one night in healthy adults (figure). if a person is woken by an alarm after only 3 cycles instead of 5, the sleep lost will be mostly: n3 sleep, because n3 is concentrated late in the night rem sleep, because rem periods grow longer in later cycles equal amounts of n3 and rem sleep neither n3 nor rem sleep, because both occur only in the first 3 cycles
a pharmacology student is sorting drugs by class. which are cns depressants? i. alcohol ii. benzodiazepines iii. amphetamine i and ii only i only ii and iii only i, ii and iii

a researcher studying cocaine in rats finds that the drug’s rewarding effect disappears when dopamine signaling is blocked in one brain region. this region is most likely the: medulla, which regulates arousal through breathing occipital cortex, which processes visual reward cues cerebellum, which stores learned drug-seeking habits nucleus accumbens, the target of the mesolimbic pathway from the ventral tegmental area

a man who regularly injects heroin in his own bedroom survives a dose that later kills him when he injects the same amount in an unfamiliar motel room. which explanation is best supported by conditioning research? his tolerance disappeared because he had not used the drug for a few hours. cues in his usual setting trigger a conditioned compensatory response that counteracts the drug, and those cues were absent in the new room. the new room’s cues produced a conditioned response that mimicked the drug, so the two effects added together. heroin is metabolized more slowly in unfamiliar environments.

a researcher finds that speakers of a language with separate basic words for light blue and dark blue tell those shades apart faster than english speakers do. she concludes that language shapes perception. what is the most important limitation of this study? language was not manipulated, so other cultural differences between the groups could explain the result. faster discrimination would actually show that language has no effect on perception. reaction time cannot measure perceptual differences between colors. the study should have tested speakers of only one language.

a 3-year-old says, “i goed to the park and seed two mouses.” which conclusion is best supported by this kind of error? children learn language only by imitating adult speech. children extract grammatical rules and apply them, even where adults use exceptions. the child has a language disorder affecting broca’s area. the child has passed the sensitive period for learning grammar.

a patient speaks rapidly with normal rhythm, saying, “the tremble went over the shimmer to get the thing,” and cannot follow simple spoken instructions. damage is most likely in which area? the cerebellum broca’s area in the left frontal lobe the primary motor cortex wernicke’s area in the left posterior temporal lobe

in a dichotic listening task, participants repeat aloud a story played to the right ear and ignore a story in the left ear. they cannot report the left-ear story, but many notice when their own name is spoken in it. this finding is most consistent with: an early-filter model, in which unattended input is fully blocked before any meaning is analyzed attenuation theory, in which unattended input is weakened but still processed for meaning attention being divided equally between the two ears inattentional blindness for visual stimuli

a company develops a new reasoning test for college admissions and compares it with an established test (table). which conclusion is best supported? the new test is valid but unreliable. the new test is reliable but shows little predictive validity for gpa. the new test is both more reliable and more valid than the established test. the new test is neither reliable nor valid.

each participant completes a reaction-time task once after a normal night of sleep and once after a night without sleep, and every participant does the rested session first. which change would best fix the main design flaw? recruit more participants and keep the same order. randomly vary the order so that half of the participants do the sleep-deprived session first. use a different reaction-time task in each session. tell participants the hypothesis so they try equally hard both times.

name: Motivation, emotion & stress
t: a man's heart races during an exam. he decides he is excited rather than anxious, and then he feels excited. which theory of emotion best fits? james lange (bodily feedback) cannon bard (simultaneous) schachter singer (two factor) yerkes dodson (arousal law)
according to the yerkes dodson law, performance on a moderately difficult task is best when arousal is: very low moderate very high unrelated to arousal
a runner trains for a marathon to win a medal and recognition. which theory of motivation best explains this? drive reduction theory incentive theory instinct theory arousal theory

in the context of psychological motivation, intrinsic motivation refers to: an involuntary spinal reflex acting solely to receive external rewards acting only to avoid punishment performing an activity for its inherent satisfaction

intrinsic motivation means doing something because: it is interesting or enjoyable in itself it earns praise or rewards from others it helps you avoid a penalty or criticism it meets expectations set by others

according to maslow, which needs must generally be met first? physiological needs like food and water safety needs like security and stability belonging needs like love and friendship esteem needs like respect and status

the six basic emotions identified by ekman across cultures include: happiness, sadness, fear, anger, surprise and disgust happiness, sadness, fear, anger, pride and shame love, jealousy, fear, anger, surprise and guilt happiness, sadness, anxiety, anger, love and disgust
the 'fight or flight' stress response is triggered mainly by the: sympathetic nervous system parasympathetic nervous system somatic nervous system cerebellum
arousal theory says people are motivated to: keep an optimal level of arousal always minimize arousal always maximize arousal avoid all stimulation

drive reduction theory proposes that behavior is motivated by: a desire to reduce internal tension from unmet biological needs a desire to maintain an optimal, moderate level of arousal innate, fixed behavior patterns shaped by evolution the pull of external incentives such as money, grades or praise

according to the james lange theory, emotion occurs when: we perceive our body's physical reaction to a stimulus body reaction and emotion happen at the same time we label arousal with a cognitive explanation the amygdala releases an emotion directly

the cannon bard theory says that: arousal and emotional experience occur simultaneously and independently emotional experience follows from the perception of bodily arousal emotion results from arousal plus a cognitive label for it emotion begins with a cognitive appraisal before any arousal
in selye's general adaptation syndrome, which stage comes after alarm? resistance exhaustion recovery denial
which hormone is the main long term stress hormone released by the adrenal cortex? cortisol insulin oxytocin melatonin

in lazarus's appraisal model, secondary appraisal is: judging whether you have the resources to cope with a stressor judging whether a situation is threatening or harmless reassessing a stressor after an initial coping attempt the body's alarm reaction during the first stage of stress

a student who used to read for fun starts getting paid per book and later stops reading when the payments end. this is the: overjustification effect drive reduction effect yerkes dodson effect incentive salience
a runner chooses between two equally appealing races scheduled on the same day. this is which type of conflict? approach approach avoidance avoidance approach avoidance double approach avoidance
smiling when you are not happy can slightly improve your mood. this supports the: facial feedback hypothesis cannon bard theory opponent process theory drive reduction theory
which coping strategy focuses on changing the stressful situation itself? problem focused coping emotion focused coping denial avoidance

chronic stress can make people more likely to get sick. which explanation best fits? long term cortisol release suppresses immune function stress increases white blood cell counts permanently stress lowers heart rate stress raises melatonin all day

self determination theory says people need three things for healthy motivation. which set is correct? autonomy, competence and relatedness food, water and shelter money, status and power arousal, drive and incentive
which brain structure, besides the amygdala, is especially important in regulating emotion through planning and reasoning? prefrontal cortex occipital lobe cerebellum medulla

workers who face high job demands but have little control over their work show more stress related illness than workers with high demands and high control. what does this suggest? perceived control reduces the impact of stress high demands alone cause all stress control increases stress job type has no effect on health

a patient's heart races after drinking too much coffee. they attend a party and feel very excited and happy. according to the two factor theory, why? they labeled their caffeine arousal as excitement because of the setting caffeine directly produced happiness without any cognitive labeling the party caused excitement first, which then raised their heart rate their arousal and happiness arose at the same time but independently

research on hunger finds that damage to the lateral hypothalamus in animals leads to a loss of interest in food, while damage to the ventromedial hypothalamus leads to overeating. what does this suggest? the hypothalamus contains areas that both start and stop eating hunger signals come mainly from the stomach, not the brain the lateral hypothalamus signals fullness and stops eating the hypothalamus controls thirst, while hunger is set elsewhere
the graph shows the yerkes dodson law. what level of arousal gives the best performance? moderate very low very high arousal has no effect
according to the hierarchy shown, a person who has just lost their home and has no food would focus mainly on which level? physiological needs esteem needs self actualization love and belonging

salmon swim upstream to spawn in the stream where they hatched, without ever being taught. which theory of motivation explains behavior as driven by inborn, unlearned patterns like this? instinct theory incentive theory arousal theory cognitive dissonance theory

getting stuck in traffic, losing your keys and arguing about whose turn it is to do the dishes are examples of which type of stressor? daily hassles catastrophic events significant life changes ambient stressors

psychologists commonly describe an emotion as having which three components? physiological, behavioral and cognitive conscious, preconscious and unconscious sensory, perceptual and motor alarm, resistance and exhaustion

when a person faces a stressor, which sequence correctly describes the hypothalamic pituitary adrenal (hpa) axis? hypothalamus releases crh → anterior pituitary releases acth → adrenal cortex releases cortisol hypothalamus releases acth → posterior pituitary releases crh → adrenal medulla releases cortisol adrenal cortex releases crh → hypothalamus releases acth → anterior pituitary releases cortisol anterior pituitary releases crh → hypothalamus releases acth → adrenal medulla releases epinephrine

a woman diets and loses 10 kg, but her metabolism slows and her hunger rises until she regains most of the weight. which idea best explains this? set point theory of body weight incentive theory of motivation the facial feedback hypothesis opponent process theory of emotion

according to masters and johnson, what is the correct order of the human sexual response cycle? excitement, plateau, orgasm, resolution plateau, excitement, orgasm, resolution excitement, orgasm, plateau, resolution arousal, orgasm, refractory, plateau

a student learns that an exam is next week. she first asks herself, 'is this a threat, a challenge, or no big deal?' in lazarus's model, this step is called: primary appraisal secondary appraisal reappraisal problem focused coping

a man has cared for his parent with dementia for two years with no breaks. he is exhausted, catches every cold that goes around and feels unable to cope. in selye's general adaptation syndrome, he is most likely in which stage? exhaustion alarm resistance recovery

eeg studies of emotion (for example, by richard davidson) found that greater resting activity in the left prefrontal cortex is most associated with: positive, approach related emotions negative, withdrawal related emotions a complete lack of emotional response higher risk of panic attacks

a medical student is offered a prestigious residency that she really wants, but it would mean moving far away from her family. which type of motivational conflict is she facing? approach avoidance approach approach avoidance avoidance multiple approach approach

a hiker sees a snake on the trail, thinks 'that could be venomous,' and only then feels fear as her heart starts pounding. which theory of emotion fits this order best? lazarus's cognitive appraisal theory the james lange theory the schachter singer two factor theory the facial feedback hypothesis

a retired surgeon has a stable income, a loving family and the respect of her colleagues. she now spends her time learning to paint, wanting to reach her full creative potential. according to maslow, which need is she pursuing? self actualization esteem love and belonging safety

on her first skydive, a woman feels terror during the jump and mild relief afterward. after 100 jumps, she feels little fear during the jump but intense exhilaration afterward. which theory explains this shift? opponent process theory drive reduction theory two factor theory self determination theory

in one year, a man gets married, moves to a new city and starts a job he wanted. he is happy about all three, yet his score on the holmes and rahe social readjustment rating scale is high. why? the scale counts any change that needs adjustment, good or bad the scale counts only negative events, so it must be scored wrong the scale measures personality traits, not life events at all positive events count only when they cause a physical illness

a patient with an incurable illness cannot change her diagnosis, so she practices meditation, journals and focuses on the meaning she finds in her family. this is an example of: emotion focused coping problem focused coping displacement approach avoidance conflict

after a frightening car accident, a mother calls her sister and gathers her children close rather than fighting or fleeing. shelley taylor proposed this pattern, linked to oxytocin release, as a stress response called: tend and befriend learned helplessness rest and digest reaction formation

walter cannon criticized the james lange theory of emotion. which point formed part of his critique? bodily arousal patterns are too similar across emotions to tell them apart emotions occur only after a person consciously labels a stimulus facial expressions of emotion differ completely from culture to culture emotions are learned through reinforcement rather than felt in the body

early research on 'type a' behavior linked it to heart disease. later studies found which component to be the most toxic predictor of coronary heart disease? hostility and anger time urgency and impatience high achievement drive working long hours

according to the yerkes dodson law, how does the optimal level of arousal for a complex surgical procedure compare with that for a simple, well practiced task like taking a pulse? it is lower for the complex task it is higher for the complex task it is the same for both tasks it is zero for the complex task

people with high need for achievement (studied by david mcclelland and john atkinson) are given a choice of tasks. which will they usually choose? moderately difficult tasks with a realistic chance of success very easy tasks where success is almost guaranteed nearly impossible tasks where failure has an excuse tasks chosen at random with no regard to difficulty

people with fully satisfied biological needs still ride roller coasters, explore new places and solve puzzles for fun. which theory is most challenged by this observation? drive reduction theory arousal theory incentive theory self determination theory

researchers give two groups of rats identical electric shocks. one group hears a warning tone 10 seconds before each shock; the other gets no warning. the warned rats develop far fewer stomach ulcers. which conclusion best fits? predictable stressors are less harmful because safe periods are clear the tone itself reduced pain by blocking the nerve signals unwarned rats received stronger shocks than the warned rats classical conditioning always increases the stress response

after gastric bypass surgery, many patients report feeling much less hungry, and their blood levels of ghrelin fall. which interpretation is best supported? less ghrelin from the bypassed stomach may contribute to reduced hunger lower ghrelin proves that patients' leptin levels must have risen the surgery eliminated the hypothalamus's role in feeding hunger is controlled only by learned habits, not hormones

which of the following is a secondary (learned) drive rather than a primary (biological) drive? the desire to earn money the urge to drink when dehydrated the urge to eat after a long fast the urge to warm up when very cold

psychologists classify stressors into types. a sudden, powerful event that affects many people at once, such as a major earthquake, is called a: cataclysmic event personal stressor daily hassle ambient stressor

a long term heroin user who always injects in the same room takes his usual dose in an unfamiliar place and nearly dies of an overdose. shepard siegel explained cases like this with which idea? familiar cues trigger a learned compensatory response that is absent in a new setting the drug is chemically stronger when it is taken in an unfamiliar place withdrawal symptoms are always more severe in new environments tolerance depends only on liver enzymes, so the setting cannot matter
hans selye used which term for positive stress that comes from a welcome challenge, such as starting a dream job? eustress distress burnout exhaustion

joseph ledoux described a fast 'low road' for fear that lets a person flinch at a snake like shape before knowing what it is. which pathway is this? thalamus directly to amygdala, bypassing the cortex thalamus to the visual cortex, then on to the amygdala hippocampus to the prefrontal cortex and back amygdala to the cerebellum, then to the muscles

expectancy value theory treats motivation as roughly expectancy × value. based on the hypothetical ratings in the table, which student is likely to be least motivated to study for a quiz? student s student p student q student r
which brain structure, rich in receptors for cortisol, is especially vulnerable to damage from long term high cortisol levels during chronic stress? hippocampus cerebellum occipital lobe pons

suzanne kobasa studied executives under heavy stress. those who stayed healthy felt committed to their work, in control of events, and saw change as a challenge. she called this trait: psychological hardiness the type a behavior pattern learned helplessness an external locus of control

a polygraph, often called a 'lie detector,' directly measures which of the following? physiological arousal such as heart rate and skin conductance electrical activity in the brain's language areas during speech whether each spoken statement is factually true changes in cortisol levels in the blood over hours

in a study by dutton and aron (1974), an attractive female interviewer gave her phone number to men who had just crossed either a high, swaying suspension bridge or a low, sturdy bridge (approximate results shown). which explanation fits the difference best? they misattributed arousal from the bridge to attraction to her fear lowered their arousal, so they felt calm and friendly their emotion came only from facial feedback while smiling their attraction came first and then caused their arousal

before a presentation, a student notices her racing heart. her coach tells her to think of it as energy that will help her perform, not as a sign of danger. which strategy is she using? cognitive reappraisal of arousal expressive suppression problem focused coping sublimation of the anxiety into effort

a man with chronic knee pain must choose between a painful surgery with months of rehabilitation and continuing to live with the pain. he strongly dislikes both options. this is which type of conflict? avoidance avoidance approach approach approach avoidance role conflict

a man keeps drinking alcohol every day mainly to stop the shakiness and anxiety he feels when he goes without it, not to feel good. which learning principle best explains why his drinking continues? negative reinforcement positive reinforcement positive punishment extinction

a patient with tension headaches watches a screen showing the electrical activity of her forehead muscles and learns to make the reading drop. which stress management technique is this? biofeedback progressive muscle relaxation systematic desensitization cognitive restructuring

after eating a large plate of pasta, a man says he is too full for another bite of pasta, yet he eats a bowl of ice cream when it is offered. which concept best explains this? sensory specific satiety set point regulation of body weight a rebound in ghrelin drive reduction

a nurse manager is driven mainly by wanting to influence others and control decisions on her unit. in david mcclelland's theory, she has a high need for: power achievement affiliation self actualization

the graph shows the yerkes dodson relationship for two tasks. a surgical resident performing a difficult new procedure is at point x. which change would most likely improve her performance? lowering her arousal, for example with slow breathing raising her arousal, for example with more caffeine keeping arousal the same, since x is already the peak adding time pressure to sharpen her focus on the task

leptin is released by fat cells and signals the hypothalamus to reduce appetite. based on the table, daily leptin injections would most likely reduce food intake and weight in which mouse? mouse a only mouse b only both mouse a and mouse b neither mouse, since leptin increases hunger

research on self determination theory has asked which rewards undermine intrinsic motivation. which reward is least likely to reduce a child's interest in drawing? unexpected praise that gives feedback about her skill a cash payment promised for every drawing she makes a prize promised only if she draws for a full hour a sticker chart announced before she starts drawing

patients with damage to the ventromedial prefrontal cortex keep choosing risky card decks that lose money in a gambling task. unlike healthy people, they show no rise in skin conductance before risky choices. which idea do these findings support? bodily emotional signals help guide good decisions emotions mainly interfere with rational decisions decisions depend only on working memory capacity the amygdala alone stores the value of choices

at the 2004 paralympic games, judo athletes who had been blind from birth showed the same facial expressions after winning and losing as sighted athletes did (matsumoto and willingham). which conclusion do these findings most strongly support? basic facial expressions are largely innate, not learned by sight facial expressions are learned mainly by watching other people blind athletes feel emotions less intensely than sighted ones facial expressions differ across cultures more than within them

people with high spinal cord injuries receive little feedback from most of their body. suppose they reported emotions just as intense as before their injury. which idea would this result most directly weaken? the james lange theory the cannon bard theory lazarus's cognitive appraisal theory the facial feedback hypothesis

in a hypothetical study, researchers raised arousal with different caffeine doses and measured scores on two tasks (table). which conclusion best fits these hypothetical data? the complex task peaked at a lower arousal level than the simple task both tasks improved steadily as arousal kept increasing the simple task peaked at a lower arousal level than the complex task arousal had little effect on performance in the complex task

in schachter and singer's 1962 study, participants were injected with epinephrine and then waited with a confederate who acted giddy and playful. which group tended to show the most euphoria? those not told the drug would cause arousal those correctly told about racing heart and shaking those given a saline placebo instead of epinephrine all groups showed the same amount of euphoria

kiecolt glaser and colleagues made a small standard skin wound on women caring for a relative with dementia and on matched women who were not caregivers (graph shows approximate results). which statement is most justified? healing took about 25% longer, but caregiving was not randomly assigned healing took about 10% longer, which proves stress slows healing healing took about 25% longer, which proves stress slows healing healing took about 50% longer, but caregiving was not randomly assigned

a friend in the room why did heart rate rise during the task while cortisol did not peak until about 20 minutes after the task began? heart rate responds to fast neural signals; cortisol needs a slower hormone cascade cortisol is released only after heart rate has returned to its baseline level heart rate is controlled by the hpa axis, which reacts faster than nerves cortisol is stored in saliva and enters the blood only after a delay

a friend in the room compared with the stress alone condition, by about what percentage did the friend's presence reduce the peak rise in cortisol above baseline? about 50% about 28% about 13% about 100%

a friend in the room according to lazarus's cognitive appraisal theory, the friend most likely lowered the stress response by changing participants': judgment of whether they had the resources to cope with the task basic physiological alarm reaction to any change in the environment long term personality traits related to anxiety and neuroticism memory of the evaluators' faces after the task had ended

a friend in the room why did all sessions begin at 2:00 p.m.? cortisol levels change across the day, so time of day had to be held constant participants tend to judge the evaluators as less stern in the afternoon than in the morning friends were most likely to be available at that time of day heart rate cannot be measured accurately in the morning hours

a friend in the room which conclusion is best supported by figure 1 and table 1 together? the friend reduced the cortisol response much more than the heart rate response the friend reduced the heart rate response much more than it reduced the cortisol response the friend prevented any cortisol response to the task the no stress task raised cortisol as much as the stress task did

which sequence correctly describes how the tsst raised salivary cortisol? pituitary releases crh → hypothalamus releases acth → adrenal medulla releases cortisol hypothalamus releases acth → anterior pituitary releases crh → adrenal cortex releases cortisol hypothalamus releases crh → posterior pituitary releases acth → adrenal medulla releases cortisol hypothalamus releases crh → anterior pituitary releases acth → adrenal cortex releases cortisol

which statement is best supported by figure 1? caregivers had lower cortisol than non-caregivers at every time point. caregivers had higher baseline cortisol but a smaller rise from baseline to peak. the two groups did not differ meaningfully at any time point. caregivers' cortisol rose more than non-caregivers' but returned to baseline faster.

which is the strongest reason the researchers cannot conclude that caregiving caused the blunted cortisol response? cortisol was measured in saliva rather than in blood. participants were not randomly assigned to be caregivers, so other differences between groups may explain the results. the sample of 60 participants was too large for a laboratory study. all participants were exposed to the same stressor.

why did all sessions begin at 2:00 p.m.? cortisol follows a daily rhythm, peaking shortly after waking, so testing at a fixed time controls for time-of-day effects. heart rate cannot be measured accurately in the morning. the tsst is only stressful when participants are tired in the afternoon. testing at one time ensured that participants were randomly assigned.

which conclusions are consistent with the passage? i. the tsst activated the sympathetic nervous system in both groups. ii. caregivers' blunted cortisol rise reflects a failure of the adrenal medulla to release hormone. iii. caregivers' cortisol peaked later than non-caregivers' cortisol. i only ii only i and iii only ii and iii only

participants were randomly assigned to low, moderate or high arousal conditions and then performed either a simple or a complex task (figure). which conclusion is best supported? higher arousal improved performance on both tasks. arousal had no meaningful effect on simple-task performance. moderate arousal produced the best performance on both tasks. high arousal improved simple-task performance relative to moderate arousal but impaired complex-task performance.

the james–lange theory states that emotions result from perceiving one's own bodily responses. which findings would challenge this theory? i. different emotions are associated with very similar patterns of autonomic arousal. ii. people with spinal cord injuries that reduce bodily feedback still report experiencing emotions. iii. holding a smiling facial expression slightly increases reported happiness. i only i and ii only ii and iii only i, ii and iii

participants receive an injection that raises their heart rate and then wait with either a cheerful or an angry confederate. those who were not told about the injection’s effects report emotions that match the confederate’s mood. this result best supports which theory? the yerkes–dodson law james–lange theory cannon–bard theory schachter–singer two-factor theory

walter cannon argued that the same bodily changes, such as a racing heart, occur in fear, anger and excitement, and that changes in the internal organs are too slow to explain how quickly emotions arise. these arguments were aimed mainly at which theory? cannon–bard theory schachter–singer two-factor theory james–lange theory lazarus’s cognitive appraisal theory

participants rate cartoons while holding a pen either between their teeth, which produces a smile-like expression, or between their lips, which prevents smiling. those in the teeth condition rate the cartoons as funnier. the independent variable in this study is: the facial expression produced by the pen position the funniness ratings of the cartoons the cartoons shown to participants the participants’ mood before the study

participants performed either a simple or a complex task under different levels of induced arousal (figure). which conclusion is best supported? performance on both tasks rose steadily as arousal increased. performance peaked at a lower arousal level for the complex task than for the simple task. arousal had no effect on performance of the complex task. the simple task peaked at a lower arousal level than the complex task.

a family that has just fled a flood spends its first days seeking food, water and safe shelter and shows little interest in a community art program. which theory best predicts this ordering of priorities? opponent-process theory self-determination theory incentive theory maslow’s hierarchy of needs

after a large dinner, a man who is no longer hungry still orders a slice of chocolate cake when he sees it on the dessert cart. which theory best explains this behavior? drive-reduction theory incentive theory arousal theory james–lange theory

preschoolers who already liked drawing were randomly assigned to expect a gold-star certificate for drawing or to draw with no reward. before the study, both groups spent about 17% of free-play time drawing. two weeks after the certificates ended, the rewarded group spent 8% of free-play time drawing and the unrewarded group spent 16%. these results best illustrate: drive reduction the overjustification effect learned helplessness the mere exposure effect

according to lazarus’s model of stress, which of the following thoughts reflect secondary appraisal? i. “do i have the time and skills to prepare for this exam?” ii. “is this exam a threat to my grade?” iii. “i can ask my study group for help.” i only i and iii only ii and iii only i, ii and iii

a caregiver has handled months of stress caring for a sick parent. after an initial burst of energy and a long period of coping, she now has frequent infections and constant fatigue. in selye’s general adaptation syndrome, she has most likely reached the: resistance stage alarm stage exhaustion stage appraisal stage

a medical resident under months of high stress has chronically elevated cortisol. which effect is most likely? increased digestion and slower heart rate enhanced immune function and lower blood glucose reduced immune function and higher blood glucose increased bone density and muscle growth

rats with lesions of the lateral hypothalamus stop eating and lose weight, whereas rats with lesions of the ventromedial hypothalamus overeat. a drug that strongly activates neurons in the lateral hypothalamus would most likely cause a well-fed rat to: begin eating lose interest in food eat less at its next meal show no change, because only the ventromedial area controls eating

a survey of 500 adults finds that those who report more stressful life events also report more colds in the past year (r = 0.35). which conclusion is most appropriate? stress and colds are associated, but these data cannot show that stress causes colds. stress causes people to catch more colds. catching colds causes people to experience more stress. stress and colds are unrelated, because r is less than 0.50.

in a stress study, participants give a speech to a panel of “experts” and are then told, falsely, that their performance was poor. which practice is most essential for this study to be ethical? a full debriefing afterward that explains the deception and the study’s true purpose paying participants only if they finish the speech telling participants the hypothesis before the study begins removing data from participants who seem upset so the results are not skewed

participants gave a stressful speech either after a short supportive talk with a friend or with no one present beforehand. salivary cortisol was measured before and 20 minutes after the speech (figure). which statement is best supported? social support lowered cortisol before the speech. social support shrank the cortisol increase from about 12 to about 5 nmol/l. cortisol rose only in the group that talked with a friend. the groups’ cortisol levels after the speech did not differ significantly.

a nursing student overwhelmed by an upcoming exam makes a detailed study schedule and joins a study group. her strategy is best described as: avoidance coping emotion-focused coping displacement problem-focused coping

name: Identity & personality
t: a student who is anxious and moody under stress would score high on which big five trait? openness conscientiousness agreeableness neuroticism
according to erikson, the main psychosocial task of adolescence is: trust vs. mistrust industry vs. inferiority identity vs. role confusion intimacy vs. isolation

a teenager says, "you shouldn't steal medicine because it's against the law, and society would fall apart if everyone broke laws." this reasoning is at which kohlberg level? preconventional conventional postconventional formal operational

self concept refers to: your overall set of beliefs about who you are your overall positive or negative evaluation of your worth your belief in your ability to succeed the way others actually perceive you

self efficacy is: your belief in your ability to succeed at a specific task your overall sense of your own worth as a person your belief that outcomes depend on your own actions your actual skill level at completing a specific task
according to freud, the part of personality that seeks immediate pleasure is the: id ego superego persona
which personality approach focuses on stable traits like extraversion? trait theory psychoanalytic theory behaviorist theory humanistic theory
defense mechanisms, in freud's theory, are used by the ego to: reduce anxiety increase id impulses create new memories improve physical health
blaming your poor exam score on the professor's unfair questions, when you didn't study, is an example of: rationalization repression sublimation regression
channeling aggressive urges into playing football is an example of: sublimation projection displacement denial
yelling at your sibling after being scolded by your boss is an example of: displacement projection reaction formation sublimation
carl rogers believed people develop best when they receive: unconditional positive regard strict punishment conditional praise only no feedback

bandura's concept of reciprocal determinism says behavior results from interactions among: personal factors, behavior and environment unconscious drives of the id, ego and superego genes, hormones and brain structure stimuli, responses and reinforcers

someone with an internal locus of control believes: their own actions largely determine what happens to them luck and chance largely determine what happens to them powerful others largely determine what happens to them their self worth depends mainly on others' approval
according to erikson, the main conflict of early adulthood is: intimacy vs. isolation trust vs. mistrust generativity vs. stagnation integrity vs. despair
erikson's final stage, in late adulthood, is: integrity vs. despair intimacy vs. isolation identity vs. role confusion industry vs. inferiority
a person who strongly dislikes a coworker acts extremely friendly toward them. which defense mechanism is this? reaction formation projection sublimation repression

kohlberg's postconventional stage is shown when someone says: 'laws should be broken if they violate basic human rights.' 'i'll do it so i don't get punished.' 'i'll follow the rules so people think i'm good.' 'rules must always be followed to keep order.'
a person who hasn't explored options but has committed to a career their parents chose is in which of marcia's identity statuses? foreclosure achievement moratorium diffusion
cooley's 'looking glass self' says our self concept is shaped by: how we imagine others see us how others actually see us how we compare ourselves to others our own private self evaluation
george herbert mead described the 'me' as: the part of the self shaped by society's expectations the spontaneous, impulsive part of self unconscious desires the part of the self that forms in old age

in vygotsky's theory, the zone of proximal development is: the range of tasks a learner can do with help but not yet alone the range of tasks a learner can already do without any help the period when a child is most sensitive to language input the gap between a child's mental age and chronological age

the big five trait of conscientiousness is most strongly linked to: being organized, dependable and goal directed seeking excitement and social attention emotional instability creativity and curiosity

personality tests that ask about behavior often find that people act differently in different situations, yet trait scores stay fairly stable over years. which view best fits both findings? interactionist: behavior comes from both traits and situations trait theory: stable traits fully determine behavior situationism: situations, not stable traits, determine all behavior psychoanalytic: unconscious conflicts drive behavior
a therapist notices a client accusing others of being dishonest while the client is often dishonest. which defense mechanism fits best? projection displacement rationalization regression
in freud's theory, which part of personality acts as the conscience, holding internalized moral standards and ideals? superego id ego preconscious
according to erikson, what is the main psychosocial conflict of infancy (birth to about 1 year)? trust vs. mistrust autonomy vs. shame and doubt initiative vs. guilt industry vs. inferiority

self esteem refers to: a person's overall evaluation of their own worth a person's belief they can succeed at a task a person's knowledge of their various social roles a person's sense that others control their fate

what is the correct order of freud's psychosexual stages? oral, anal, phallic, latency, genital anal, oral, phallic, genital, latency oral, phallic, anal, latency, genital oral, anal, latency, phallic, genital
in freud's model, the ego operates mainly according to the: reality principle pleasure principle morality principle fixation principle

which statement correctly distinguishes suppression from repression? suppression is conscious; repression is unconscious repression is conscious; suppression is unconscious both are conscious forms of forgetting on purpose both are unconscious and work in exactly the same way

gordon allport described a single trait so dominant that it shapes nearly everything a person does, such as a lifelong devotion to helping the poor. he called this a: cardinal trait central trait secondary trait source trait

hans eysenck's model of personality is built on which three dimensions? psychoticism, extraversion and neuroticism openness, agreeableness and conscientiousness id, ego and superego autonomy, competence and relatedness

a clinician shows a client ambiguous inkblots and asks what they look like, believing the answers reveal hidden conflicts. this projective test (the rorschach) comes from which perspective? psychodynamic behaviorist trait social cognitive

carl jung proposed that all humans share inherited images and themes, such as the 'hero' or the 'wise old man,' stored in the: collective unconscious personal unconscious libidinal energy of the id preconscious

a college sophomore has tried biology, music and business classes and is actively talking with mentors, but has not yet chosen a path. in marcia's model, which identity status is she in? moratorium foreclosure identity diffusion identity achievement

a 50 year old nurse feels deeply fulfilled training new nurses and volunteering at a youth clinic. which of erikson's stages is she successfully resolving? generativity vs. stagnation intimacy vs. isolation integrity vs. despair identity vs. role confusion

a 9 year old who keeps struggling with schoolwork compared with classmates starts to say, 'i'm just bad at everything.' which erikson stage is most relevant? industry vs. inferiority initiative vs. guilt trust vs. mistrust autonomy vs. shame and doubt
