asked whether a man should steal a drug to save his dying wife, a child answers, 'no, because he'll get caught and go to jail.' which of kohlberg's levels does this reasoning reflect? preconventional conventional postconventional formal operational

after a new baby sister arrives, a 5 year old who was fully toilet trained starts wetting the bed and asking for a bottle. which defense mechanism does this illustrate? regression reaction formation sublimation projection

a physician diagnosed with cancer talks only about survival statistics and drug mechanisms, avoiding any discussion of how she feels. which defense mechanism is she most likely using? intellectualization rationalization reaction formation sublimation

a child playing on a baseball team understands what the pitcher, catcher and outfielders are each expected to do and how they fit together. according to george herbert mead, the child has reached which stage? game stage, taking the role of the generalized other play stage, taking the role of one other at a time preparatory stage, simply imitating others looking glass stage, imagining how others judge him

according to e. tory higgins's self discrepancy theory, a student who feels she falls short of what her parents believe she ought to be is most likely to feel: anxiety and guilt sadness and disappointment pride and confidence boredom and apathy

carol gilligan criticized kohlberg's theory of moral development mainly because it: was based largely on males and overlooked an ethic of care relied on infants who were too young to reason about rules placed too much weight on caring for others over justice ignored the role of the unconscious in moral decisions

eysenck proposed a biological basis for introversion. according to his theory, why do introverts tend to avoid loud parties? they have higher baseline cortical arousal, so extra stimulation is unpleasant they have lower baseline cortical arousal, so they need more stimulation they lack the dopamine receptors needed to feel any pleasure socially they were punished for socializing, so the behavior was extinguished

a man's view of himself as a successful, confident person clashes with his real experience of failing repeatedly at work, and he feels anxious. carl rogers would describe this as: incongruence between his self concept and his experiences conditions of worth being fully replaced by unconditional regard a fixation at the anal stage of psychosexual development low self monitoring caused by an external locus of control

a woman's self esteem rises when her hometown hospital wins a national award, and she starts describing herself as 'one of the best trained nurses around.' which theory best explains this? social identity theory psychosexual theory drive reduction theory trait theory

in a twin study, identical twins raised apart have extraversion scores that correlate at about 0.45, while fraternal twins raised together correlate at about 0.20. which conclusion is best supported? genes have a sizable influence on extraversion, and shared family environment adds little shared family environment is the main cause of extraversion, and genes add little extraversion is fully inherited, so environment plays no role in it at all extraversion cannot be measured reliably, so no conclusion can be reached

in langer and rodin's nursing home study, one floor of residents was given choices and responsibility for caring for a plant; another floor had staff do everything for them. the first group became happier and more active, and fewer had died 18 months later. what does this most support? increasing a sense of personal control improves well being and health caring for plants has a direct biological effect on the immune system elderly people prefer that staff make all decisions for them happiness is mostly genetic, so environment has little effect

jerome kagan found that 4 month old infants who cried and thrashed in response to unfamiliar sights and sounds were more likely to be shy and cautious as children years later. this finding best supports the idea that: personality partly reflects inborn temperament that is fairly stable personality is shaped only by parenting styles after infancy shyness is caused by unresolved conflicts in the oral stage infant reactivity has no lasting connection to later personality traits
a person's internal sense of being a man, a woman, both, or neither is called their: gender identity sexual orientation sex assigned at birth gender role

behaviorist theorists such as b. f. skinner explained personality mainly as: patterns of behavior shaped by a history of reinforcement unconscious conflicts among the id, ego and superego inborn traits that stay fixed and unchanged across the whole lifespan an inner drive to grow toward self actualization

in freud's theory, the oedipus complex, in which a child has unconscious desire for the opposite sex parent and rivalry with the same sex parent, arises during which psychosexual stage? phallic oral anal latency
carl jung used which term for the public 'mask' a person presents to others to fit social expectations? persona shadow anima ego ideal

children come to sort toys, jobs and behaviors into 'for boys' and 'for girls,' then use these categories to guide their own behavior. sandra bem's explanation of this process is: gender schema theory psychoanalytic identification theory social identity theory kohlberg's theory of moral development

hazel markus and paula nurius proposed that 'possible selves' images of who we hope to become and who we fear becoming mainly serve to: motivate and guide behavior toward future goals defend the ego against anxiety from the id store memories of past events in order fix personality permanently by early childhood

alfred adler, a student of freud who later broke away, believed that a central force in personality is: the drive to overcome feelings of inferiority inherited archetypes in the collective unconscious sexual energy passing through childhood stages stable traits that are measured by questionnaires

in many east asian cultures, people tend to define themselves mainly through their relationships and group memberships. markus and kitayama called this view of the self: interdependent self construal independent self construal the looking glass self self discrepancy

after failing an exam, a student feels better by thinking about classmates who did even worse. in leon festinger's social comparison framework, this is: downward social comparison upward social comparison self handicapping reaction formation

which statement best describes how erik erikson's theory differs from freud's? erikson stressed social conflicts and development across the whole lifespan erikson stressed sexual urges and ended development at adolescence erikson rejected all stages and studied only adult traits erikson focused on how reinforcement shapes observable behavior

a 4 year old pretends to be her mother cooking dinner, then pretends to be a firefighter, taking on one specific role at a time. according to george herbert mead, she is in which stage? play stage preparatory stage game stage formal operational stage

asked whether a man should steal a drug to save his wife, a teen says, 'yes, because a good husband would, and people would think badly of him if he didn't.' which of kohlberg's stages does this reasoning reflect? stage 3: good interpersonal relationships stage 2: individualism and exchange stage 4: maintaining social order stage 5: social contract and rights

a 20 year old has not explored any career or value options and shows no interest in committing to one. in james marcia's model, he is in which identity status? identity diffusion identity foreclosure identity moratorium identity achievement

a heavy smoker who has just been diagnosed with emphysema insists that his breathing trouble is only a lingering cold and refuses to discuss the diagnosis. which defense mechanism is he using? denial projection sublimation displacement

a 2 year old insists on dressing and feeding himself. his parents scold him harshly for every spill, and he starts to doubt that he can do things on his own. which of erikson's stages is involved? autonomy vs. shame and doubt trust vs. mistrust initiative vs. guilt industry vs. inferiority in school

a patient loves trying unusual foods, visiting art museums and discussing abstract ideas. which big five trait would she most likely score high on? openness conscientiousness agreeableness neuroticism

a new nurse feels she is a worthwhile and likable person overall, but she doubts she can start an iv on an infant. which description fits her best? high self esteem but low self efficacy for that task low self esteem but high self efficacy for that task an external locus of control for all life outcomes low self esteem and low self efficacy in general

at work, at parties and with family, a man carefully watches others and changes how he acts to fit what each situation seems to call for. he is best described as: a high self monitor a low self monitor high in neuroticism showing reaction formation

according to e. tory higgins's self discrepancy theory, a student who falls short of the concert pianist he personally hoped to become is most likely to feel: disappointment and sadness anxiety and guilt anger directed at others pride and contentment

which is a common criticism of trait theories of personality? they describe behavior well but explain little about why traits develop they rely too heavily on unconscious drives that can never be measured directly they predict behavior equally well in every possible situation they claim personality is shaped only by reinforcement history

researchers recorded two children's aggression across situations at a summer camp (hypothetical data shown). both children have the same overall average. which conclusion best fits the 'if...then' view of walter mischel and yuichi shoda? each child shows a stable, distinctive pattern across situations the children have identical personalities, since averages match aggression is random, so personality cannot be measured here situations alone determine aggression, so the children are alike

which is the strongest scientific criticism of freud's psychoanalytic theory? many of its claims can explain any outcome, so they are hard to falsify it places far too much weight on observable, measurable behaviors in the lab it ignores childhood and focuses only on adult experiences it was tested mainly in large, randomized controlled trials

cross cultural studies found that kohlberg's highest (postconventional) stages are rare in many small scale, non western societies. critics argue this mainly shows that: his top stages reflect western, individualist values people in those societies cannot reason about morality moral reasoning is fixed entirely by genes at birth his stages are too easy, so nearly everyone reaches them

in a hypothetical study of adults with snake phobia, participants received one of four treatments, then rated their self efficacy and were asked to hold a harmless snake (table). which conclusion best fits these hypothetical data and albert bandura's theory? direct success experiences raised self efficacy and behavior most watching a model was the strongest source of self efficacy encouragement alone was as effective as guided practice self efficacy ratings were unrelated to approach behavior

walter mischel's early studies found that preschoolers who waited longer for a second marshmallow later had higher sat scores. a larger, more diverse 2018 study (watts, duncan and quan) found that waiting time's link with achievement at age 15 was about half as strong as earlier work suggested, and it shrank by about two thirds after controlling for family background and early cognitive ability. which conclusion is best supported? waiting time partly reflects background factors that also shape achievement teaching children to wait would by itself raise their later test scores delay of gratification has no link at all with later achievement the original studies proved that self control causes school success

a first-year student plans to become a pharmacist because both parents are pharmacists and says she has never seriously considered other careers. her identity status is best classified as: diffusion foreclosure moratorium achievement

which conclusion is best supported by table 1? most students reached identity achievement by the fourth year. the percentage of students in moratorium doubled from year 1 to year 4. the percentage in achievement more than tripled, while the percentage in diffusion was cut in half. foreclosure was the most common status in both years.

given the information about students who did not complete the fourth-year assessment, table 1 most likely: understates the decrease in diffusion for the original sample is unaffected, because the original sample was randomly selected proves that diffused students are more likely to leave college overstates how much identity development occurred in the original sample

which can be concluded from the first-year correlation between exploration and anxiety? i. students who explored more tended to report more anxiety. ii. exploring identity options causes anxiety. iii. about 10% of the variance in anxiety scores is shared with exploration scores. i only ii only i and iii only i, ii and iii

according to erikson's theory, students who resolve the crisis studied here would next be expected to face which psychosocial stage? industry vs inferiority intimacy vs isolation generativity vs stagnation integrity vs despair

in a study of 500 adults, conscientiousness scores were correlated with the number of missed medical appointments over one year (r = −0.45). which conclusion is justified? increasing a person's conscientiousness would reduce the number of appointments they miss. more conscientious people tended to miss fewer appointments, and the two variables share about 20% of their variance. conscientiousness explains 45% of the variation in missed appointments. the negative correlation shows that the relationship between the variables is weak.

after being criticized by her supervisor, a nurse says nothing at work but snaps at her younger brother when she gets home. which defense mechanism does this illustrate? displacement projection sublimation reaction formation

in a study of attachment, toddlers are briefly separated from and then reunited with their mothers in a laboratory playroom. researchers classify a toddler as “securely attached” if he is distressed at separation and quickly comforted on reunion. this classification rule is best described as: a measure of test–retest reliability the independent variable a confounding variable an operational definition of secure attachment

coworkers describe a new employee as organized, dependable and careful to meet every deadline. in the five-factor model, she would most likely score high in: openness to experience conscientiousness agreeableness extraversion

a student who believes she can master organic chemistry studies more, earns better grades and then feels even more confident. bandura would describe this interplay among her beliefs, behavior and environment as: reciprocal determinism the collective unconscious unconditional positive regard the looking-glass self

a therapist accepts a client fully, without judging her choices, hoping to reduce the gap between how the client sees herself and who she would like to be. this approach is most closely associated with: b. f. skinner’s behaviorism sigmund freud’s psychoanalytic theory carl rogers’s humanistic theory hans eysenck’s trait theory

researchers measured extraversion in pairs of relatives (table). which conclusion is best supported? genes contribute substantially to extraversion, while the shared family environment contributes little. the shared family environment is the main source of similarity in extraversion. extraversion is determined entirely by genes. fraternal twins raised together are more similar than identical twins raised apart.

a 78-year-old retired teacher looks back on her life with satisfaction, feels that her choices were meaningful, and calmly accepts that death is approaching. erikson would say she has successfully resolved the crisis of: identity vs role confusion generativity vs stagnation intimacy vs isolation integrity vs despair

a 19-year-old plans to become a pharmacist because her parents are pharmacists. she has never considered other careers or questioned this plan. in marcia’s model, her identity status is: identity diffusion moratorium identity achievement foreclosure

asked whether a man should steal a drug he cannot afford in order to save his dying wife, a student answers, “no, because if everyone broke laws whenever they felt like it, society would fall apart.” this reasoning is most typical of which level of kohlberg’s theory? preconventional, focused on self-interest and fair exchange preconventional, focused on avoiding punishment postconventional, focused on universal ethical principles conventional, focused on maintaining law and social order

a 4-year-old watches juice poured from a short, wide glass into a tall, thin glass and insists the tall glass now holds more. according to piaget, this child: is in the formal operational stage and reasons abstractly is in the sensorimotor stage and lacks object permanence is in the concrete operational stage and reasons logically about volume is in the preoperational stage and has not yet mastered conservation

a 9-year-old in piaget’s concrete operational stage would typically be able to do which of the following? i. recognize that a flattened ball of clay contains the same amount as before ii. mentally reverse an action, such as pouring water back into its original glass iii. systematically test hypotheses about an abstract problem i only ii only i and ii only i, ii and iii

a tutor watches a student struggle with a stoichiometry problem she cannot solve alone, then gives hints that let her solve it, gradually removing the hints as she improves. this approach most closely reflects: kohlberg’s conventional morality piaget’s stage of formal operations vygotsky’s zone of proximal development and scaffolding erikson’s industry vs inferiority

in a study of adolescent identity, two trained coders independently read each interview transcript and classify the teen into one of marcia’s four identity statuses. they assign the same status for 92% of transcripts. this figure is best described as evidence of the measure’s: external validity construct validity test–retest reliability inter-rater reliability

a researcher tests 20-year-olds and 70-year-olds on the same day and finds that the older adults score much lower on a computer-based reasoning test. she concludes that reasoning declines with age. what is the most serious problem with this conclusion? the study is longitudinal, so dropout may bias the result. testing both groups on the same day introduces order effects. the sample should have included only 70-year-olds. age is confounded with cohort differences, such as lifelong experience with computers.

a researcher measures conscientiousness with a self-report questionnaire given to job applicants and finds that almost all of them score very high. which change would best improve the validity of the measure? shorten the questionnaire so applicants finish faster give the same questionnaire again one week later increase the number of applicants who complete the questionnaire add ratings from people who know each applicant well, such as former supervisors

name: Psychological disorders
t: a patient hears voices that no one else hears. this symptom of schizophrenia is classified as: a positive symptom a negative symptom a cognitive symptom a mood symptom
a person feels persistent fear that is out of proportion to a specific harmless object. this is most consistent with: aphasia specific phobia anterograde amnesia narcolepsy
which manual is used in the united states to classify psychological disorders? dsm 5 tr icd 3 the mcat outline the big five inventory

the biopsychosocial model explains disorders as resulting from: biological, psychological and social factors together biological factors, such as genes and brain chemistry unresolved unconscious conflicts from early childhood learned behaviors shaped by reinforcement history

major depressive disorder involves: at least two weeks of depressed mood or lost interest, plus other symptoms episodes of elevated mood and energy lasting at least one week chronic low mood lasting at least two years with milder, persistent symptoms recurrent, unexpected panic attacks with persistent fear of more
bipolar i disorder is defined by: at least one manic episode only depressive episodes constant mild sadness repeated panic attacks

generalized anxiety disorder involves: excessive, hard to control worry about many things intense fear of one specific object or situation recurrent, unexpected panic attacks and fear of more intrusive memories and avoidance after a trauma
repeated unwanted thoughts that cause anxiety, and rituals done to reduce it, describe: obsessive compulsive disorder generalized anxiety disorder specific phobia bipolar disorder
which disorder can develop after a traumatic event, with flashbacks, avoidance and hypervigilance? post traumatic stress disorder (ptsd) dissociative identity disorder panic disorder schizophrenia

which is a negative symptom of schizophrenia? flat affect (little emotional expression) hallucinations (false sensory perceptions) delusions (fixed false beliefs) disorganized speech (derailed thought)

the dopamine hypothesis of schizophrenia proposes: too much dopamine activity in certain brain pathways too little dopamine activity throughout the brain too little serotonin activity in mood related pathways too much gaba activity in the prefrontal cortex
which is a key feature of dissociative identity disorder? two or more distinct identity states hallucinations of voices repeated panic attacks extreme mood swings

which personality disorder is marked by disregard for others' rights and lack of remorse? antisocial personality disorder borderline personality disorder avoidant personality disorder obsessive compulsive personality disorder

unstable relationships, self image and emotions, along with intense fear of abandonment, describe: borderline personality disorder narcissistic personality disorder schizoid personality disorder paranoid personality disorder

somatic symptom disorder involves: excessive worry about physical symptoms that disrupts daily life intentionally faking physical symptoms for external gain neurological symptoms like paralysis with no medical cause persistent fear of having a serious illness despite few or no symptoms

a patient has sudden episodes of intense fear with a pounding heart and shortness of breath, and now worries constantly about having another. the most likely diagnosis is: panic disorder generalized anxiety disorder specific phobia social anxiety disorder
a child has trouble paying attention, is very restless and acts impulsively at school and home. the most likely diagnosis is: adhd autism spectrum disorder conduct disorder bipolar disorder

autism spectrum disorder is characterized mainly by: difficulties with social communication and restricted, repetitive behaviors persistent inattention, hyperactivity and impulsivity beginning in early childhood intrusive thoughts and repetitive rituals that reduce anxiety below average intellectual functioning and adaptive skills

selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (ssris) work by: blocking serotonin reuptake, so more serotonin stays in the synapse blocking serotonin receptors, so less serotonin signal is received inhibiting the enzyme that breaks down serotonin and other monoamines increasing serotonin release from presynaptic vesicles

cognitive behavioral therapy (cbt) for depression mainly aims to: change unhelpful thought patterns and behaviors uncover unconscious childhood conflicts change brain chemistry with drugs interpret dreams

exposure therapy for phobias works through: gradual exposure to the feared stimulus until fear extinguishes pairing the feared stimulus with an unpleasant stimulus exploring the unconscious conflicts that caused the fear rewarding avoidance of the feared stimulus to lower anxiety

the diathesis stress model proposes that disorders develop when: an underlying vulnerability interacts with stressful life events enough stress causes a disorder regardless of vulnerability a genetic vulnerability causes a disorder regardless of stress learned helplessness develops after uncontrollable events
seasonal affective disorder (depression with a seasonal pattern) is often treated with: bright light therapy antipsychotics exposure therapy surgery

a medication blocks dopamine receptors and reduces a patient's hallucinations, but the patient develops tremors and stiffness. why? blocking dopamine in the basal ganglia causes parkinson like effects blocking dopamine in the cerebellum causes tremor and poor balance excess serotonin from the drug causes muscle rigidity and tremor blocking acetylcholine at muscles causes stiffness and tremor

a researcher notes that schizophrenia occurs in about 1% of the general population, but the identical twin of an affected person develops it about 40 50% of the time. what does this pattern suggest? genes contribute, but environment matters since concordance isn't 100% schizophrenia is purely genetic, since twins share nearly all dna schizophrenia is purely environmental, since twins share a home genes matter little, since most identical twins remain unaffected

in the dsm 5 tr, post traumatic stress disorder is classified in which category? trauma and stressor related disorders anxiety disorders dissociative disorders obsessive compulsive and related disorders
persistent depressive disorder (dysthymia) in adults requires depressed mood for most of the day, more days than not, for at least: 2 years 2 weeks 6 months 10 years

a patient is convinced that the government has implanted a chip in his tooth to track him, despite clear evidence that it is not true. this is an example of: a delusion a hallucination an obsession a compulsion

avoidant, dependent and obsessive compulsive personality disorders belong to which dsm 5 tr cluster? cluster c (anxious or fearful) cluster a (odd or eccentric) cluster b (dramatic or erratic) cluster d (impulsive or detached)

a college student intensely fears being judged during class presentations and at parties, so she avoids them; this has lasted for over a year. the most likely diagnosis is: social anxiety disorder agoraphobia generalized anxiety disorder panic disorder

agoraphobia is best described as intense fear of: situations where escape or help might be hard to get being judged or embarrassed by other people one specific object or animal, such as spiders or dogs having a serious undiagnosed illness

after a frightening argument, a patient suddenly cannot move her right arm. neurological testing finds no damage, and the symptom does not fit any known neurological disease. dsm 5 tr calls this: functional neurological symptom disorder illness anxiety disorder factitious disorder imposed on self somatic symptom disorder

how does illness anxiety disorder differ from somatic symptom disorder? illness anxiety involves few or no symptoms but heavy fear of illness illness anxiety involves many symptoms but no worry about them illness anxiety is always caused by a real medical disease illness anxiety involves faking symptoms for money or benefits

a man often feels as if he is watching himself from outside his body, as though in a movie, but he knows this feeling is not real. this describes: depersonalization/derealization disorder dissociative identity disorder schizophrenia dissociative amnesia with dissociative fugue
in large u.s. surveys, which category of mental disorders is the most common in a given year? anxiety disorders schizophrenia spectrum disorders dissociative disorders personality disorders

a 22 year old has had hallucinations, disorganized speech and delusions for 3 months. medical causes and substance use have been ruled out. based on duration, the most fitting diagnosis is: schizophreniform disorder schizophrenia brief psychotic disorder schizoid personality disorder

a woman is found working at a diner in another state. she cannot recall who she is or how she got there, and she has no memory of her previous life after a traumatic loss. the most likely diagnosis is: dissociative amnesia with dissociative fugue dissociative identity disorder major neurocognitive disorder with memory loss depersonalization/derealization disorder

a patient demands special treatment from staff, exaggerates his achievements, needs constant admiration and shows little empathy for other patients. which personality disorder fits best? narcissistic personality disorder histrionic personality disorder obsessive compulsive personality disorder avoidant personality disorder

a man dresses eccentrically, believes he can sense others' thoughts, has odd speech and few close friends, but does not have sustained hallucinations or delusions. which personality disorder fits best? schizotypal personality disorder schizoid personality disorder obsessive compulsive personality disorder antisocial personality disorder

an adult cannot make everyday decisions without lots of reassurance, lets her partner choose her clothes and job, and panics at the thought of being left to care for herself. which disorder fits best? dependent personality disorder borderline personality disorder avoidant personality disorder histrionic personality disorder

a man's apartment is so filled with old newspapers and boxes that he cannot use his kitchen. he becomes very distressed at any attempt to discard them. which disorder fits best? hoarding disorder obsessive compulsive personality disorder illness anxiety disorder generalized anxiety disorder

a woman has a history of major depressive episodes. she now has 5 days of elevated mood, little need for sleep and fast speech; friends notice, but she keeps working normally and is never hospitalized or psychotic. the most likely diagnosis is: bipolar ii disorder bipolar i disorder cyclothymic disorder persistent depressive disorder

brain imaging of people with schizophrenia most consistently shows which structural difference compared with controls? enlarged ventricles and reduced cortical gray matter smaller ventricles and more cortical gray matter enlarged hippocampi and thicker frontal lobe gray matter no measurable structural differences

two patients both check things repeatedly. patient 1 finds her checking senseless and distressing; patient 2 believes his strict rules and perfectionism are simply the right way to live. which is most likely? patient 1 has ocd; patient 2 has obsessive compulsive personality disorder patient 1 has obsessive compulsive personality disorder; patient 2 has ocd both patients have ocd, since both show repeated checking both patients have obsessive compulsive personality disorder

for more than 2 years, an adult has had many periods of mild highs and mild lows. none meet the full criteria for a hypomanic or major depressive episode. the best diagnosis is: cyclothymic disorder bipolar ii disorder persistent depressive disorder borderline personality disorder

autopsy of a patient with progressive memory loss shows beta amyloid plaques, neurofibrillary tangles of tau and loss of acetylcholine producing neurons. which treatment aims to make up for the neurotransmitter loss? a cholinesterase inhibitor to slow acetylcholine breakdown a dopamine receptor blocker to lower dopamine signaling an ssri to block the reuptake of serotonin at synapses a benzodiazepine to enhance gaba activity at synapses

ssris block serotonin reuptake within hours of the first dose, yet patients with depression usually need 2 6 weeks to feel better. what does this delay suggest? recovery depends on slower brain changes, not just higher serotonin ssris do not actually change serotonin levels in the synapse depression is caused only by having too much serotonin patients must first become tolerant to the drug's side effects

dogs first exposed to shocks they could not escape later failed to escape shocks even when they could easily jump a barrier. dogs never exposed to inescapable shock learned to escape quickly. how is this finding applied to human depression? learned helplessness: experiences of no control can lead to passivity and hopelessness classical conditioning: the barrier became a conditioned stimulus for pleasure and calm drive reduction: the dogs' hunger drive was stronger than their drive to avoid pain habituation: repeated shocks made the dogs stop noticing the pain of later shocks

ketamine and pcp block nmda type glutamate receptors. in healthy volunteers, they can produce hallucinations, flat affect and disorganized thinking. what does this best support? reduced glutamate signaling may contribute to schizophrenia's symptoms schizophrenia is caused only by having too much dopamine activity schizophrenia symptoms come only from the drugs patients take nmda receptors play no part in perception or thinking at all

fourteen months after her husband died, a 60 year old woman still feels intense longing for him nearly every day, feels part of herself has died, and cannot return to work or social activities. she has no prior psychiatric history and does not meet criteria for a major depressive episode. which dsm 5 tr diagnosis fits best? prolonged grief disorder post traumatic stress disorder adjustment disorder persistent depressive disorder

for most dsm 5 tr diagnoses, symptoms must do more than exist. they must also: cause clinically significant distress or impairment be confirmed by a brain scan or blood test begin before the person reaches adulthood appear in at least two family members
in the dsm 5 tr, obsessive compulsive disorder is placed in which category? obsessive compulsive and related disorders anxiety disorders trauma and stressor related disorders personality disorders
lithium is a mood stabilizer used mainly to treat which disorder? bipolar i disorder schizophrenia generalized anxiety disorder attention deficit/hyperactivity disorder
compared with men, women are diagnosed with major depressive disorder: about twice as often about half as often about equally often about ten times as often

after david rosenhan's 1973 pseudopatient study, one hospital was told that fake patients would try to get admitted over the next 3 months. staff rated 41 of 193 new admissions as likely pseudopatients, but rosenhan had sent none. what does this follow up most directly suggest? staff could not reliably tell real patients from healthy people in this setting staff were able to spot every pseudopatient once they were warned most of the 193 new admissions were healthy people faking symptoms diagnostic labels have no effect on how staff interpret behavior

electroconvulsive therapy (ect) is most often used today for: severe depression that has not responded to other treatments mild anxiety in patients who have never been treated by anyone specific phobias, as the first treatment tried attention problems in school aged children

aaron beck proposed that people with depression hold a 'cognitive triad' of negative views about: themselves, the world and the future their parents, their peers and their teachers the past, the present and their dreams their body, their mind and their emotions

a clinician treats depression only as a chemical imbalance and focuses solely on finding the right medication, without considering stress, thinking patterns or relationships. this clinician is using the: biomedical model biopsychosocial model diathesis stress model sociocultural model

compared with first generation antipsychotics such as haloperidol, second generation drugs such as risperidone and clozapine generally: also block serotonin receptors and cause fewer movement side effects work only on negative symptoms and do not affect hallucinations increase dopamine release in the striatum to calm the patient carry no risk of weight gain or other metabolic side effects
schizophrenia most typically first appears: in late adolescence or early adulthood in early childhood, usually before age 5 in middle age, around age 50 in late life, after age 70

about twice a week for 6 months, a man eats very large amounts of food quickly, feels out of control while eating, and feels ashamed afterward. he does not vomit, fast or over exercise to make up for it. the most likely diagnosis is: binge eating disorder bulimia nervosa anorexia nervosa, binge eating/purging type avoidant/restrictive food intake disorder

a college student spends hours each day checking a small scar on her chin in mirrors and covering it with makeup. friends say they can barely see it, but she avoids classes because of it. the most likely diagnosis is: body dysmorphic disorder illness anxiety disorder social anxiety disorder anorexia nervosa

for 6 months, a 45 year old accountant has been convinced that a famous actor is secretly in love with her and sends her coded messages. she has no hallucinations, her speech is organized, and she still works well. the most likely diagnosis is: delusional disorder schizophrenia schizotypal personality disorder brief psychotic disorder

after her house burns down, a 30 year old suddenly develops delusions and disorganized speech. medical causes and drugs are ruled out, and her symptoms go away completely after 12 days. the most likely diagnosis is: brief psychotic disorder schizophreniform disorder schizophrenia post traumatic stress disorder

three weeks after giving birth, a woman has had 2 weeks of depressed mood, poor sleep even when the baby sleeps, guilt and loss of interest. which dsm 5 tr diagnosis fits best? major depressive disorder, with peripartum onset persistent depressive disorder adjustment disorder with depressed mood, postpartum bipolar ii disorder

a therapist asks a patient with contamination fears to touch a doorknob and then not wash his hands, repeating this until his anxiety fades on its own. this treatment is: exposure and response prevention systematic desensitization with relaxation aversive conditioning psychodynamic free association

after many years on a first generation antipsychotic, a patient develops involuntary lip smacking, grimacing and tongue movements that persist even after the dose is lowered. this side effect is called: tardive dyskinesia catatonia neuroleptic induced flat affect serotonin syndrome

for 2 years, a woman has had nearly continuous hallucinations and delusions. during most of that time she also met criteria for a major depressive episode, but for one 3 week stretch her psychotic symptoms continued while her mood was normal. the most likely diagnosis is: schizoaffective disorder, depressive type major depressive disorder with psychotic features schizophrenia bipolar i disorder

dexamethasone is a synthetic glucocorticoid that normally signals the brain to cut acth release. the graph shows hypothetical morning cortisol levels before and after a dose. what do the results for the patients with major depressive disorder (mdd) suggest? weakened negative feedback in the hpa axis an adrenal gland that cannot make cortisol too little crh released by the hypothalamus normal hpa regulation in both groups

patient 1 secretly injects herself with insulin to cause low blood sugar, with no goal except to be cared for as a sick person. patient 2 fakes back pain to get opioid prescriptions to sell. which is correct? patient 1 has factitious disorder; patient 2 is malingering patient 1 is malingering; patient 2 has factitious disorder both patients have functional neurological symptom disorder both patients have somatic symptom disorder

a patient with parkinson's disease takes l dopa combined with carbidopa, a drug that cannot cross the blood brain barrier. what is carbidopa's main purpose? it blocks l dopa's conversion to dopamine outside the brain it converts l dopa to dopamine faster inside the brain it blocks dopamine receptors in the brain to reduce tremor it replaces the dopamine neurons lost from the substantia nigra

a patient with anorexia nervosa sometimes binges and then vomits. why would a clinician not also diagnose bulimia nervosa? binge purge episodes occurring only during anorexia fit its binge eating/purging type bulimia nervosa requires binges at least five times every day for a whole year bulimia can only be diagnosed in patients who are above normal weight dsm 5 tr does not allow anyone to have two diagnoses at the same time

a patient taking a monoamine oxidase inhibitor (maoi) for depression eats aged cheese and cured salami. within an hour, his blood pressure rises dangerously high. what best explains this? the drug blocked breakdown of dietary tyramine, which released excess norepinephrine the drug blocked serotonin receptors, so the blood vessels suddenly constricted aged cheese contains cortisol, which adds to the drug's effect on the heart the drug raised gaba levels, which directly stimulated the heart muscle

pet studies of antipsychotics (such as kapur and colleagues, 2000) related how many d2 receptors a dose blocks to clinical response and to movement side effects. the schematic graph summarizes this pattern. which target occupancy offers the best balance? about 65 78% about 40 55% about 85 95% any level above 50%, since effects are similar

the table shows results from a hypothetical trial of treatments for major depressive disorder. which conclusion is best supported by these hypothetical data? gains from cbt lasted better after treatment ended than gains from an ssri alone the ssri alone gave the most lasting benefit after treatment ended the placebo pill produced no improvement in any of the patients combined treatment had both the highest response rate and the lowest relapse rate

family history, life stress and teen depression which pattern in figure 1 best supports the view that vulnerability and stress work together? high stress raised mdd rates far more in teens whose parent had depression high stress raised mdd rates by the same amount in both family groups family history raised mdd rates only among the low stress teens mdd rates were similar in all four groups of teens in the study

family history, life stress and teen depression to be diagnosed with major depressive disorder under dsm 5, a teen must have had: at least five symptoms over two weeks, including depressed (in teens, possibly irritable) mood or lost interest depressed mood on most days for at least two years, with no other symptoms required at all at least one episode of abnormally elevated, expansive mood lasting a week or more, with or without depression symptoms that began within one month of a major negative life event

family history, life stress and teen depression why did the researchers exclude teens who had already had a depressive episode at age 14? so that measured life events would come before, not after, the onset of mdd so that every teen in the study would have a parent who had been diagnosed with mdd so that the interviewer would know which teens had a family history so that each group would contain exactly the same number of teens

family history, life stress and teen depression among teens with a parent who had depression, how many times more likely were high stress teens than low stress teens to develop mdd? 4 times 6 times 3 times 18 times

family history, life stress and teen depression the researchers caution that family history is not purely genetic. which planned change best addresses this concern? studying adopted teens, so genetic and rearing parents are different people asking the interviewer to learn each teen's family history before the final interview counting only life events reported by the teens rather than by parents raising the cutoff for high life stress from two events to four events

which conclusion is best supported by figure 1? combined treatment was clearly more effective than erp alone. the ssri alone was as effective as erp plus placebo. combined treatment was not clearly better than erp alone, but both outperformed placebo. no treatment was clearly more effective than placebo.

what was the main purpose of having symptoms rated by independent evaluators who did not know participants' conditions? to reduce rater bias, since erp could not be hidden from participants or therapists to ensure that the four groups had similar baseline scores to increase how well the results generalize to patients outside the study to prevent participants from dropping out of the erp conditions

according to learning theory, compulsions in ocd persist mainly because they: are positively punished by the anxiety that follows them are negatively reinforced by the temporary reduction in anxiety they produce are positively reinforced by praise from family members have undergone extinction during repeated performance

which purposes were served by including the pill placebo alone condition? i. controlling for improvement caused by expecting medication to help ii. controlling for symptom improvement that occurs with time alone, such as regression toward the mean iii. allowing the effect of erp to be isolated by comparison with the erp + placebo condition i only i and ii only ii and iii only i, ii and iii

which explanation best accounts for the pattern in table 1? ssris damaged serotonin receptors, so symptoms returned more often after treatment ended. participants given the ssri were more severely ill at baseline than erp participants. erp was given only to participants least likely to relapse. learning acquired during erp persists after therapy ends, while the ssri's benefit depends largely on continued drug action.

on january 1, 200 residents of a town of 10,000 had a diagnosis of schizophrenia. during the following year, 10 additional residents received a new diagnosis. which statement is correct? the prevalence on january 1 was 2%, and the annual incidence was about 1 per 1,000 people at risk. the incidence on january 1 was 2%, and the annual prevalence was about 1 per 1,000. the prevalence on january 1 was 0.1%, and the annual incidence was 2%. prevalence and incidence were equal, because both count people with the disorder.

in a randomized trial for major depressive disorder, participants received placebo or one of two doses of a new antidepressant for 8 weeks (figure). which conclusion is best supported? both doses were clearly more effective than placebo. only the high dose was clearly more effective than placebo. the low dose was clearly more effective than the high dose. neither dose was clearly more effective than placebo, because placebo also produced improvement.

for the past 3 weeks, a 34-year-old has felt sad most of the day, lost interest in her hobbies, slept poorly, felt worthless and had trouble concentrating. she has never had a manic or hypomanic episode. the most likely diagnosis is: bipolar ii disorder persistent depressive disorder (dysthymia) major depressive disorder cyclothymic disorder

a 25-year-old has had 10 days of decreased need for sleep, racing thoughts, grandiose plans and reckless spending that led to hospitalization. which diagnosis is most consistent with this episode? bipolar ii disorder bipolar i disorder major depressive disorder generalized anxiety disorder

a patient with schizophrenia hears voices commenting on his actions, shows a flat facial expression and believes the government implanted a chip in his tooth. which of these are positive symptoms? i. hearing voices ii. flat affect iii. the belief about the chip i only ii only ii and iii only i and iii only

a psychiatrist reviews several findings about patients with psychosis. which provides the strongest support for the dopamine hypothesis of schizophrenia? drugs that block d2 dopamine receptors reduce hallucinations and delusions. patients often have enlarged brain ventricles. people born in late winter have a slightly higher risk of schizophrenia. symptoms usually begin in late adolescence or early adulthood.

a 28-year-old has had several sudden episodes of racing heart, shortness of breath and fear of dying that peak within minutes and come “out of the blue.” for two months she has worried constantly about having another attack. the most likely diagnosis is: specific phobia generalized anxiety disorder panic disorder illness anxiety disorder

six months after a car crash, a paramedic has nightmares and intrusive memories of the crash, avoids driving past the site, startles easily and feels detached from friends. which diagnosis is most likely? major depressive disorder with psychotic features acute stress disorder specific phobia of cars posttraumatic stress disorder

after witnessing a violent assault, a woman suddenly cannot move her right arm. neurological exams and imaging are normal, and she is not faking the weakness. which diagnosis is most consistent? factitious disorder illness anxiety disorder conversion disorder (functional neurological symptom disorder) somatic symptom disorder

a patient has two distinct identities that each take control of her behavior at different times, along with gaps in memory for everyday events. which diagnosis fits best? bipolar i disorder schizophrenia dissociative identity disorder borderline personality disorder

a 30-year-old has a long history of lying, stealing and fighting that began at age 12, shows no remorse after hurting others, and repeatedly ignores obligations at work. which personality disorder is most likely? schizoid personality disorder avoidant personality disorder obsessive-compulsive personality disorder antisocial personality disorder

a patient who started an ssri five days ago asks why she does not feel better yet. which finding poses the greatest challenge to the simple idea that depression is caused only by a lack of synaptic serotonin? drugs that deplete monoamines can trigger depressive symptoms in some people. ssris raise synaptic serotonin within hours, but mood usually improves only after several weeks. ssris reduce depressive symptoms more than placebo in many trials. some antidepressants increase both serotonin and norepinephrine.

the figure shows the approximate lifetime risk of schizophrenia for people who have a relative with the disorder, compared with the general population. which conclusion is best supported? genes contribute substantially to risk, but environmental factors must also matter. schizophrenia is caused entirely by genes. the shared family environment fully explains the pattern. risk does not depend on how closely a person is related to the patient.

researchers plan a trial of a new therapy for depression. which features would strengthen their ability to conclude that the therapy itself caused any improvement? i. random assignment to the therapy or a control condition ii. symptom ratings by clinicians who do not know each patient’s condition iii. letting patients choose whether to receive the therapy i only i and ii only i and iii only i, ii and iii

a study finds that patients with depression have lower levels of a serotonin breakdown product in their cerebrospinal fluid than healthy controls do. which conclusion is most justified? low serotonin causes depression. depression is associated with altered serotonin metabolism, but the direction of causation is unclear. depression causes the brain to stop making serotonin. serotonin is unrelated to depression.

patients with depression received medication, cognitive behavioral therapy (cbt) or both for 12 weeks (figure). which conclusion is best supported? cbt was more effective than medication at week 12. medication worked faster than cbt, with a clear advantage at week 4. at week 12, combined treatment produced lower scores than either treatment alone, while medication and cbt alone ended at similar scores. none of the treatments reduced depression scores over time.

a 20-year-old college student of normal weight repeatedly eats large amounts of food in a short time, feels out of control during these episodes, and then makes herself vomit. which diagnosis is most likely? bulimia nervosa anorexia nervosa binge-eating disorder avoidant/restrictive food intake disorder

name: Social processes & attitudes
t: an experienced surgeon performs a routine procedure faster when students are watching. this illustrates: social loafing social facilitation deindividuation groupthink

a patient collapses in a crowded waiting room and several minutes pass before anyone helps. the best explanation is: the bystander effect, through diffusion of responsibility deindividuation, through loss of self awareness in a crowd group polarization, through discussion that strengthens views social facilitation, through arousal from others' presence
a committee of doctors who mildly favor a new treatment discuss it and finish strongly in favor of it. this is: groupthink group polarization social facilitation conformity to an authority figure

a smoker who knows smoking causes cancer tells himself, "my grandfather smoked and lived to 95." this is an attempt to reduce: cognitive dissonance learned helplessness the just world bias role strain
which term describes behavior adjusted to conform with group expectations? conformity sensitization habituation negative reinforcement

in asch's line judgment experiments, many participants: gave obviously wrong answers to match the group changed their private beliefs about the line lengths conformed less when the group was unanimous obeyed the experimenter's orders to give wrong answers

in milgram's obedience experiments, most participants: gave what they believed were the maximum shocks when instructed refused to continue as soon as the learner began to protest gave stronger shocks than the experimenter instructed them to give saw through the deception and knew the shocks were not real
an attitude has which three components (the abc model)? affective, behavioral and cognitive attention, belief and conformity arousal, behavior and conditioning ability, bias and culture

socialization is the process by which people: learn the norms, values and behaviors of their society inherit behavioral traits from their parents' genes mature physically through predictable developmental stages move up or down in social class across their lifetimes

deindividuation is most likely when people: are anonymous in a large, aroused group are identifiable within a small, calm group are alone and highly self aware are being watched by a familiar audience

social loafing is: putting in less effort when working in a group performing better on easy tasks when others watch adopting more extreme views after group discussion going along with group opinion to fit in
changing your behavior to fit in or be accepted is: normative social influence informational social influence obedience compliance through reciprocity

the foot in the door technique works by: getting someone to agree to a small request first, then a bigger one making a large request first, then a smaller, more reasonable one giving a small favor first so the person feels obligated to return it getting agreement first, then revealing hidden extra costs

according to the elaboration likelihood model, the central route to persuasion involves: careful thinking about the strength of the arguments cues like the speaker's attractiveness or fame emotional appeals and catchy, memorable slogans the sheer number of arguments offered, not their quality
a deviant act in sociology is best defined as: a behavior that violates social norms a behavior that violates written laws a behavior that is statistically rare a behavior that causes harm to others

labeling theory proposes that: being labeled deviant can lead people to adopt a deviant identity deviance arises when people lack legitimate means to reach goals deviance is learned through interaction with deviant peers weak social bonds make people more likely to act deviantly

a student votes for a candidate because a famous celebrity endorses them, without reading the platform. this is: the peripheral route to persuasion the central route cognitive dissonance informational influence

participants in the stanford prison experiment quickly took on harsh 'guard' roles. this suggests that: social roles and situations can strongly shape behavior personality traits mainly determine how people act in roles harsh behavior mostly reflects participants' prior attitudes obedience to direct orders explains most harmful behavior

merton's strain theory explains deviance as arising when: people lack legitimate ways to reach goals their society values people are labeled deviant and come to accept that identity people learn deviant values from close friends and family people's bonds to family and community are weak

differential association theory proposes that people learn deviance from: interacting with others who engage in deviant behavior being labeled as deviant by authority figures lacking legitimate means to achieve social goals inheriting traits that increase impulsive behavior

after spending an hour on a very boring task, participants paid $1 to tell others it was fun rated the task as more enjoyable than those paid $20. why? low pay caused more dissonance, so they changed their attitude to fit the lie higher pay caused more dissonance, so those participants disliked the task low pay made the task feel harder, so they valued their effort more higher pay made participants feel guilty, so they rated the task lower
a group of friends who mildly support a policy become strongly in favor after discussing it together. this is: group polarization groupthink social loafing deindividuation

a hospital wants staff to wash hands more often. posters saying 'most of your coworkers wash their hands every time' work better than posters about germs. which principle explains this? descriptive social norms: people follow what most others do injunctive norms: people follow what authorities approve of cognitive dissonance: people change attitudes to match actions obedience: people follow direct orders from authority figures

in a study, people who were told that a famous expert supported a claim agreed more, even when the argument was weak. which persuasion factor is at work? source credibility (a peripheral cue) argument strength (central route) cognitive dissonance group polarization

members of a planning team never raise doubts about a risky plan because they want to keep the group harmonious, and the plan fails. this is: groupthink group polarization social facilitation the bystander effect

participants heard someone having a seizure, with different numbers of other people believed to be listening (graph). which concept best explains the trend? diffusion of responsibility social facilitation group polarization the foot in the door effect

a coworker with no authority over you asks you to cover her shift, and you agree. changing your behavior in response to a direct request like this is called: compliance obedience conformity deindividuation

when a student talks loudly during a lecture, nearby classmates glare and shush him. in sociology, this reaction is an example of: an informal negative sanction a formal positive sanction a formal negative sanction an informal positive sanction
wearing pajamas to a formal wedding would violate a casual, everyday social norm that carries little moral weight. such norms are called: folkways mores taboos formal laws
during early childhood, which agent of socialization usually has the greatest influence? the family the mass media the workplace the peer group

a first year medical student fumbles more than usual while placing an iv when an attending physician is watching. according to zajonc, why? an audience raises arousal, which impairs performance on new, hard tasks an audience lowers arousal, which makes all tasks more difficult an audience causes social loafing, so the student tries less hard an audience always improves performance, so another cause is needed

on her first day, a new hospital intern is unsure which entrance to use during a fire drill, so she follows the other staff. changing behavior because you believe others know what is correct is: informational social influence normative social influence obedience to an authority figure group polarization

new army recruits have their hair cut, wear uniforms and follow strict schedules as their old identities are stripped away and replaced. erving goffman called settings like boot camp or prisons 'total institutions.' this process is: resocialization anticipatory socialization primary socialization assimilation

according to ajzen's theory of planned behavior, a person's intention to get a flu shot is best predicted by which combination? attitude, subjective norms and perceived behavioral control id, ego and superego working in balance consistency, distinctiveness and consensus information alarm, resistance and exhaustion

workers in one factory report nausea and dizziness after a rumor about toxic fumes spreads, but inspectors find no chemical exposure. this form of collective behavior is best described as: mass psychogenic illness a short lived fashion fad group polarization diffusion of responsibility

a patient hides his hiv diagnosis from coworkers because he fears it would cause them to see him as discredited and less acceptable. erving goffman called this kind of devalued attribute a: stigma master status folkway sanction

a clinic volunteer first asks a donor to fund a $10,000 equipment purchase. after the donor refuses, she asks for a $100 donation instead, and the donor agrees. which technique is this? door in the face foot in the door lowball technique that's not all technique

a car dealer gets a customer to agree to buy a car for $20,000, then says that the price will actually be $21,500 because of 'fees.' the customer still buys it. which technique did the dealer use? lowball technique door in the face foot in the door norm of reciprocity

a pre med student begins wearing a white coat to volunteer shifts, reads medical journals and practices speaking like the doctors she shadows, even though she has not yet started medical school. this is: anticipatory socialization resocialization in a total institution primary socialization deindividuation

a teen shoplifts once on a dare and still sees himself as a good kid. after he is arrested, his school and neighbors treat him as a 'delinquent,' and he begins to see himself that way and steals more. lemert would call the later stealing: secondary deviance primary deviance anomie differential association

nursing students working on a group project are putting in little effort. which change would most likely reduce this social loafing? grade each member's identifiable contribution separately make the group larger so that each member feels less pressure give only one shared grade to the whole group at the end let members submit their work without names attached

a health class shows teens weak versions of tobacco ad arguments and then helps them refute each one. later, the teens resist real tobacco ads better than classmates who did not get this training. this is: attitude inoculation foot in the door cognitive dissonance peripheral route persuasion

residents who survived a grueling intern year often insist that it was valuable and should not be made easier for future interns. which concept best explains this? effort justification the overjustification effect social facilitation normative social influence

in the 1930s, richard lapiere traveled with a chinese couple and was refused service at only 1 of about 250 hotels and restaurants. yet when he later mailed letters asking whether they would serve chinese guests, over 90% of the replies said no. what does this study suggest? stated attitudes do not always predict actual behavior people's behavior always matches their written attitudes prejudice was nearly absent among business owners then mailed surveys are always more accurate than observation

in variations of asch's line judgment experiment, what happened when just one other confederate gave the correct answer before the participant spoke? conformity dropped sharply compared with a unanimous majority conformity rose because the dissenter made participants nervous conformity stayed the same because the majority was still large participants conformed to the dissenter instead of the majority

in milgram's obedience studies, which change most clearly decreased obedience? the experimenter gave orders by telephone rather than in person the study was run at yale rather than at a rundown office the learner was in another room rather than right beside them the experimenter wore a lab coat and stood beside the teacher

according to the elaboration likelihood model, a patient is most likely to process a pamphlet about a new medication through the central route when he: is highly motivated and able to think carefully about it is tired, distracted and has little time to read it cares mainly about how attractive the pamphlet looks has no personal connection to the medication at all

a woman is asked whether she likes jazz. she thinks, 'i listen to jazz stations a lot, so i guess i like it.' which theory best explains how she formed this attitude? self perception theory cognitive dissonance theory social identity theory drive reduction theory

in hofling's hospital study, an unknown 'doctor' phoned nurses and told them to give 20 mg of an unfamiliar drug, though the label said 10 mg was the maximum dose. almost all of the nurses (21 of 22) were about to give it before being stopped. which conclusion best fits? obedience to perceived authority can override training and safety rules nurses conformed because they saw other nurses giving the drug the nurses were persuaded by strong arguments via the central route the nurses showed social loafing because they worked in large teams

in a dark room, a still point of light appears to move (the autokinetic effect). muzafer sherif found that people estimating the movement in groups gradually converged on a shared estimate, and they kept using it when later tested alone. what does this show? groups create norms in ambiguous situations, and people internalize them people ignore others when a task is uncertain and rely on themselves conformity happens only when the correct answer is obvious to all group estimates converge because members are paid to agree
a driver gets a speeding ticket and must pay a fine. in sociology, this is an example of: a formal negative sanction an informal negative sanction a formal positive sanction a folkway violation

in the 1890s, norman triplett observed that cyclists rode faster when racing against others than when riding alone against the clock. this was an early demonstration of: social facilitation social loafing deindividuation group polarization
during adolescence, which agent of socialization typically gains the most influence compared with earlier childhood? the peer group the family the workplace religious institutions
a dance challenge spreads quickly on social media, becomes hugely popular for a few weeks, and then fades. this form of collective behavior is best called a: fad riot moral panic mass hysteria

news outlets and politicians spread exaggerated fears that a new music style is turning teens into criminals, though crime rates have not changed. sociologist stanley cohen called this kind of reaction: a moral panic a fad groupthink cultural diffusion

serge moscovici found that a small minority in a group could sway the majority's judgments. the minority was most influential when it: held its position consistently over time changed its answers often to seem flexible agreed with the majority on most trials stayed silent and let the majority speak first

people read a persuasive article that was attributed to a source with low credibility. at first they were unconvinced, but weeks later their attitudes had shifted toward the article's position. this is called: the sleeper effect the mere exposure effect the inoculation effect the overjustification effect

a teen has close ties to his family, is committed to plans for college, spends after school hours in sports and believes the law should be followed. travis hirschi's theory predicts he is unlikely to commit crimes because of strong: social bonds strain between goals and means differential association with deviant peers labels applied by authorities

fear based health messages, such as graphic warnings about smoking, are most likely to change behavior when they: also give clear, doable steps to avoid the threat arouse as much fear as possible, whatever the advice avoid mentioning the audience's personal risk come from a source the audience sees as biased

a two sided message presents the opposing view and then refutes it. compared with a one sided message, it tends to persuade best when the audience: is well informed or initially disagrees already agrees and knows little about the issue is distracted and paying little attention is mainly swayed by the speaker's looks

a pre med student badly wants to get into medical school but, short on study time, buys stolen exam answers. in robert merton's strain theory, which adaptation is this? innovation ritualism retreatism rebellion

on halloween, researchers left trick or treaters alone with a candy bowl and a request to take only one piece. some were asked their names and addresses; others were not (approximate results shown). which concept do these results best support? deindividuation social facilitation normative social influence group polarization

a woman chooses between two toasters she likes equally. after buying one, she rates it much better than before and rates the one she rejected as worse. which process does this best show? reducing dissonance after a decision using the foot in the door technique showing the mere exposure effect engaging in group polarization

a hospital board has fallen into groupthink in past decisions. which change would most likely prevent it? assigning a devil's advocate and having the leader share her view last having the leader state her preferred plan clearly at the very start keeping outside experts away to protect group harmony requiring a quick, unanimous vote to avoid long arguments

a medical resident enjoys hard thinking and carefully weighs evidence. according to the elaboration likelihood model, a persuasive pamphlet will most likely influence her through: the central route, based on argument quality the peripheral route, based on attractive models the peripheral route, based on the number of claims neither route, since she will resist all persuasion

a sociologist notes that a poor teen caught shoplifting gets jail time, while a wealthy executive who embezzles millions pays a fine. she argues that laws and enforcement mainly protect the interests of powerful groups. which perspective on deviance is she using? conflict theory functionalism differential association theory social bond theory

the graph shows approximate results from solomon asch's line judgment studies in which the size of the unanimous, incorrect majority was varied. what does it show? conformity rose sharply up to about 3 people, then leveled off conformity rose steadily as each extra person joined the group conformity was highest when only one person disagreed majority size had no effect on the amount of conformity

a drug company representative brings free lunches and small gifts to a clinic. afterward, some physicians feel they 'owe' the company and prescribe its drugs more often. which principle is at work? the norm of reciprocity the door in the face technique the bystander effect group polarization

milgram's original obedience studies went up to 450 volts. for ethical reasons, jerry burger's 2009 partial replication stopped at 150 volts. why was 150 v a reasonable stopping point for estimating obedience? in milgram's data, most who passed 150 v went on to the maximum in milgram's data, no participant ever obeyed past 150 v at 150 v the learner fell silent and stopped responding shocks above 150 v would have injured the learner

in a study by latane and darley, smoke poured into a room while participants filled out forms (approximate results shown). why did so few people report the smoke when two calm confederates ignored it? they used others' calm as a sign it wasn't an emergency they feared punishment for interrupting the experiment they could not see the smoke clearly with others present they believed the confederates had already reported it

davidson and jaccard (1979) measured women's attitudes at different levels of specificity and then tracked whether they used birth control pills over the next 2 years (approximate correlations shown). which conclusion is best supported? attitudes predict behavior best when they match the behavior's specificity general attitudes predict specific behaviors better than specific ones attitudes are unrelated to behavior at every level of measurement specific attitudes predict poorly because people lie on surveys

in one version of asch's line judgment study, the participant heard the group's wrong answers but wrote his own answer privately. conformity dropped sharply. this suggests that conformity in the original study was driven largely by: normative social influence informational social influence deindividuation social facilitation

in a study by johnson and downing, anonymous participants dressed in hooded robes resembling ku klux klan robes or in nurses' uniforms could shock a learner. those in nurses' uniforms gave fewer shocks than controls. what does this suggest about deindividuation? it makes people more responsive to the norms the situation cues it always increases aggression, whatever the setting or the costume it occurs only when people are identified by name it reduces the impact of clothing on behavior

darley and batson (1973) asked seminary students to walk to another building to give a talk, either about jobs or about the parable of the good samaritan. on the way they passed a man slumped in a doorway. the talk topic had little effect, while time pressure had the effect shown (approximate data). which conclusion is best supported? situational time pressure predicted helping more than the ideas on their minds thinking about the good samaritan made students far more likely to help students in a hurry helped more because they were more physically aroused helping depended mainly on stable personality traits, not situations

in a hypothetical study, students read a message favoring a new graduation exam policy. researchers varied argument strength, source expertise and how much the policy affected the students. the table shows mean agreement (1 9). which conclusion fits these hypothetical data? argument quality mattered under high relevance; expertise mattered under low source expertise mattered under high relevance; arguments under low argument quality and expertise mattered equally in both conditions neither argument quality nor expertise affected agreement at all

correcting misperceived drinking norms the situation described in the first paragraph, in which most students privately doubt a practice but wrongly assume that others support it, is best described as: pluralistic ignorance groupthink deindividuation group polarization

name: Social interaction

a reference group is a group that: people use to evaluate themselves people always belong to has no influence is made up of strangers only

an in group is: a group a person identifies with a group a person dislikes any group of strangers a group of three people
which describes a dyad? a group of two people a group of three a large organization a crowd

a nurse feels torn because her job requires both caring for patients and enforcing strict hospital rules that frustrate them. this is: role strain role conflict role exit status inconsistency

aggression is more likely when people are frustrated and blocked from a goal. this is the: frustration aggression hypothesis contact hypothesis social facilitation effect mere exposure effect

in a study, roommates who were randomly assigned became friends more often than people living farther apart. which factor does this best illustrate? proximity similarity physical attractiveness reciprocity

a new nurse imitates the communication style of experienced coworkers to fit into the unit. this is an example of: workplace (occupational) socialization role strain from competing demands within the unit groupthink among the nursing staff social facilitation by coworkers
during intake, a clinic records each patient's age, sex assigned at birth and race. all three describe which kind of status? ascribed statuses achieved statuses master statuses social roles

after 30 years as an icu nurse, rosa retires. for months she still thinks of herself as a nurse, then slowly builds a new identity as a hospice volunteer. this process is called: role exit role strain role conflict role taking
two hundred students share a large biology lecture. they rarely talk and meet only to finish the course. sociologists would call them a: secondary group primary group reference group dyad

two suspects are questioned separately. each does better for himself by betraying the other, yet if both betray, both end up worse off than if both had stayed silent. this game theory situation is the: prisoner's dilemma tragedy of the commons zero sum game hawk dove game

a sociologist contrasts a small farming village, where ties rest on kinship and shared tradition, with a large city where most ties are impersonal and based on self interest. in ferdinand tonnies' terms, the village is an example of: gemeinschaft (community) gesellschaft (society) organic solidarity a secondary group

members of an isolated new guinea group with little exposure to outside media correctly matched photos of facial expressions to stories about emotional events. this finding most supports the idea that: basic facial expressions of emotion are largely universal display rules about emotion are identical in every culture facial expressions are learned mainly from mass media facial expressions are unrelated to what people feel
a hockey player trips an opponent only to stop a scoring chance, not out of anger. this is best described as: instrumental aggression hostile aggression displaced aggression relational aggression

a patient advocacy group starts with every member voting on every decision. ten years later, a small board makes all decisions and works mainly to keep its own positions. robert michels called this pattern the: iron law of oligarchy iron cage of rationality mcdonaldization of society bureaucratic ritualism

an urgent care chain schedules every visit for exactly 12 minutes, uses scripted questions and ranks doctors by patients seen per hour. which concept does this best illustrate? mcdonaldization iron law of oligarchy charismatic authority anomie
