a new graduate finds her first nursing job through a former classmate's cousin whom she met once, rather than through her close friends. this is best explained by: the strength of weak ties, which reach new information loyalty within her primary group of close friends the mere exposure effect from repeated contact role strain within her closest friendships

in a study of dating couples, observers rated each partner's attractiveness separately. partners' ratings were much more similar than chance would predict. this supports the: matching hypothesis mere exposure effect halo effect proximity effect

peahens prefer to mate with peacocks that have the largest, most colorful tails, even though such tails make males easier for predators to catch. this is an example of: intersexual selection (mate choice) intrasexual selection (male competition) natural selection for survival kin selection

an infant in the strange situation approaches the returning caregiver, then freezes, looks dazed and backs away. this pattern has been linked most strongly to: disorganized attachment, often tied to frightening care avoidant attachment, caused by warm, consistent care secure attachment, caused by responsive caregiving ambivalent attachment, caused by an easy temperament

vampire bats that fail to feed often receive regurgitated blood from roostmates, including unrelated bats that shared with them before. unrelated bats that never share are less likely to get help. this best supports: reciprocal altruism kin selection sexual selection purely selfless altruism

in elephant seals, a few males mate with most females, and males are several times larger than females. why does this polygynous mating system tend to produce such large differences in body size? intense male male competition favors larger males females prefer smaller, less aggressive males monogamy pushes both sexes toward equal size males provide more parental care, needing mass

in a hawk dove model, a population settles at a stable mix of aggressive and peaceful individuals that no rare new strategy can outperform. game theorists call this mix: an evolutionarily stable strategy a purely zero sum strategy a prisoner's dilemma outcome a product of group selection

a ground squirrel's alarm call lowers its own expected reproduction by 1 offspring but saves its full siblings, adding an expected 3 offspring to them in total. using hamilton's rule (rb > c), with r = 0.5 for full siblings, the alarm call: should be favored, because 0.5 × 3 = 1.5 exceeds 1 should not be favored, since the caller loses 1 offspring should be favored only if siblings later repay the caller should not be favored, since rb must exceed 2c to count

the just world hypothesis is the belief that: people get what they deserve the world is unpredictable everyone is equal bad things happen to good people

ethnocentrism is: judging other cultures by the standards of your own judging each culture by its own standards and values adopting the customs of a dominant culture rejecting your own culture in favor of another

the actor observer bias means people tend to: explain their own behavior by situation, but others' by personality explain their own behavior by personality, but others' by situation credit successes to themselves and failures to the situation overestimate personality causes for everyone's behavior equally

the halo effect occurs when: one positive trait leads to positive judgments about other traits one negative trait outweighs many positive traits in judgments first impressions anchor all later judgments of a person people see their own group as more varied than other groups

stereotype threat is: underperforming from worry about confirming a stereotype of one's group treating group members unfairly because of a stereotype about them rising to meet others' high expectations about one's abilities holding negative attitudes toward members of another group

according to the contact hypothesis, prejudice is reduced when groups: interact as equals working toward shared goals compete with each other for limited resources are kept apart to reduce chances for conflict learn facts about each other without direct contact

institutional discrimination is: unfair treatment built into the policies of organizations or society unfair treatment by one prejudiced individual toward another person negative attitudes that members of one group hold about another oversimplified, generalized beliefs about the traits of a social group
prejudice toward people in other groups, combined with favoring your own, is linked to: in group bias the mere exposure effect the halo effect altruism
a professor assumes a student who failed an exam is lazy, ignoring that the student was ill. this is: the fundamental attribution error the self serving bias the just world hypothesis the halo effect
someone says 'i won the game because i'm talented, but lost because the referee was unfair.' this is: self serving bias fundamental attribution error actor observer bias hindsight bias

kelley's covariation model uses consistency, distinctiveness and consensus to decide whether a behavior is caused by the person or the situation. if everyone reacts the same way (high consensus) and the person reacts this way only in this situation (high distinctiveness), the cause is most likely: the situation the person's personality random chance biology

a hiring manager unknowingly rates resumes with typically male names more favorably than identical resumes with typically female names. this shows: implicit (unconscious) bias explicit prejudice self serving bias stereotype threat

a medical student notices that after hearing a patient's diagnosis, she 'knew it all along.' this is: hindsight bias confirmation bias anchoring the halo effect

a physician learns that a patient's family expects to make medical decisions together. she tries to understand the practice within the family's own cultural values instead of judging it. she is practicing: cultural relativism ethnocentrism xenocentrism cultural assimilation

a coworker says a nurse snapped at a patient "because she's just a rude person." this explanation is a: dispositional (internal) attribution situational (external) attribution self serving attribution consensus attribution

meeting a cheerful new colleague, sam assumes she must also be generous and trustworthy, based on his beliefs about which traits naturally go together. this reflects: implicit personality theory the just world hypothesis the actor observer bias stereotype threat

staff at one hospital describe their own team as full of different personalities, but say the staff at a rival hospital are "all the same." this illustrates: the out group homogeneity effect the false consensus effect the halo effect group polarization

one group hears a person described as "intelligent, industrious, impulsive, critical, stubborn, envious." another hears the same list in reverse order. the first group rates the person more favorably. this shows: the primacy effect in impression formation the recency effect in impression formation the halo effect of physical attractiveness the false consensus effect

a manager has a positive view of a resident for months, but after one recent serious error, that error dominates her whole impression of him. this illustrates: the recency effect the primacy effect the halo effect the out group homogeneity effect

a student who skips most lectures estimates that 80% of classmates also skip, when the true figure is 20%. this illustrates: the false consensus effect the fundamental attribution error the optimism bias social loafing

most young adults in a survey say they are less likely than the average person their age to be hurt in a car crash. this is: optimism bias the false consensus effect the just world hypothesis hindsight bias

a family insists that imported products are always better than those made in their own country and looks down on local customs. this attitude is called: xenocentrism ethnocentrism cultural relativism assimilation

at a summer camp, two groups of boys grew hostile after contests in which only one group could win prizes. hostility dropped after the groups worked together on a series of shared goals, such as fixing the camp's water supply. the rise in hostility best supports: realistic conflict theory the just world hypothesis stereotype threat the mere exposure effect

during a recession, many residents blame a small immigrant community for job losses that were actually caused by factory automation. this best illustrates: scapegoating cultural relativism stereotype threat the out group homogeneity effect

neighbors begin avoiding the parents of a child with a highly stigmatized illness, even though the parents are healthy. erving goffman called this spread of disgrace to people linked to a stigmatized person: courtesy stigma master status labeling stereotype threat

a landlord refuses to rent to applicants of one religion, even though city laws and policies forbid it. this is an example of: individual discrimination institutional discrimination prejudice without discrimination stereotype threat

after hearing that a stranger was robbed while walking home at night, several people say, "she should have known better." which belief most likely drives this reaction? the just world hypothesis the out group homogeneity effect cultural relativism the primacy effect

before a guest lecture, half a class read that the speaker was "rather warm" and half that he was "rather cold"; the rest of the description was identical. after the same lecture, the 'warm' group rated him as more considerate and sociable. this shows that: central traits strongly shape overall impressions recent information outweighs earlier information actual behavior overrides prior descriptions self serving bias distorts people's self ratings

older adults scored lower on a memory test when told it measured age related memory decline than when told it measured general learning. the best explanation is: stereotype threat self serving bias the fundamental attribution error belief perseverance

in a 'jigsaw' classroom, each student in a mixed ethnicity group learns one part of a lesson and must teach it to the others, because everyone is tested on the whole lesson. prejudice drops over time. the method works mainly through: cooperative interdependence toward a shared goal exposure alone, without any need to cooperate rewards for the single best student in each group teacher praise for the least prejudiced students

maria yells at a nurse. she also yells at other staff in other settings (low distinctiveness), has yelled at this nurse before (high consistency), and no one else yells at this nurse (low consensus). kelley's covariation model predicts observers will attribute her behavior to: maria's personality (an internal cause) the nurse's behavior (an external cause) temporary circumstances of that one day the hospital setting (a situational cause)

a person attributes an out group member's kind act to luck or a special situation, but attributes the same person's rude act to the 'nature' of their group. thomas pettigrew called this: the ultimate attribution error the actor observer bias the self serving bias the false consensus effect

men talked by phone with women they were told (at random) were attractive or unattractive. listeners who heard only the women's side of the call rated the 'attractive' women as warmer and friendlier. this best demonstrates: behavioral confirmation (a self fulfilling prophecy) a halo effect existing only in the men's minds stereotype threat felt by the women themselves the matching hypothesis of romantic attraction

rosenthal and jacobson told teachers that some randomly chosen students were about to 'bloom' intellectually. those students later showed larger iq gains. which explanation is best supported by later research? teachers gave them more warmth, attention and feedback those students truly had higher ability at the start those students worked harder after seeing their scores graders scored those students' tests more generously

participants were falsely told they were very good at telling real suicide notes from fake ones. even after learning the feedback was made up, they still believed they had above average skill. this is: belief perseverance hindsight bias the false consensus effect the primacy effect in memory

boys were sorted into groups by a trivial preference (which of two painters they liked) and never met their group members. when dividing rewards, many picked options that maximized the gap between groups, even when that gave their own group less overall. which theory best explains this? social identity theory realistic conflict theory kin selection theory social exchange theory

in the 1930s, a researcher toured the u.s. with a chinese couple and was refused service at only 1 of about 250 hotels and restaurants. months later, most places that answered a mailed letter said they would not serve chinese guests. what does this study most directly show? stated prejudice does not always predict discrimination discrimination always follows from stated prejudice institutional policies caused the in person refusals the couple's presence created stereotype threat

students read an essay praising fidel castro. some were told the writer chose that position freely; others were told a debate coach assigned it. even in the assigned condition, readers rated the writer as fairly pro castro. this finding best shows: the fundamental attribution error (correspondence bias) the actor observer bias, since readers were the actors the self serving bias in judging the writer's essay belief perseverance after the readers were debriefed

after a depression diagnosis, a man starts to believe he is weak and worthless, accepting society's negative stereotypes about mental illness as true of himself. this is: self stigma courtesy stigma public stigma stereotype threat

theodor adorno and colleagues linked prejudice to a personality pattern marked by rigid obedience to authority, conventional thinking and hostility toward out groups. they called it the: authoritarian personality type a personality machiavellian personality social dominance personality

erving goffman described stigma based on race, religion or nationality, which can be passed down through families, as: tribal stigma abominations of the body blemishes of individual character courtesy stigma
in bernard weiner's attribution theory, the causes people give for success and failure are classified by locus, stability and: controllability consensus distinctiveness consistency

the grid shows the stereotype content model (fiske, cuddy, glick and xu). which emotion belongs in the cell marked ? (groups seen as competent but cold, such as wealthy professionals)? envy pity contempt admiration

jim believes society works best when some groups stay on top and others stay at the bottom, and he opposes policies that promote equality between groups. this reflects high: social dominance orientation belief in a just world collectivist orientation cultural relativism

a medical student spills coffee on his white coat before rounds and is sure everyone noticed, but almost nobody did. overestimating how much others notice us is the: spotlight effect false consensus effect actor observer bias illusion of control

before working with a group of refugees, some volunteers feel tense and worry about saying the wrong thing, so they avoid contact. walter and cookie stephan called this: intergroup anxiety stereotype threat courtesy stigma intergroup scapegoating

a job applicant is polite and agreeable throughout an interview. according to correspondent inference theory (jones and davis), this tells observers little about her true personality mainly because: politeness is expected of anyone in that situation politeness is always caused by a stable inner trait interviews produce behavior with high distinctiveness observers can never make inferences about others

aggressive children who are bumped by a peer in an unclear situation are more likely than other children to assume it was done on purpose. kenneth dodge described this as: hostile attribution bias self serving attribution bias just world belief belief perseverance

coach ruiz shouted at a player during practice today. using the information in the table and kelley's covariation model, the most likely cause is: unusual circumstances today coach ruiz's irritable personality something about the player himself the team's rules on discipline

a student asks to borrow class notes. classmates are much more willing to help when he missed class because of an eye infection than when he went to the beach. weiner would explain the difference mainly by the: perceived controllability of the cause perceived stability of the cause student's internal locus of control low consensus of his behavior

in a 1974 study by langer and abelson, therapists watched the same videotaped interview of a young man. those told he was a 'patient' rated him as much more disturbed than those told he was a 'job applicant'. this best illustrates how: a label shapes how identical behavior is interpreted the man acted differently in the two versions of the tape therapists are always more accurate than untrained raters job applicants tend to hide their psychological problems

in a hypothetical study, managers with power over hiring spent less time reading details about each applicant and relied more on group stereotypes than coworkers with no say in hiring. this fits the idea that: power lowers the need to attend to individuals stereotypes are used only by low status people power makes social judgments more accurate more details always increase stereotyping

after two rival hospitals merge, leaders stress that everyone now belongs to one 'valley health' team, and bias between the former staff groups drops. this best illustrates: recategorization into a common in group realistic conflict over scarce resources the out group homogeneity effect scapegoating of the former rival

a runner who exercises every day believes that very few people her age exercise regularly, though most actually do. this is the: false uniqueness effect false consensus effect spotlight effect unrealistic optimism bias

white students who simply knew that a white friend had a close black friend reported less prejudice toward black people, even though they had no such friendships themselves. this is the: extended contact effect mere exposure effect jigsaw classroom effect superordinate goal effect

participants read statements describing acts by members of a large group a and a small group b (table; hypothetical). later, most overestimated how many undesirable acts group b members did. what best explains this? pairing two rare things makes them seem linked group b truly did a larger share of bad acts participants belonged to group a and disliked b small groups are always seen as more desirable

black and white seventh graders wrote briefly about values important to them; a control group wrote about unimportant values. black students' grades improved, narrowing the racial gap, while white students' grades were unchanged. the best explanation is that the exercise: reduced threat by affirming the students' self worth taught study skills that raised every student's grades lowered teachers' expectations of the white students created stereotype threat for the white students only

residents' ratings of neighborhood disorder were predicted by the share of black and poor residents, even after controlling for disorder (litter, graffiti) recorded by trained observers. this suggests that: stereotypes about groups shape how places are perceived observers' recordings of disorder were not accurate residents perceive their surroundings without any bias at all racial makeup directly causes more physical disorder

in a survey, people who believe the public sees psychiatric patients as dangerous are less likely to seek therapy for their own symptoms, even when the symptoms are severe. this pattern is best described as: label avoidance driven by public stigma courtesy stigma from family members stereotype threat during treatment the belief in a just world

women told that a math test shows gender differences scored lower than women told it did not, and they also did worse on a working memory task given during the session. what does this suggest? threat uses up working memory needed for the test women naturally have less working memory than men the instructions only lowered the women's effort weak working memory is what causes the stereotypes

white participants who reported low prejudice reviewed job candidates whose qualifications were strong, ambiguous or weak (hypothetical data in the graph). which conclusion is best supported? bias appears when a decision can be justified on other grounds participants were biased against black candidates in every case ambiguous resumes lowered both candidates' ratings by the same amount the low prejudice participants showed no racial bias at all

physicians took an implicit association test and then read cases of patients with identical heart attack symptoms who differed only by race. doctors with stronger implicit pro white bias were less likely to recommend clot dissolving drugs for black patients, although self reported bias was low and did not predict decisions. which conclusion is best supported? implicit bias predicted decisions that self reports missed explicit attitudes are the best predictor of care black patients need clot dissolving drugs less often the doctors were consciously hiding their true racial views

white participants did worse on a golf task when it was described as measuring 'natural athletic ability', while black participants did worse when it was described as measuring 'sports intelligence'. what does this show about stereotype threat? any group can be affected when a relevant stereotype is made salient it only affects groups that have low social status in society black athletes truly have less sports intelligence than white athletes telling people a task's purpose always lowers their scores
test framing and performance what is the independent variable in this study? math test score self rated anxiety how the test was described students' math course grades
test framing and performance the women's results in the diagnostic condition best illustrate: stereotype threat the self serving bias social loafing the halo effect

test framing and performance why did the researchers randomly assign students to conditions? to keep students from guessing the hypothesis being tested to balance pre existing differences, like math skill, across conditions to make the sample representative of the wider population to guarantee equal numbers of men and women in each of the two conditions

test framing and performance which additional result would most strongly support the idea that anxiety caused the women's lower scores? men reported the same anxiety in both conditions, and their scores did not differ in the diagnostic condition, higher anxiety women scored lower, and reducing anxiety raised scores women's scores were lower in the diagnostic condition whether or not they felt anxious women in both conditions reported having earned similarly high grades in prior math courses

explaining lateness: self, others and culture the mean attribution index of the u.s. observers best illustrates which tendency? the fundamental attribution error the self serving attributional bias the just world hypothesis the false consensus effect

explaining lateness: self, others and culture which conclusion is best supported by figure 1? the gap between actors and observers was smaller in the south korean sample south korean actors made more dispositional attributions than u.s. actors on average, observers in both samples favored dispositional explanations culture affected the actors' index more than it affected the observers' index

explaining lateness: self, others and culture besides perspective, which difference between the actor and observer conditions could explain the actor observer gap? actors knew far more about the circumstances than the short description gave observers participants were randomly assigned to the two conditions separately within each country the attribution index combined two separate ratings into a single score participants in both conditions rated the same kind of event, arriving late

explaining lateness: self, others and culture which statement best describes a limitation of the researchers' conclusion about culture? nationality was not randomly assigned, so other sample differences may explain the results perspective was not manipulated by the researchers, so actor and observer scores cannot be compared the index could take negative values, so its mean cannot be interpreted each sample was randomly divided, so the two countries cannot be compared

explaining lateness: self, others and culture suppose u.s. actors instead recalled a time they arrived early and were praised for it. compared with their index for lateness, their index would most likely be: lower, because people credit their own successes to their personal qualities higher, because people credit their own successes to circumstances unchanged, because actors always explain their own actions by their circumstances identical to the u.s. observers' index for a stranger's lateness

which best describes the results of experiment 1? a main effect of choice only: high choice raised attitudes for both essay types. an interaction: choice had a large effect after counterattitudinal essays but not after proattitudinal essays. a main effect of essay type only: counterattitudinal essays raised attitudes equally in both choice conditions. no effects: all post-essay attitudes stayed within the original range of 3 or below.

what is the main purpose of the proattitudinal essay conditions? to increase the sample size so that the study has more power to make the counterattitudinal essays seem more persuasive to show that choice and essay-writing by themselves do not shift attitudes when behavior matches beliefs to measure students' attitudes before the manipulation

the results of experiment 2 most directly support cognitive dissonance theory over which alternative explanation? self-perception theory, which says people infer their attitudes from their behavior without needing arousal the foot-in-the-door effect, which says small requests increase later compliance social facilitation, which says an audience improves performance on simple tasks the mere exposure effect, which says repeated exposure increases liking

which change to experiment 1 would best reduce the threat of experimenter bias? allowing students to choose which essay to write having a second experimenter, unaware of each student's condition, give the post-essay attitude scale recruiting students who favored the tuition increase giving the attitude scale one week later instead of immediately

which statements about experiment 1 are correct? i. regression toward the mean explains why only the high-choice counterattitudinal group changed. ii. the findings may not generalize to students who already favored the tuition increase. iii. random assignment allows a causal conclusion about the effect of choice. i only i and iii only ii and iii only i, ii and iii

which of the following are examples of discrimination rather than only a stereotype or prejudice? i. a manager declines to interview applicants with foreign-sounding names. ii. a man believes that older adults are bad with technology. iii. a landlord feels uneasy around tenants of a different religion. i only ii only i and iii only i, ii and iii

researchers want to (1) estimate how strongly u.s. adults endorse belief in a just world and (2) test whether reading a news story about an assault victim increases victim blaming. which statements about their methods are correct? i. randomly sampling participants from all u.s. adults would improve the external validity of the estimate in aim 1. ii. randomly assigning participants to read the assault story or a neutral story would support a causal conclusion for aim 2. iii. random assignment alone would ensure that results for aim 2 apply to all u.s. adults. i only i and ii only ii and iii only i, ii and iii

a driver who is cut off on the highway immediately thinks, “what a selfish jerk,” without considering that the other driver might be rushing to a hospital. this illustrates: the fundamental attribution error the self-serving bias the just-world hypothesis the false consensus effect

a medical student says she failed her anatomy exam because it was unfair and she had a cold, but says her classmate failed because he is lazy. her explanations best illustrate: the halo effect the actor–observer bias a self-fulfilling prophecy the mere exposure effect

students rated how much each of several causes explained their grade on a recent exam. among students with high grades, 78% chose “my ability or effort” as the main cause and 12% chose “an easy test.” among students with low grades, 18% chose “my ability or effort” and 64% chose “an unfair or hard test.” these data best illustrate: the false consensus effect the fundamental attribution error the self-serving bias the just-world hypothesis

everyone in a theater laughs at a comedian (high consensus). maya laughs at this comedian but rarely at other comedians (high distinctiveness), and she laughs every time she sees him (high consistency). according to kelley’s covariation model, maya’s laughter will most likely be attributed to: the comedian, an external cause maya’s personality, an internal cause chance circumstances on one night maya’s mood on that particular day

a nurse who smokes knows that smoking causes cancer. according to cognitive dissonance theory, which response would reduce her discomfort without changing her behavior? fully accepting that smoking is harmful while continuing to smoke as before quitting smoking with the help of nicotine patches deciding that the health risks of smoking are exaggerated for people like her increasing the number of cigarettes she smokes each day

students who went through a difficult, embarrassing initiation to join a study club rate the club’s dull meetings as more valuable than students who joined with no initiation. this best illustrates: the mere exposure effect effort justification, a form of dissonance reduction social loafing the foot-in-the-door technique

tired commuters glance at a vaccine poster featuring a smiling celebrity, while infectious disease nurses read a detailed fact sheet comparing infection rates. according to the elaboration likelihood model, which statement is most accurate? the commuters are likely swayed by peripheral cues, while the nurses process the arguments centrally, which tends to produce more lasting attitude change. both groups use the central route, because the topic is health. the commuters process the arguments centrally, because celebrities draw attention to facts. the nurses rely on peripheral cues, because they are already experts.

a public health researcher wants attitudes about exercise to predict actual gym attendance. which conditions generally make attitudes better predictors of behavior? i. the attitude is strong and comes to mind easily. ii. the attitude is measured at the same level of specificity as the behavior. iii. strong social pressure pushes against acting on the attitude. i and ii only ii only i and iii only i, ii and iii

researchers tell teachers, falsely, that certain students are about to show an “intellectual growth spurt.” by year’s end, those students have improved more than their classmates, a self-fulfilling prophecy. which feature of the design best supports the claim that teacher expectations caused the gains? the students’ improvement was measured at the end of the year. the teachers were told which students to expect gains from. the “growth spurt” students were chosen at random rather than by prior ability. the study was carried out in real classrooms rather than a laboratory.

after hearing that a coworker was robbed while walking home at night, a man says, “she should have known better than to walk alone that late; people like that bring it on themselves.” his reaction best illustrates: the just-world hypothesis the self-serving bias the halo effect in-group favoritism

participants are randomly assigned by coin toss to a “blue” or “green” group and then divide points between anonymous members of each group. they give more points to their own group. why is assignment by coin toss central to this study’s conclusion? it shows that mere categorization, not preexisting similarity or history, is enough to produce in-group favoritism. it ensures that the sample represents the general population. it keeps participants from knowing which group they belong to. it guarantees that participants will favor the out-group.

a researcher uses the implicit association test, which measures how much faster people sort words when two concepts share a response key, as a measure of implicit bias. a critic notes that many people’s scores change a lot when they retake the test a few weeks later. the critic’s concern is mainly about the test’s: sampling bias random assignment internal validity as an experiment test–retest reliability

participants rated two appliances as equally desirable, chose one to keep, and then rated both again (figure). which interpretation is best supported? choosing lowered ratings of both items, consistent with regret after any decision. after the choice, ratings of the chosen item rose and ratings of the rejected item fell, consistent with dissonance reduction. ratings did not change, because both items were rated 6.0 before the choice. only the rejected item’s rating changed, consistent with the mere exposure effect.

a landlord believes young tenants are irresponsible, feels annoyed when young people apply, and rejects their applications. which part of this scenario is discrimination? rejecting the young applicants believing that young tenants are irresponsible feeling annoyed by young applicants assuming that all young people are alike

a school district wants to test whether jigsaw classrooms, in which each student must teach part of the lesson to a mixed-ethnicity group, reduce prejudice. which design would provide the strongest evidence? measure prejudice in jigsaw classrooms at the end of the year only randomly assign classrooms to jigsaw or standard instruction and measure prejudice before and after compare schools that already chose jigsaw methods with schools that did not ask teachers whether they believe jigsaw methods reduce prejudice

name: Social structure & demographics
t: a sociologist studies how patients and nurses create shared meanings through small gestures during hospital visits. which perspective is she using? functionalism conflict theory symbolic interactionism social constructionism of institutions

a hospital's stated purpose is to treat patients, but it also becomes a place where neighborhood residents form friendships. the friendships are a: manifest function latent function dysfunction social norm

in stage 2 of the demographic transition model, a country typically experiences: high birth rates and high death rates; slow growth high birth rates and falling death rates; rapid growth falling birth rates and low death rates; slowing growth low birth rates and low death rates; stable population

functionalism views society as: a system of parts that work together to maintain stability a struggle between groups over power and resources a product of meanings created in everyday interactions the result of individuals weighing costs and benefits

conflict theory views society as: shaped by group competition over limited resources and power a stable system whose parts each serve a useful function built from shared symbols people create in interaction the outcome of individuals' rational cost benefit choices

symbolic interactionism focuses on: how people create meaning through everyday interactions how large institutions keep society stable over time how economic classes compete for power and resources how biological drives shape human social behavior
a society's shared beliefs about what is good and important are its: values norms laws symbols
material culture includes: physical objects, like tools and buildings shared beliefs, like values and religion symbols, like language and gestures rules for behavior, like norms and laws
mores are: norms with strong moral importance informal norms for routine behavior formal norms written into law shared ideas about what is desirable
rational choice theory says people: weigh costs and benefits before acting act only on emotion follow tradition without thinking have no free will

social constructionism argues that: many social categories, like race and gender, arise from shared agreement social categories like race and gender reflect fixed biological types social structures fully determine people's identities and choices individuals' rational choices create all social categories

culture lag is: when non material culture takes time to catch up with new technology when material culture lags behind changes in a society's values and norms when a minority group slowly adopts the dominant culture when people feel disoriented on entering a new culture
the fertility rate refers to: the average number of children born per woman the number of deaths per 1000 movement of people into a country the percentage of elderly people
moving from rural areas into cities is called: urbanization gentrification globalization emigration

gentrification occurs when: wealthier newcomers raise costs and displace residents of low income areas low income residents move into wealthier areas, lowering housing costs residents leave cities for suburbs, shrinking the urban tax base rural residents move to cities in search of jobs and services
a country has high birth rates, rapidly falling death rates and a population pyramid with a wide base. which stage of the demographic transition is it most likely in? stage 2 stage 1 stage 4 stage 5

a population pyramid that is roughly the same width from bottom to top suggests: low birth and death rates and a stable population high birth rates and rapid population growth low birth rates and a shrinking, aging population high death rates among working age adults
factors that drive people away from their home country, such as war or poverty, are called: push factors pull factors assimilation factors fertility factors

assimilation is the process by which: a minority group adopts the culture of the dominant group a minority group keeps its own culture alongside others groups blend equally to form a new, shared culture a dominant group forcibly removes a minority group

the dependency ratio compares: dependents (children and elderly) to working age people the number of births to the number of deaths in one year unemployed adults to employed adults immigrants to emigrants in a population

durkheim used the term anomie to describe: a breakdown of social norms that leaves people without guidance strong social bonds that tightly regulate people's behavior workers' alienation from the products of their labor the shared beliefs that unite members of a society

weber described bureaucracy as having: a clear hierarchy, written rules and specialized roles flexible roles assigned by personal relationships a flat structure with decisions made by consensus leadership based mainly on a leader's personal charisma and appeal

a conflict theorist studying a hospital would most likely focus on: how power and resources are unequally shared among staff and patients how the hospital's parts work together to keep society stable how patients and staff create shared meanings in interaction how each individual weighs the personal costs and benefits of their choices

a country's population is aging quickly because of low fertility and longer life expectancy. which policy challenge is most likely? funding healthcare and pensions for a larger elderly population building more schools for a growing number of children reducing high infant mortality in a young population controlling rapid population growth caused by persistently high fertility

a symbolic interactionist studying medical care would most likely examine: how patients and doctors interpret a diagnosis as they talk how national healthcare spending varies across income groups how hospitals compete for patients, funding and power how the healthcare system helps keep society stable

the graph shows a rapidly growing population's age structure, with the largest share in the youngest group and steadily smaller older groups. which demographic transition stage fits best? stage 2: high birth rate and falling death rate stage 4: low birth and death rates stage 5: birth rate below death rate stage 1: high birth and death rates, little growth

a country's age structure is shown, with roughly equal shares in most age groups. which demographic transition stage fits best? stage 4: low birth and death rates, slow growth stage 2: high birth rate, falling death rate stage 1: high birth and death rates stage 3 with a recent baby boom
a sociologist describes a group of people who share a language, ancestry and cultural traditions. she is referring to their: ethnicity race social class master status

an international nursing student feels anxious, confused and homesick during her first weeks in a country with very different customs. she is experiencing: culture shock culture lag cultural diffusion assimilation
unlike sex, gender refers to: socially constructed roles and expectations chromosomes and anatomy at birth hormone levels measured in the blood sexual attraction to other people

a patient with the flu is excused from work. according to talcott parsons' 'sick role', what is she expected to do in return? want to get well and seek competent medical help accept full blame for having caused her illness keep working at full capacity while she is sick avoid doctors and recover without outside help

in a large modern city, a surgeon depends on farmers, electricians and pharmacists because each does a specialized job. emile durkheim called social cohesion based on this kind of interdependence: organic solidarity mechanical solidarity gemeinschaft anomie

a sociologist studies why women physicians are paid less than men in the same specialty and how unpaid caregiving at home shapes their careers. which perspective is she most likely using? feminist theory functionalism symbolic interactionism rational choice theory

a couple stays together because each partner feels the relationship's rewards (support, companionship) outweigh its costs. which theory explains relationships this way? social exchange theory conflict theory feminist theory social constructionism

yoga, which began in south asia, is now practiced in gyms around the world. this spread of a cultural practice from one society to others is called: cultural diffusion culture lag cultural assimilation culture shock

a commune rejects private property, money and the wider society's focus on career success, and lives by opposing values. sociologists call this group a: counterculture subculture reference group secondary group

restlessness in children and heavy drinking were once seen as normal variation or moral failings, but are now often defined and treated as medical conditions. this process is called: medicalization secularization social reproduction gentrification

besides reading and math, elementary students learn to wait their turn, obey authority and arrive on time. sociologists call these unofficial lessons the: hidden curriculum formal curriculum culture lag teacher expectancy effect

followers obey a movement's founder because they believe she has extraordinary personal qualities, not because of laws or custom. max weber would call this: charismatic authority traditional authority rational legal authority coercive power

country x exports mostly raw coffee and minerals, imports most manufactured goods and has very low wages. in wallerstein's world systems theory, country x is most likely a: periphery nation core nation semi periphery nation post industrial nation
in a community, nearly everyone marries a partner from their own religious and ethnic group. this marriage pattern is called: endogamy exogamy polygamy cohabitation

a new hospital parking policy is meant to save money, and it does. however, in a result no one planned or foresaw, patients start missing appointments because the parking is now far away. in robert merton's terms, the missed appointments are a: latent dysfunction manifest function latent function manifest dysfunction
in one year, a city of 1,000,000 people has 20,000 births, 8,000 deaths, 5,000 immigrants and 2,000 emigrants. what is its population growth rate? 1.5% 1.2% 0.3% 1.9%

a country's total fertility rate has stayed at 1.5 for decades, and it has little immigration. in the long run, its population will most likely: shrink, since 1.5 is below replacement (about 2.1) grow slowly, since any rate above 1.0 adds people stay stable, since 1.5 is close to replacement grow quickly as the population pyramid widens

protests in a region began not when residents were poorest, but after incomes rose and residents began comparing themselves with richer neighboring regions. which theory of social movements fits best? relative deprivation theory resource mobilization theory absolute deprivation theory labeling theory

a group splits off from a large, established church, saying the church has abandoned its original teachings. the new group is in strong tension with the surrounding society. sociologists classify it as a: sect church (ecclesia) denomination cult (new religious movement)

a critic argues that parsons' sick role fits a patient with lifelong diabetes poorly. which point best supports this critique? chronic illness has no cure, so role exemption can't be temporary chronic patients are not expected to see a doctor or seek help the sick role was designed to apply only to mental illness the sick role requires patients to keep working while ill

max weber argued that the 'protestant ethic' helped modern capitalism develop. what was his main point? religious values of hard work and thrift encouraged investment religion is an opiate that keeps workers from rebelling capitalism created protestantism to justify its profits shared rituals create the mechanical solidarity of markets

a country in stage 2 of the demographic transition has a crude birth rate of 40 per 1,000 and a crude death rate of 15 per 1,000 per year, with no migration. about how long will its population take to double? about 28 years about 18 years about 47 years about 2.5 years

in country y, death rates are already low. over 30 years, girls' schooling rises, families move to cities and contraception becomes common, while the birth rate falls from 35 to 18 per 1,000. which demographic transition stage is country y moving through? stage 3: falling birth rates and slowing growth stage 1: high birth rates and high death rates stage 2: high birth rates and falling death rates stage 4: low, stable birth and death rates

thomas malthus warned that, without checks such as famine or disease, human population tends to grow: exponentially, while the food supply grows only linearly linearly, while the food supply grows exponentially exponentially, at exactly the same rate as the food supply linearly, at the same rate as the food supply

the statement "if people define situations as real, they are real in their consequences" (the thomas theorem) is most closely tied to which perspective? symbolic interactionism structural functionalism conflict theory rational choice theory

hospital staff follow the ceo's directions because she holds an office defined by written rules and was appointed through formal procedures. max weber called this: rational legal authority traditional authority charismatic personal authority coercive authority

anthropologist george murdock listed practices found in every known society, such as funeral rites, family structures and incest taboos. these are called: cultural universals cultural relativism cultural diffusion folkways

as a country moves through the demographic transition, its leading causes of death shift from infections and malnutrition to heart disease and cancer. abdel omran called this shift the: epidemiologic transition nutrition transition medicalization of death demographic dividend

after birth rates fall, a country has, for a few decades, many working age adults compared with children and elderly people, which can boost economic growth. this is called the: demographic dividend dependency burden population momentum replacement fertility

a movement works to pass laws banning smoking in public places but does not seek to change society as a whole. in david aberle's typology, it is a: reformative movement revolutionary movement redemptive movement alternative movement

a sociologist argues that a patients' rights movement succeeded not because grievances grew, but because it gained money, skilled organizers, media access and allied groups. this view is: resource mobilization theory relative deprivation theory mass society theory smelser's value added theory

over a century, fewer people in a country attend religious services, and schools, hospitals and courts once run by churches come under government control. this trend is: secularization fundamentalism medicalization cultural lag

several ethnic groups in a city keep their own languages, festivals and schools while sharing equal political and legal rights. this pattern is called: cultural pluralism cultural assimilation amalgamation segregation

using the hypothetical population pyramid (each bar's length is the percent of the total population in that sex and age group), what is this country's total dependency ratio? about 67 dependents per 100 working age people about 40 dependents per 100 working age people about 17 dependents per 100 working age people about 150 dependents per 100 working age people
a town has 4,800 men and 6,000 women aged 80 and older. what is the sex ratio of this age group? 80 men per 100 women 125 men per 100 women 44 men per 100 women 20 men per 100 women
a country of 50 million people records 600,000 births in one year. what is its crude birth rate? 12 per 1,000 people 1.2 per 1,000 people 120 per 1,000 people 83 per 1,000 people

a hypothetical country's population pyramid is shown. which description fits best? below replacement fertility, so the population may shrink high fertility and rapid growth, as in stage 2 high birth and death rates, as in stage 1 falling deaths but still very high fertility

the graph shows a country's crude birth and death rates as it passes through the demographic transition. at which labeled time is the rate of natural increase (population growth) highest? time b time a time c time d

immigrants from one mexican village settle in the same chicago neighborhood because earlier migrants from the village help newcomers find housing and jobs. this pattern is called: chain migration forced migration return migration gentrification

the table shows hypothetical survey support for a health policy by age group in three years. which kind of effect best explains the change between 2010 and 2020? a period effect a cohort effect an age (life cycle) effect a sampling effect

name: Stratification & health disparities
t: a woman whose parents were farmworkers becomes a physician. this is an example of: horizontal mobility intragenerational downward mobility intergenerational upward mobility social reproduction

children from wealthier families often know how to talk with teachers and navigate college applications, which helps them succeed. sociologists call these learned advantages: economic capital cultural capital social mobility meritocracy

social stratification refers to: the ranking of groups in a society by wealth, power and prestige the movement of individuals and families between social classes over time the division of society into distinct cultural subgroups the passing of class position from parents to children
socioeconomic status (ses) is usually measured by: income, education and occupation income, age and family size education, religion and ethnicity occupation, health and marital status
a society in which status is based mainly on individual achievement is a: meritocracy caste system monarchy plutocracy
in a caste system, social position is: fixed at birth based on merit easily changed chosen in adulthood

relative poverty means: having much less than others in the same society lacking the resources needed for basic survival living below a fixed, government set income line being poor for a short time due to job loss
social mobility describes: movement between social positions moving to a new city physical fitness keeping the same social position throughout life

social capital refers to: the benefits that come from social networks and relationships the financial assets, like money and property, a person owns the education, tastes and skills that signal social class the prestige attached to a person's occupation

social reproduction refers to: the passing of social class status from one generation to the next the movement of children into a higher class than their parents the process by which people learn their society's norms the replacement of a population through births over time

residential segregation can contribute to health disparities by: concentrating poverty and limiting access to healthy food, housing and care increasing genetic similarity among people living in the same area spreading pollution and other health risks evenly across all city neighborhoods raising local demand for healthcare, which improves clinic quality

epidemiologists use 'incidence' to mean: the number of new cases of a disease in a population during a period the total number of existing cases in a population at one time the number of deaths from a disease in a population during a period the proportion of a population that is immune to a disease

prevalence refers to: the total number of existing cases at a given time the number of new cases during a given period the number of deaths from a disease in a period the average length of time each case lasts
morbidity refers to: the rate of illness in a population the rate of death in a population the rate of births in a population the average life expectancy in a population

name: Quick reasoning drills
t: passage: a museum replaced chronological displays with thematic rooms. visitors reported finding connections among distant cultures, but some said it became harder to understand how ideas changed over time. the curator argued that neither layout was neutral: each invites a different kind of comparison. what is the passage’s central claim? exhibition organization shapes interpretation thematic displays are always superior visitors dislike all museums chronological displays contain fewer objects
